Note that "inu no niku" can also mean the "dog's meat" in the sense: Meat eaten by the dog. I'd say this is more likely, pork also is "butaniku" and not "buta no niku". Don't worry about this too much, it should be easily clear from context.

phrases.reading: わたし の ゆめ は
phrases.lemmaField: 私 の 夢 は
phrases.translation: As for my dream... [it's living in Japan].

phrases.reading: おれ の あいて は だれ
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 の 相手 は 誰
phrases.translation:
As for my opponent: Who [is it]?
Or less literally: Who's my opponent?
phrases.notes: aite: "other party" or "the other", this can mean either opponent or partner / ally. This is a bit confusing, but usually clear from context, read more about this here.

phrases.reading: ぼく の もの
phrases.lemmaField: 僕 の もの
phrases.translation: [This is] mine? lit. my thing?

phrases.reading: すき な たべもの は
phrases.lemmaField: 好き だ 食べ物 は
phrases.translation: As for like food / food [you] like... [what is it]?
phrases.notes:
tabemono: food

Here, the listener is a new student at school and is ambushed with questions. She is a bit overwhelmed and asks "e - what?" before the speaker asks "suki na tabemono ha?". The "e" and the "suki" mix a bit, which makes it a bit harder to understand. This is from K-ON season 1 Episode 9 (very beginning), if you want to check yourself.

phrases.japanese: 人間の食べるものじゃないな
phrases.reading: にんげん の たべる もの じゃない な
phrases.lemmaField: 人間 の 食べる もの じゃ な
phrases.romaji: ningen no taberu mono janai na
phrases.translation: [Don't eat this, because it's] not a thing eaten by humans.
phrases.notes:
Note the subtle difference between "tabemono" and "taberu mono": The first is food, the second is a "mono/thing" described by the clause "taberu". In practice, "tabemono" is more common.

Why is "no" being used here? In short: In a relative clause, "ga" may be replaced by "no". The clause in this case is "ningen no taberu" and describes "mono". Note that you can also say "ningen ga taberu mono", have a look at the references for details.

phrases.reading: しあわせ の あじ
phrases.lemmaField: 幸せ の 味
phrases.translation: The taste of happiness.

phrases.reading: ここ の いえ の ひと いる
phrases.lemmaField: ここ の 家 の 人 いる
phrases.romaji: koko no ie no hito iru
phrases.translation:
"Is the owner of this house there"? or: "are the people of this house there"?
In English, you'd rather say: Is anyone home?
phrases.notes:
It's a question without question marker, this is introduced later in the deck.

koko: here, this place (close to the speaker)

In this example, "no/の" links three items together: here no house no person -> owner of people of this house.

The world god only knowns, season 3, episode 7, around 10:00.
phrases.source: The World God Only Knows S3 (jp eng)

phrases.reading: おれ の ゆめ だ
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 の 夢 だ
phrases.translation: [This] is my dream.

phrases.reading: ごめん わたし の せい だ
phrases.lemmaField: ごめん 私 の せい だ
phrases.translation: Sorry, [it's] my fault.
phrases.notes: sei: fault

phrases.reading: ぼく の じんせい の いみ は
phrases.lemmaField: 僕 の 人生 の 意味 は
phrases.romaji: boku no jinsei no imi ha
phrases.translation: As for the meaning of [my] life...
phrases.notes: jinsei: (human) life

phrases.reading: かのじょ の りょうしん だった
phrases.lemmaField: 彼女 の 両親 だ
phrases.translation: [The people you just saw] were her parents.
phrases.notes:
ryoushin: (both) parents
kanojo: she (sometimes also girlfriend)

phrases.reading: いみ の ない じんせい
phrases.lemmaField: 意味 の ない 人生
phrases.translation: [Without you, it's ] a life that is meaningless.
phrases.notes: Interesting here is that I can easily understand this sentence, but wasn't able to explain, why "no" is used (and not "ga"). It seems like in relative clauses, the "ga"-particle may be replaced by "no", see link to Japanese stack exchange. The takeaway message is: You don't have to understand all the grammar in order to understand a sentence.

phrases.reading: こころ の ちから
phrases.lemmaField: 心 の 力
phrases.translation: The power of the heart... [what's that supposed to mean?!]
phrases.notes: kokoro: mind; heart; spirit

phrases.reading: おれ は うみ の おとこ ぞ
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 は 海 の 男 ぞ
phrases.romaji: ore ha umi no otoko zo
phrases.translation: A "guy of the sea" is possibly a sailor or someone who likes the sea.
phrases.notes: "zo" is a sentence ending particle used by males. It adds force and is used o e.g. express strong intent or to persuade someone.

phrases.japanese: ここにいる全ての人が
phrases.reading: ここ に いる すべて の ひと が
phrases.lemmaField: ここ に いる 全て の 人 が
phrases.romaji: koko ni iru subete no hito ga
phrases.translation: In this example, the clause "koko ni iru" describes "subete no hito". All the people, who are here. The "ga" in the end indicates that the sentence continues.

phrases.japanese: 彼女は私の大事な仲間だ
phrases.reading: かのじょ は わたし の だいじ な なかま だ
phrases.lemmaField: 彼女 は 私 の 大事 だ 仲間 だ
phrases.romaji: kanojo ha watashi no daiji na nakama da
phrases.translation: As for her, [she's] my important fellow.

phrases.japanese: じゃわたしの家こっちだから
phrases.reading: じゃ わたし の いえ こっち だ から
phrases.lemmaField: じゃ わたし の 家 こっち だ から
phrases.romaji: ja watashi no ie kocchi da kara
phrases.translation: [I go this way] because my house is in this direction.
phrases.notes: Note that Tae Kim covers "kara" later. It usually connects two sentences in the following fashion: Reason kara result, meaning: because of reason, result happened. If the result is clear from context, it is often omitted, just as in this example. I'll pick this up in more detail later.

phrases.reading: せんせい の すき な もの
phrases.lemmaField: 先生 の 好き だ もの
phrases.translation: [This is] the teacher's like-it-item (an item the teacher likes).
phrases.source: 今からあなたを脅迫します

phrases.japanese: 大丈夫の意味が分からない
phrases.reading: だいじょうぶ の いみ が わからない
phrases.lemmaField: 大丈夫 の 意味 が 分かる
phrases.translation: [I] don't get the meaning of "ok" -> nothing is ok here!
phrases.notes: Imagine two persons in a dangerous situation. Person A said: daijoubu - safe / secure / ok. Person B responds with this sentence.
phrases.source: さよなら絶望先生 (Sayonara, Zetsubou-Sensei)

phrases.reading: だれ の せい だ よ
phrases.lemmaField: 誰 の せい だ よ
phrases.translation: Whose fault is it?!
phrases.notes: This sounds a bit like the speaker was accused of doing something. He defends himself by saying: Come on, think again? Who is at fault?! Not me!

phrases.reading: わたし の なかま が いる
phrases.lemmaField: 私 の 仲間 が いる
phrases.translation: My comrade / ally is there [with me].

phrases.reading: ここ が ぼく の いえ
phrases.lemmaField: ここ が 僕 の 家
phrases.translation:
Here is my house.
koko: here, this place (close to the speaker)
phrases.source: Mahoutsukai no Yome (The Ancient Magus Bride) ep 1-12

phrases.reading: ここ は わたし の しんしつ
phrases.lemmaField: ここ は 私 の 寝室
phrases.translation: As for here, [it's] my bedroom.

phrases.reading: わたし の じんせい は わたし の もの
phrases.lemmaField: 私 の 人生 は 私 の もの
phrases.romaji: watashi no jinsei ha watashi no mono
phrases.translation: My life is my item -> my life belongs to me!

phrases.japanese: ごめんなさい私のせいだ
phrases.reading: ごめんなさい わたし の せい だ
phrases.lemmaField: ごめんなさい 私 の せい だ
phrases.translation: Sorry, it's my fault.
phrases.source: Erased - 僕だけがいない街

phrases.reading: できる おとこ だ
phrases.lemmaField: できる 男 だ
phrases.translation: Someone here is a can-do-it-guy -> a capable guy.
phrases.notes: dekiru: to be able (in a position) to do

phrases.japanese: できる人がいないから
phrases.reading: できる ひと が いない から
phrases.lemmaField: できる 人 が いる から 出来る
phrases.translation: [We're in trouble] because someone who can do [it] is not there.
phrases.notes: Note that Tae Kim covers "kara" later. It usually connects two sentences in the following fashion: Reason kara result, meaning: because of reason, result happened. If the result is clear from context, it is often omitted, just as in this example. I'll pick this up in more detail later.

phrases.japanese: 私一人ぼっちじゃないもの
phrases.reading: わたし ひとりぼっち じゃない もの
phrases.lemmaField: 私 一人ぼっち じゃ もの
phrases.translation: [Don't worry, you can leave.] It's not that I am alone
phrases.grammarNote: Ignore the "mono" here.
phrases.notes:
hitoribocchi: loneliness; solitude

Isn't something missing here? On the previous cards, similar examples always started with "watashi ha". In casual speech, particles are often omitted. This is no good practice for beginners, but for sure something to be aware of.

In this sentence "mono" is actually used for emphasis as explained here. This is also explained on jisho (#6). Don't worry about this for now, I will add more examples later.

The "watashi" here sounds a bit like "atashi". atashi is also a valid word for "I" but only used by females.

phrases.reading: おれ の ここ に ある
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 の ここ に ある
phrases.translation: [The plan is] "ore no koko ni" -> all in my head.
phrases.grammarNote: Have a look at the picture: Where's the guy pointing at?
phrases.notes: The speaker is pointing at his head and refers to it as "koko - here". The no in this example has the same meaning as on the previous cards, it simply links "ore" to "koko", which literally means "my koko/here". Since he is referring to his head (which is "atama" in Japanese), you could also say: "ore no atama ni aru".

phrases.reading: だれ の せい だ
phrases.lemmaField: 誰 の せい だ
phrases.translation: Whose fault is it?!
phrases.grammarNote: This card is related to the next one
phrases.notes: This again sounds a bit like the speaker was accused of doing something. He defends himself by saying: Come on, think again? Who is at fault?! Not me!
phrases.source: Sakurasou no Pet na Kanojo (jp eng)

phrases.reading: ぼく の
phrases.lemmaField: 僕 の
phrases.translation: [It's] mine.
phrases.notes:
If it is clear, what's meant from context, the target of "no" can be omitted. Remember the last card? "dare no sei da". Instead of saying "boku no sei da" you can just say: "boku no".

Keep in mind that "no" in this case would link a property to a noun, e.g. boku no sei / ie / inu. This is important for the next cards.
phrases.source: Mahoutsukai no Yome (The Ancient Magus Bride) ep 1-12

phrases.reading: めんま の
phrases.lemmaField: めんま の
phrases.translation: [This was] menma's.
phrases.grammarNote: menma is the nickname of a character.
phrases.notes: In this example, the target of "no" is again clear from context, for example somenone may ask: Who's dog is this? Answer: "menma no inu". Since it's clear from context that you're talking about a dog, you can say: "menma no".

phrases.reading: しぬ の は こわくない
phrases.lemmaField: 死ぬ の は 怖い
phrases.translation: As for dying, [it's] not scary.
phrases.notes: shinu + no enables to attach the topic marker "ha". This is very similar to the English nominalization (appending "-ing" to the verb).

phrases.reading: しぬ の は こわい
phrases.lemmaField: 死ぬ の は 怖い
phrases.translation: As for dying, it's scary.
phrases.notes: shinu + no enables to attach the topic marker "ha". This is very similar to the English nominalization (appending "-ing" to the verb).

phrases.reading: あやまる の は こっち だ
phrases.lemmaField: 謝る の は こっち だ
phrases.translation: As for apologizing, it's me who should do it [and not you].
phrases.notes:
ayamaru: to apologize

The "me" is expressed by "kocchi" here, remember: "kocchi" is the colloquial form of "kochira" and means: this way (direction close to the speaker or towards the speaker). It can be used as pronoun (i.e. meaning "me, us") in some cases. Don't worry about that, but read the stackexchange ref if you're interested.

There's also: acchi/achira and socchi/sochira.

verb + no enables to attach the topic marker "ha". This is very similar to the English nominalization (appending "-ing" to the verb).

phrases.reading: かつ の は わたし だ
phrases.lemmaField: 勝つ の は 私 だ
phrases.translation: As for winning, it's me -> I win.
phrases.notes: verb + no enables to attach the topic marker "ha". This is very similar to the English nominalization (appending "-ing" to the verb).

phrases.japanese: 人を殺すのは悪いことだ
phrases.reading: ひと を ころす の は わるい こと だ
phrases.lemmaField: 人 を 殺す の は 悪い こと だ いいこと 良いこと
phrases.romaji: hito wo korosu no ha warui koto da
phrases.translation: Killing people is a bad thing!
phrases.notes:
koto: thing, matter (abstract / intangible)

Whereas English uses the word “thing” to refer to anything that exists, Japanese generally divides existence into the physical and non-physical. mono is usually a tangible thing, such as a wallet, a cabbage, a door, or a coin, while koto is an intangible thing, such as a win, a habit, a wish, or an incident.

verb + no enables to attach the topic marker "ha". This is very similar to the English nominalization (appending "-ing" to the verb).

phrases.reading: くらい の が こわい とか
phrases.lemmaField: 暗い の が 怖い とか
phrases.translation: As for darkness, it is scary.
phrases.notes:
kurai: dark; gloomy

In this example, "no" is used for nominalizing an adjective, this again allows to add the "ga" particle (similar to "ha" on the previous cards).
Remember that "toka" is a colloquial way of making a sentence more vague, just like adding "or something" in English.

phrases.reading: くらい ところ とか
phrases.lemmaField: 暗い 所 とか
phrases.translation: [What are you afraid of? - Many things, for example] dark places.
phrases.notes:
tokoro: place; spot; scene; site

Japanese also has many words that can be used instead of "no", for example "tokoro". So instead of saying "kurai no ha", you can also refer to something slightly more specific: a "kurai tokoro" - dark place instead of the more general nominalized "kurai". you already learned "mono", this acts the same way.

phrases.reading: じかん と の しょうぶ だ
phrases.lemmaField: 時間 と の 勝負 だ
phrases.translation: [It's] a battle with/against time (which means: we're running out of time)
phrases.notes:
shoubu: match, contest

The use of both particles "to" and "no" combines their meaning. This becomes more clear in the following (constructed) example:
watashi no shoubu: my (own) battle
watashi to no shoubu: the battle with/against me

Reminder: "to" means with here, it also has a few other meanings covered later.

phrases.reading: わたし と の やくそく は
phrases.lemmaField: 私 と の 約束 は
phrases.translation: What about the promise [you made] with/to me?
phrases.notes:
yakusoku: promise

Remark: Here, the "no" particle is again combined with "to" to combine their meaning:
watashi no yakusoku: my promise, i.e. the promise I made to someone else.
watashi to no yakusoku: Here, "no" modifies "yakusoku" as being a promise mate with/to me.

phrases.japanese: 友達の力ってすごいのね
phrases.reading: ともだち の ちから って すごい の ね
phrases.lemmaField: 友達 の 力 って すごい の ね
phrases.romaji: tomodachi no chikara tte sugoi no ne
phrases.translation: [This happened] because the power of friendship is amazing.
phrases.notes:
tte: colloquial "ha"

The "no" particle attached at the end of a sentence can also add an explanatory tone. Note that a single "no" at the end may sound feminine. Guys likely add a "da" to add more force.

phrases.reading: ともだち じゃない の
phrases.lemmaField: 友達 じゃ の
phrases.translation: [Why don't you ask her? - I can't because] we're not friends or more literal: The thing is that we're not friends.
phrases.notes:
"no" at the end of a sentence conveys an explanatory tone.
Note that a single "no" at the end may sound feminine. Guys likely add a "da" to add more force.

phrases.reading: おれ が わるい の だ
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 が 悪い の だ
phrases.translation: [You don't need to apologize] because I am to blame (i.e. it's my fault).
phrases.notes:
"no" at the end of a sentence conveys an explanatory tone.
Note that a single "no" at the end may sound feminine. Guys likely add a "da" to add more force, like in this example.
Remark: "warui" means "bad, poor, undesireable", but when used like this, it means "at fault, to blame", see also here.

phrases.reading: おれ が わるかった の だ
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 が 悪い の だ
phrases.translation: [I apologized] because I was at fault.
phrases.notes:
"no" at the end of a sentence conveys an explanatory tone.
Note that a single "no" at the end may sound feminine. Guys likely add a "da" to add more force, like in this example.

phrases.reading: はんぶん の ちから で かつ
phrases.lemmaField: 半分 の 力 で 勝つ
phrases.translation: [We] win with [only] half [of our] power.
phrases.notes: hanbun: half

phrases.reading: わたし は かった の だ
phrases.lemmaField: わたし は 勝つ の だ
phrases.translation: ...because I won.
phrases.notes: Remember that I wrote: "no" at the end of a sentence sounds feminine, guys rather add a "da"? Here we have a girl doing the same thing. Things like this happen all the time, maybe she want's to sound strong or something. Over time, you'll get a sense for that.

phrases.reading: ゆめ を みた の
phrases.lemmaField: 夢 を 見る の
phrases.translation: [This] was a dream?
phrases.notes:
This is a question without question indicator.
"no" in the end of a question adds the nuance of "I want an explanation" to the question. So in this case, someone may want to know, why someone else woke up: yume wo mita no?
The weird thing here is that this does not sound feminine (according to Tae Kim, the reason might be that the declarative "da" cannot be used in questions (p. 67)).

phrases.reading: なに が わるい の
phrases.lemmaField: 何 が 悪い の
phrases.translation: What is bad [about this]?
phrases.notes:
This is a question without question indicator.
"no" in the end of a question adds the nuance of "I want an explanation" to the question. The weird thing here is that this does not sound feminine (according to Tae Kim, the reason might be that the declarative "da" cannot be used in questions (p. 67)).
phrases.source: Terrace House-Boys x Girls Next Door

phrases.reading: ここ に いた の
phrases.lemmaField: ここ に いる の
phrases.translation: The speaker is searching for some living being and asks: Was [he / she / it, clear from context] here? (With a "please explain" connotation).

phrases.japanese: できるとかできないとかじゃないのよね
phrases.reading: できる とか できない とか じゃない の よ ね
phrases.lemmaField: できる とか できる とか じゃ の よ ね
phrases.romaji: dekiru toka dekinai toka janai no yo ne
phrases.translation: It's not about being able or not being able [to do something], again in an explanatory tone.
phrases.notes:
In contrast to "to" and "ya", toka can also be attached to verbs.
yo ne: combination of the sentence ending particles "yo" (new point you're trying to make) and "ne" (seeking aggreement). Don't worry about the somewhat technical rules here, "yo" and "ne" are very often used in conversations, you'll hear many many examples.
phrases.source: Toaru Kagaku no Railgun S (Railgun S02, JP only)

phrases.reading: おれ みた ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 見る ん だ んだ
phrases.translation: [No need to hide this] because I already saw it.
phrases.notes:
In practice, the "no da/の だ" is often spelled as "n da/ん だ", maybe because it is easier to pronounce.

Isn't something missing here? On the previous cards, similar examples always started with "ore ha". In casual speech, particles are often omitted. This is no good practice for beginners, but for sure something to be aware of.

phrases.reading: わたし ゆめ が ある ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: 私 夢 が ある ん だ
phrases.romaji: watashi yume ga aru n da
phrases.translation: [I'm looking forward to the future] because I have a dream (a dream is there).
phrases.grammarNote: Isn't a particle missing here?
phrases.notes: Isn't something missing here? On the previous cards, similar examples always started with "watashi ha". In casual speech, particles are often omitted. This is no good practice for beginners, but for sure something to be aware of.
phrases.source: Erased - 僕だけがいない街

phrases.reading: じかん が ない ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: 時間 が ない ん だ
phrases.translation: [I can't come] because time is not there -> I don't have time.
phrases.grammarNote: The speaker is speaking fast, this often results in skipped vowels and sounds slurred. If this is too hard to understand, just skip the card, it does not add anything new.

phrases.japanese: 僕たちには分かるんだ
phrases.reading: ぼくたち に は わかる ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: 僕たち に は 分かる ん だ
phrases.romaji: bokutachi ni ha wakaru n da
phrases.translation: [Something is] understood by us.
phrases.notes:
A question on what the "ni" is supposed to mean came up here. I actually didn't notice it when I added the card, sorry if this caused any trouble. I'd suggest you don't worry about it much for now, you can simply omit it and the meaning of the sentence will not change much.

If you're still curious, here's the explanation: As we learned before, "ni" marks the target of the verb "wakaru". In this sentence, it indicates that the understanding of something applies only or mostly to "bokutachi". So "something is understood by us (and maybe not by someone else). Read more on this here.

phrases.reading: ぼく じゃない ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: 僕 じゃ ん だ
phrases.translation: [He doesn't talk to me] because it's not me [who should do this].
phrases.notes: "n da" can be attached to all kinds of conjugations to add an explanatory tone, similar to "no". In this case, the penguin says in an explanatory tone: "boku janai" - not me.

phrases.reading: なに が あった ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: 何 が ある ん だ
phrases.translation: What happened (literally: what was there)?
phrases.notes:
Remark 1: This is a question without question marker. Moreover, the pronunciation of the sentence does not sound like a question, but it starts with a question word.
Remark 2: For people wondering why a question is ending on "da", have a look at this discussion. In short, it makes the speaker's demand for information stronger.

phrases.reading: しらなかった ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: 知る ん だ
phrases.translation: [I did this] because [I] didn't know [better].
phrases.notes:
shiranakatta: negative past tense of shiru

The negative past tense is very easy to construct: Simply replace the "i" in the negative verb ending -nai by "katta".

phrases.reading: だれ と いる ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: 誰 と いる ん だ
phrases.translation: Who is with [you]?

phrases.reading: わすれた ん じゃない
phrases.lemmaField: 忘れる ん じゃ
phrases.translation: [I] didn't forget (in an explanatory tone).
phrases.notes: The "da" in "n da" can also be conjugated (to "janai" in this case).

phrases.japanese: おはよう今日は早いね
phrases.reading: おはよう きょう は はやい ね
phrases.lemmaField: おはよう 今日 は 早い ね 速い
phrases.translation: Good morning, [you are] early today, aren't you?
phrases.notes: hayai: fast, early

phrases.reading: はやく ねる の よ
phrases.lemmaField: 早い 寝る の よ
phrases.translation: [Oh, you feel sick? Then] go to bed quickly.
phrases.notes: Adjectives describe nouns. They can easily be transformed to adverbs in Japanese, which describe verbs. For i-adjectives, replace "i" by "ku".

phrases.reading: うしなう もの は おおきい ぞ
phrases.lemmaField: 失う もの は 大きい ぞ
phrases.translation: The thing [we] lose [if this happens] is big.
phrases.notes: ookii: big; large; great

phrases.reading: おれ つよく なる
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 強い なる
phrases.translation: I become strong.
phrases.notes:
naru: to become; to get

Reminder: Changing the "i" of an i-adjective to "ku" makes it an adverb that describes the following verb.

phrases.reading: おおきく なった な
phrases.lemmaField: 大きい なる な
phrases.translation: [It] grew big, didn't it!
phrases.notes: natta: past of naru

phrases.reading: きれい に なった ね ふく
phrases.lemmaField: きれい に なる ね 服
phrases.translation: [They] became clean, didn't they? The clothes [I mean].
phrases.notes:
fuku: clothes (esp. western clothes)

Remember that "kirei" is a na-adjective, even though it ends on a n "i". For na-adjectives, simply use [adjective + ni] to use them as adverb (i.e. to describe a verb).

Pay attention to the pronunciation here, there is a short pause after "kirei ni natta ne". It also sounds like a soft questions. Sounds like the speaker forgot to mention what actually became clean and adds it (the clothes of course!) afterwards.

phrases.japanese: 悪い人じゃないんだよね
phrases.reading: わるい ひと じゃない ん だ よ ね
phrases.lemmaField: 悪い 人 じゃ ん だ よ ね
phrases.romaji: warui hito janai n da yo ne
phrases.translation: [Someone clear from context] isn't a bad person (in an explanatory tone due to "n da").

phrases.reading: なに を する
phrases.lemmaField: 何 を する
phrases.translation: What [should we] do? Note that the meaning of "should we" is implicit.
phrases.notes:
suru: to do
Remark: Most resources teach this as "to do", but in fact it is more general. Don't worry about this for now, it's covered in more detail later.

phrases.reading: なに を する
phrases.lemmaField: 何 を する
phrases.translation: What [are you] do[ing]?! Note that just from the changed intonation, the sentence meaning changed. Also note that the stuff in square brackets is not explicitly stated in Japanese, the meaning in this case however is that of the English sentence.
phrases.notes:
suru: to do
Remark: Most resources teach this as "to do", but in fact it is more general. Don't worry about this for now, it's covered in more detail later.

phrases.reading: やくそく する
phrases.lemmaField: 約束 する
phrases.translation: [I] promise.
phrases.notes:
The verb "suru" is slightly special. Together with a noun, you can omit the "wo"-particle, the entire compound then acts as a verb. When you look up such a noun on jisho, you'll notice the word type to be "noun, suru verb".

suru: to do
Remark: Most resources teach this as "to do", but in fact it is more general. Don't worry about this for now, it's covered in more detail later.

phrases.reading: でんわ は しない
phrases.lemmaField: 電話 は する
phrases.translation: As for phoning/calling, [I] don't do [it].
phrases.notes:
shinai: negative of suru

The negative form of suru is one out of few verb conjugation exceptions (Tae Kim p. 46).

phrases.reading: つよく なった な
phrases.lemmaField: 強い なる な
phrases.translation: [You] became strong.
phrases.notes: natta: past of naru

phrases.reading: いかない
phrases.lemmaField: 行く
phrases.translation: [I] don't go.
phrases.notes: ikanai: negative of iku

phrases.reading: きょう は こない よ
phrases.lemmaField: 今日 は 来る よ
phrases.translation: As for today [the panda] doesn't come. They're talking about the panda who doesn't attend his job at the zoo today.
phrases.notes:
konai: negative of kuru.

The negative form of kuru is one out of few verb conjugation exceptions (Tae Kim p. 46).

phrases.reading: ぼく が かった
phrases.lemmaField: 僕 が 勝つ
phrases.translation:
I won.
Note that the plain past tense of "katsu - to win" and "kau - to buy" is the same.

phrases.reading: こなかった
phrases.lemmaField: 来る
phrases.translation: [Someone] didn't come.
phrases.notes: konakatta: past negative of kuru

phrases.japanese: 私ずっと分からなかった
phrases.reading: わたし ずっと わからなかった
phrases.lemmaField: 私 ずっと 分かる
phrases.translation: I never realized [this].
phrases.notes: wakaranakatta: past negative of wakaru

phrases.reading: いただきます
phrases.lemmaField: いただく いただきます
phrases.translation: "itadakimasu" is actually a phrase Japanese people say before starting a meal. The dictionary form is "itadaku", but I think the teineigo-form is used more often.
phrases.notes:
itadaku: to receive
itadakimasu: polite / teineigo conjugation of itadaku

A plain verb is made more polite by somehow appending "-masu".

phrases.reading: はなします
phrases.lemmaField: 話す
phrases.translation: hanashimasu: polite/teineigo of hanasu (to speak, talk)
phrases.notes: A plain verb is made more polite by somehow appending "-masu".
phrases.source: Mahoutsukai no Yome (The Ancient Magus Bride) ep 1-12

phrases.reading: わかります
phrases.lemmaField: 分かる
phrases.translation: wakarimasu: polite/teineigo of wakaru (to understand)
phrases.notes:
In this example, the "u" of "masu" is pronounced very clearly. It is usually omitted, see next card.

Fast Japanese speakers even tend to skip more vowels.

phrases.reading: わかります
phrases.lemmaField: 分かる
phrases.translation: wakarimasu: polite/teineigo of wakaru (to understand)
phrases.grammarNote: Skipped "u" in the end, this is the more common pronunciation.

phrases.reading: さあ いそぎます よ
phrases.lemmaField: さあ 急ぐ よ
phrases.translation:
isogimasu: polite/teineigo of isogu (to hurry)
sa: well now; all right (it's sort of a filler, safe to ignore here I'd say)

phrases.reading: たのみます よ
phrases.lemmaField: 頼む よ
phrases.translation: tanomimasu: polite/teineigo of tanomu (to request; to beg; to ask)

phrases.reading: さけ
phrases.lemmaField: 酒
phrases.translation: sake: alcoholic beverage
phrases.notes: Remark: In western languages, "sake" refers to Japanese rice wine. In Japanese, sake is a broader category that refers to any type of alcoholic beverage, no matter where it comes from. The Japanese rice wine is called nihonshu/日本酒 in Japanese.

phrases.reading: おさけ のみます
phrases.lemmaField: お酒 飲む
phrases.translation: [We] drink sake [there].
phrases.notes:
nomimasu: polite/teineigo of nomu (to drink)
osake: polite/teineigo for sake (alcoholic beverage)

Some nouns also have a teineigo form. In this case they start with an additional "o/お" or "go/ご". Note that "o" or "go" can't be added to all nouns, you'll need to learn this from the respective context. I'll add some more examples soon.
phrases.source: Terrace House- Boys & Girls in the City

phrases.reading: よぶ
phrases.lemmaField: 呼ぶ
phrases.translation: yobu: to call out (to); to call; to invoke
phrases.grammarNote: Look at what the guy is doing...
phrases.notes: Obviously, the speaker wants to yobu someone with his phone. Do you remember the Japanese word for phone?
phrases.source: The Daily Lives of High School Boys (EP 1-12)

phrases.reading: わたし も たべます
phrases.lemmaField: 私 も 食べる
phrases.translation: I also [will] eat [this]! The speaker says this in anticipation of some super delicious food someone else has already tasted.
phrases.notes:
tabemasu: polite/teineigo of taberu (to eat)

Remark: You could also translate this as "I also want to eat this" in English, which was the translation of this card up to deck version 14. Since there's a dedicated form for saying "want to" in Japanese (covered later), I changed the translation.

phrases.reading: ぺんぎん を みます
phrases.lemmaField: ペンギン を 見る
phrases.translation: [I] see a penguin.
phrases.notes:
pengin: penguin
mimasu: polite/teineigo of miru (to see)

phrases.reading: ぜったい かちます
phrases.lemmaField: 絶対 勝つ
phrases.translation: [I will] totally win (the speaker is talking to his teacher and wants to convince him).
phrases.notes:
An interesting point here is that Japanese does not have a future tense. The present tense is used for both present and future, future is either expressed by context as in this example (the date of the contest is known to both). Or if it is unknown, it is stated by using time words as "tomorrow" or "next week". That's actually a lot simpler than in English. For this reason, some people also avoid the term "present tense" and say that there's past and non-past only.

kachimasu: polite/teineigo of katsu (to win)
zettai: definitely; absolutely; unconditionally

phrases.reading: はいはい まちます よ
phrases.lemmaField: はいはい 待つ よ
phrases.translation: Ok, ok, [I'll] wait!
phrases.notes: machimasu: polite/teineigo of matsu (to wait)

phrases.reading: かいます
phrases.lemmaField: 買う
phrases.translation: kaimasu: polite/teineigo of kau (to buy)
phrases.grammarNote: Ok, the intonation/pitch is sort of bad here.
phrases.source: Ouran High School Host Club (jp eng)

phrases.reading: おれ も たたかいます
phrases.lemmaField: オレ も 戦う
phrases.translation: [I will] also fight.
phrases.notes: tatakaimasu: polite/teineigo of tatakau (to fight, to wage war)

phrases.japanese: すみません少し急ぎます
phrases.reading: すみません すこし いそぎます
phrases.lemmaField: すみません 少し 急ぐ
phrases.translation: Sorry, [I need to] hurry a bit.
phrases.notes: sukoshi: small quantity; a little; few

phrases.reading: けいさつ よびます よ
phrases.lemmaField: 警察 呼ぶ よ
phrases.translation: [Hey, don't do that! I'll] call the police!
phrases.notes:
yobimasu: polite/teineigo of yobu (to call out (to); to call; to invoke)
keisatsu: police

phrases.reading: さいご まで たたかいます
phrases.lemmaField: 最後 まで 戦う
phrases.translation: [I] fight till the end.
phrases.notes: saigo: end; conclusion

phrases.reading: やくそく します
phrases.lemmaField: 約束 する
phrases.translation: [I] promise [this to you].
phrases.notes:
shimasu: polite/teineigo of suru (to do)

"suru" is one out of two conjugation exceptions for teneigo / -masu.

phrases.reading: また きます
phrases.lemmaField: また 来る
phrases.translation: [I] come again.
phrases.notes:
mata: again; once more
kimasu: polite/teineigo of kuru (to come)

"kuru" is the other one out of two conjugation exceptions for teneigo / -masu.

phrases.reading: ぼく も いきます
phrases.lemmaField: 僕 も 行く
phrases.translation: ikimasu: polite/teineigo of iku (to go)

phrases.reading: おります
phrases.lemmaField: 降りる
phrases.translation: orimasu: polite/teineigo of oriru (to descend (e.g. a mountain); to go down; to get off (bus / train)
phrases.source: JoJos Bizarre Adventure 黄金の風 (26-39)

phrases.reading: だいじ な はなし が あります
phrases.lemmaField: 大事 だ 話 が ある
phrases.translation: Important conversation is there -> [I] need to talk about [something] important.
phrases.notes: arimasu: polite/teineigo of aru (to be there, to exist for inanimate things)
phrases.source: Terrace House-Boys x Girls Next Door

phrases.reading: しあわせ に なります
phrases.lemmaField: 幸せ に なる
phrases.translation: [Something] will become happiness / good fortune. Probably something these people are about to do makes them happy.
phrases.notes: narimasu: polite/teineigo of naru (to become, to get)

phrases.reading: ねむく なります
phrases.lemmaField: 眠い なる
phrases.translation: nemui: sleepy
phrases.notes: Refresher: Replacing "i" by "ku" in an i-adjective makes it an adverb (i.e. it can be used to describe a verb, just as in this example).
phrases.source: さよなら絶望先生 (Sayonara, Zetsubou-Sensei)

phrases.japanese: 好きな人がいますよね
phrases.reading: すき な ひと が います よ ね
phrases.lemmaField: 好き だ 人 が いる よ ね
phrases.romaji: suki na hito ga imasu yo ne
phrases.translation: There's a person you like, right?
phrases.notes: imasu: polite/teineigo of iru (to be there, to exist for animate things)
phrases.source: Boku no Hero Academia S3 (ep 1-25 jp_en)

phrases.reading: ええ あそびます わ よ
phrases.lemmaField: ええ 遊ぶ わ よ
phrases.translation:
asobimasu: polite/teineigo of asobu (to play)
wa yo: female emphatic sentence-ending particle​

phrases.japanese: 僕は書きますよ内申書に
phrases.reading: ぼく は かきます よ ないしんしょ に
phrases.lemmaField: 僕 は 書く よ 内申書 に
phrases.romaji: boku ha kakimasu yo naishinsho ni
phrases.translation: kakimasu: polite/teineigo of kaku (to write)
phrases.grammarNote: Ignore "naishinsho ni"
phrases.notes: naishinsho means "school record (on a student); transcript (of grades)". It's not a frequent word, so just ignore it - I couldn't find a better example for "kakimasu".

phrases.japanese: おもしろいことになるよたぶんね
phrases.reading: おもしろい こと に なる よ たぶん ね
phrases.lemmaField: おもしろい こと に なる よ たぶん ね
phrases.romaji: omoshiroi koto ni naru yo tabun ne
phrases.translation: [Something] becomes an interesthing thing / matter. perhaps...
phrases.notes: tabun: perhaps; probably
phrases.source: Ouran High School Host Club (jp eng)

phrases.japanese: すみませんすぐ行きます
phrases.reading: すみません すぐ いきます
phrases.lemmaField: すみません すぐ 行く
phrases.translation: Sorry, [I] go immediately!
phrases.notes:
sugu: immediately; at once; right away
sugu can also mean soon, which is a little less urgent.

phrases.japanese: 多分すぐ死にますよ俺は
phrases.reading: たぶん すぐ しにます よ おれ は
phrases.lemmaField: 多分 すぐ 死ぬ よ 俺 は
phrases.romaji: tabun sugu shinimasu yo ore ha
phrases.translation: Maybe I soon die. This sentence is just for the sake of completeness to conclude the teineigo-conjugation of verbs. It contains "shinu", which ends on the rare "nu".
phrases.notes: shinimasu: polite/teineigo of shinu (to die)

phrases.reading: のみもの を のみます か
phrases.lemmaField: 飲み物 を 飲む か
phrases.translation:
nomimono: beverage (notice the similarity to nomu - to drink)
ka (always written in Hiragana as か): Question marker particle
phrases.grammarNote: Finally, the question marker! Tae Kim introduces it a little later, but I need it on the following cards.
phrases.notes: "ka" explicitly marks a sentence as question. I'm sure you remember all those questions without "ka": In casual speech it is often omitted, the question is formed by intonation.

phrases.reading: いきます か
phrases.lemmaField: 行く か
phrases.translation: [Do you] go [there]?
phrases.grammarNote: Finally, the question marker! Tae Kim introduces it a little later, but I need it on the following cards.
phrases.notes:
ka (always written in Hiragana as か): Question marker particle

"ka" explicitly marks a sentence as question. I'm sure you remember all those questions without "ka": In casual speech it is often omitted, the question is formed by intonation.

phrases.reading: しらない の か
phrases.lemmaField: 知る の か
phrases.translation: [You] don't know [this]?

phrases.reading: わたし は いきません
phrases.lemmaField: 私 は 行く
phrases.translation: As for me, [I] don't go.
phrases.notes:
ikimasen: negative polite/teineigo of iku (to go)

The negative polite teineigo form is simply built by using "-masen" instead of "-masu".

phrases.reading: わかりません
phrases.lemmaField: 分かる
phrases.translation: wakarimasen: negative polite/teineigo of wakaru (to understand)

phrases.reading: おもいません
phrases.lemmaField: 思う
phrases.translation: omoimasen: negative polite/teineigo of omou (to think, to believe)

phrases.reading: ありません
phrases.lemmaField: ある
phrases.translation: arimasen: negative polite/teineigo of aru (to be, to exist)

phrases.reading: いみ が わかりません
phrases.lemmaField: 意味 が 分かる
phrases.translation: As for the meaning [of something that just happened], [I] don't understand.

phrases.reading: やくそく は できません
phrases.lemmaField: 約束 は できる
phrases.translation: As for promise, [I] can't do.
phrases.notes:
yakusoku: promise
dekimasen: negative polite/teineigo of dekiru (to be able to)

phrases.reading: せんせい いません か
phrases.lemmaField: 先生 いる か
phrases.translation: Teacher, aren't [you] there?
phrases.notes: imasen: negative polite/teineigo of iru (to be there, to exist for animate things)

phrases.reading: はい しません
phrases.lemmaField: はい する
phrases.translation: This sentence could be the answer to the order "Don't do this" - yes, [I] don't do [it]. Or the question "So he doesn't do his homework?" - yes, [he] doesn't do [it].
phrases.notes: shimasen: negative polite/teineigo of suru (to do)
phrases.source: Honzuki - Ascendance of a Bookworm S1 (JP Only)

phrases.reading: ありません でした
phrases.lemmaField: ある です
phrases.translation: [Something inanimate] wasn't there.
phrases.notes: In order to get the negative past teineigo, simply add "deshita" to the negative form.

phrases.reading: しりません でした
phrases.lemmaField: 知る です
phrases.translation: [I] didn't know [this] / [I] wasn't aware [of this].
phrases.notes: In order to get the negative past teineigo, simply add "deshita" to the negative form.

phrases.japanese: 喧嘩にもなりませんでしたよ
phrases.reading: けんか に も なりません でした よ
phrases.lemmaField: 喧嘩 に も なる です よ
phrases.romaji: kenka ni mo narimasen deshita yo
phrases.translation: [Something, maybe a conversation] didn't become a fight (the speaker was asked: "Did you fight"? before). Ignore the "mo" in this sentence for now: We learned it meant "also", but in negative sentences it's used a bit different. I'll explain this in more detail later.
phrases.notes:
kenka: quarrel; brawl; fight

Remark: The "ni" particle is often used together with "naru" in practice, see ref.
phrases.source: Sakurasou no Pet na Kanojo (jp eng)

phrases.japanese: 全然分かりませんでした
phrases.reading: ぜんぜん わかりません でした
phrases.lemmaField: 全然 分かる です
phrases.translation: [I] completely didn't understand -> in the sense: I understood nothing.
phrases.notes: zenzen: wholly; entirely; completely

phrases.reading: わかりました
phrases.lemmaField: 分かる
phrases.translation: "got it."
phrases.notes:
wakarimashita: past polite/teineigo of wakaru (to unterstand)

The past polite/teineigo form is simply built by using "-mashita" instead of "-masu".

phrases.reading: わすれました
phrases.lemmaField: 忘れる
phrases.translation: [I] forgot [it].
phrases.notes:
wasuremashita: past polite/teineigo of wasureru (to forget)

The past polite/teineigo form is simply built by using "-mashita" instead of "-masu".

phrases.reading: できました か
phrases.lemmaField: できる か
phrases.translation: Could [you] do/finish [it]? Meaning: Are you done? is it done?
phrases.notes:
dekimashita: past polite/teineigo of dekiru (to be able to, to finish)

The past polite/teineigo form is simply built by using "-mashita" instead of "-masu".

phrases.japanese: はいありがとうございました
phrases.reading: はい ありがとう ございました
phrases.lemmaField: はい ありがとう ござる
phrases.translation: Remember "arigatou gozaimasu" as polite way to thank someone? If the thing you're thanking for happened a while a go in the past, you use "gozaimashita". "gozaimasu" is used to thank fo something that happened just now.

phrases.reading: おそく なりました
phrases.lemmaField: 遅い なる
phrases.translation: Literally, the sentence reads [something] became late. It means that either the speaker or someone else was late.

phrases.reading: たべました ね
phrases.lemmaField: 食べる ね
phrases.translation: [We] ate [everything on the table, didn't we].

phrases.reading: つよく なりました
phrases.lemmaField: 強い なる
phrases.translation: [You / it / someone] became strong.

phrases.reading: かいました
phrases.lemmaField: 買う
phrases.translation: [I] bought [it].
phrases.source: Ouran High School Host Club (jp eng)

phrases.reading: やくそく しました よ
phrases.lemmaField: 約束 する よ
phrases.translation: [Someone / I] made a promise.

phrases.reading: おいしい です
phrases.lemmaField: おいしい です
phrases.translation: [It's] tasty.
phrases.notes:
desu: politeness marker

According to Tae Kim, Everything that does not end on a verb will become polite by adding "desu" (p. 79). That may be a bit vague, but you'll face "desu" so often that it will become easily clear from context. Technically, it is the teineigo conjugation of "da", but the uses of "desu" can be very different from "da". Therefore I follow Tofugu's definition and simply describe "desu" as politeness marker. You already see one difference in this example: "desu" is attached to an i-adjective, which is not possible for "da".

phrases.reading: おいしかった です
phrases.lemmaField: おいしい です
phrases.translation: [It] was tasty.
phrases.notes:
desu: politeness marker

According to Tae Kim, Everything that does not end on a verb will become polite by adding "desu" (p. 79). That may be a bit vague, but you'll face "desu" so often that it will become easily clear from context. Technically, it is the teineigo conjugation of "da", but the uses of "desu" can be very different from "da". Therefore I follow Tofugu's definition and simply describe "desu" as politeness marker. You already see one difference in this example: "desu" is attached to an i-adjective, which is not possible for "da".

phrases.reading: わるくない です ね
phrases.lemmaField: 悪い です ね
phrases.translation: [That's] not bad.
phrases.notes:
desu: politeness marker

According to Tae Kim, Everything that does not end on a verb will become polite by adding "desu" (p. 79). That may be a bit vague, but you'll face "desu" so often that it will become easily clear from context. Technically, it is the teineigo conjugation of "da", but the uses of "desu" can be very different from "da". Therefore I follow Tofugu's definition and simply describe "desu" as politeness marker. You already see one difference in this example: "desu" is attached to an i-adjective, which is not possible for "da".
phrases.source: Ouran High School Host Club (jp eng)

phrases.reading: わるくない です よ
phrases.lemmaField: 悪い です よ
phrases.translation: [You're] not to blame / don't worry, it's not bad.
phrases.notes:
desu: politeness marker

According to Tae Kim, Everything that does not end on a verb will become polite by adding "desu" (p. 79). That may be a bit vague, but you'll face "desu" so often that it will become easily clear from context. Technically, it is the teineigo conjugation of "da", but the uses of "desu" can be very different from "da". Therefore I follow Tofugu's definition and simply describe "desu" as politeness marker. You already see one difference in this example: "desu" is attached to an i-adjective, which is not possible for "da".
phrases.source: さよなら絶望先生 (Sayonara, Zetsubou-Sensei)

phrases.japanese: あれ怖くなかったですか
phrases.reading: あれ こわくなかった です か
phrases.lemmaField: あれ 怖い です か
phrases.translation: Eh, wasn't [that] scary?
phrases.notes:
desu: politeness marker
are: huh?, eh?

According to Tae Kim, Everything that does not end on a verb will become polite by adding "desu" (p. 79). That may be a bit vague, but you'll face "desu" so often that it will become easily clear from context. Technically, it is the teineigo conjugation of "da", but the uses of "desu" can be very different from "da". Therefore I follow Tofugu's definition and simply describe "desu" as politeness marker. You already see one difference in this example: "desu" is attached to an i-adjective, which is not possible for "da".

phrases.reading: かわいい です よ ね
phrases.lemmaField: かわいい です よ ね
phrases.translation: It's cute, isn't it?
phrases.grammarNote: "desu" again after an i-adjective. That's not possible for "da".

phrases.japanese: とても楽しかったです
phrases.reading: とても たのしかった です
phrases.lemmaField: とても 楽しい です
phrases.translation: [Something] was very enjoyable / fun.
phrases.notes: totemo: very

phrases.reading: きょう は いい てんき だ ね
phrases.lemmaField: 今日 は いい 天気 だ ね
phrases.romaji: kyou ha ii tenki da ne
phrases.translation: As for today, weather is good, isn't it.
phrases.notes: tenki: weather

phrases.reading: うみ たのしかった です ね
phrases.lemmaField: 海 楽しい です ね
phrases.translation: [Going to] the sea was fun, wasn't it

phrases.reading: おもしろく ありません
phrases.lemmaField: 面白い ある
phrases.translation: omoshiroi (interesting) in this example becomes omoshiroku arimasen (not interesting). This is the grammatically correct way for a polite negative i-adjective. In practice, you'll encounter "omoshirokunai desu" more often though.
phrases.grammarNote: The sentence is cut off a bit, I couldn't find a better one.
phrases.source: さよなら絶望先生 (Sayonara, Zetsubou-Sensei)

phrases.japanese: おおいしくありませんでしたか
phrases.reading: お おいしく ありません でした か
phrases.lemmaField: お おいしい ある です か
phrases.translation: oishii (yummy) in this example becomes oishiku arimasen deshita (was not yummy). This is the grammatically correct way for a polite past negative i-adjective. In practice, you'll encounter "oishikunakatta desu" more often though.

phrases.reading: さむくない です か
phrases.lemmaField: 寒い です か
phrases.translation: Isn't [it] cold [over there]?
phrases.notes: samui: cold (e.g. weather)​

phrases.reading: しずか だ
phrases.lemmaField: 静か だ
phrases.translation: [It] is quiet.
phrases.notes: shizuka: quiet; silent

phrases.reading: とても しずか です
phrases.lemmaField: とても 静か です
phrases.translation: [It] is very quiet.

phrases.reading: ‪ きれい でした ね ‬
phrases.lemmaField: ‪ きれい です ね ‬
phrases.translation: [Something] was pretty / lovely.

phrases.reading: にんげん です よ
phrases.lemmaField: 人間 です よ
phrases.translation: [He's] a human being [not an alien].

phrases.reading: わたし は すき です
phrases.lemmaField: 私 は 好き です
phrases.translation: As for me, [I] like [it].

phrases.japanese: 相手が悪かったですね
phrases.reading: あいて が わるかった です ね
phrases.lemmaField: 相手 が 悪い です ね
phrases.translation: [Your] partner was at fault, wasn't he?
phrases.notes: aite: "other party" or "the other", this can mean either opponent or partner / ally. This is a bit confusing, but usually clear from context, read more about this here.
phrases.source: BOFURI - Itai no wa Iya nano de Bougyoryoku ni Kyokufuri Shitai to Omoimasu (ep 1-12 w_en)

phrases.reading: おそい です よ
phrases.lemmaField: 遅い です よ
phrases.translation: [You're] late!

phrases.reading: おもしろい いもうとさん です ね
phrases.lemmaField: 面白い 妹さん です ね
phrases.translation: [Your] sister is interesting, isn't she (sounds like she did something weird).

phrases.reading: せんせい も すき です よ
phrases.lemmaField: 先生 も 好き です よ
phrases.translation: [I, the teacher] like [that] too...
phrases.notes: The speaker refers to herself in 3rd person. Depending on the context however, this can also mean that someone else talks about something the teacher likes. Don't worry about those details, from context this is usually clear (updated in v14).

phrases.reading: じょうだん です よ
phrases.lemmaField: 冗談 です よ
phrases.translation: [Something said before] is a joke.

phrases.reading: じょうだん じゃない です よ
phrases.lemmaField: 冗談 じゃ です よ
phrases.translation: This is not a joke [I am serious]!

phrases.reading: たのしみ です
phrases.lemmaField: 楽しみ です
phrases.translation: [Something] is enjoyment / anticipation.
phrases.notes: When you're looking forward to something, you can say "tanoshimi" or "tanoshimi desu".

phrases.japanese: 買い物早かったですね
phrases.reading: かいもの はやかった です ね
phrases.lemmaField: 買い物 早い です ね
phrases.translation: Shopping was fast, wasn't it.

phrases.japanese: 本当の私じゃないです
phrases.reading: ほんとう の わたし じゃない です
phrases.lemmaField: ほんとう の 私 じゃ です
phrases.translation: [This] is not the real me. This refers e.g. to the picture someone might have in mind about the speaker or to something the speaker did.
phrases.notes: hontou: truth; reality; actuality; fact

phrases.reading: かぜ じゃない です
phrases.lemmaField: 風邪 じゃ です
phrases.translation: kaze: (common) cold; influenza

phrases.reading: うみ です ね
phrases.lemmaField: 海 です ね
phrases.translation: It's the sea, isn't it.
phrases.notes: This can be the answer to several questions: What is his favorite vacation destination? What is on this unclear picture? etc.

phrases.reading: ちゅうがくせい
phrases.lemmaField: 中学生
phrases.translation: The speaker is asking: [Are you] junior high school student? (continues on next card)
phrases.grammarNote: This card and the next two belong together. It's a conversation between two girls, the speaker here is the older one.
phrases.notes: chuugakusei: junior high school student

phrases.reading: なんで こども が いる の
phrases.lemmaField: 何で 子ども が いる の 子供たち 子どもたち
phrases.translation: [Are you] junior high school student (previous card)? Why [is] a kid here?
phrases.notes:
nande: why?; what for?
kodomo: kid, child

We already learned a word for "why": naze, which is slightly more formal than "nande".

phrases.reading: こども じゃない です
phrases.lemmaField: 子ども じゃ です
phrases.translation: [I] am not a kid!
phrases.notes:
kodomo: kid, child

The older one is using plain, the younger one polite speech.

phrases.reading: ぼく の いえ です よ
phrases.lemmaField: 僕 の 家 です よ
phrases.translation: [This] is my house!
phrases.source: Ore no Imouto ga konna ni Kawaii Wake ga Nai_

phrases.reading: きれい でした
phrases.lemmaField: きれい です
phrases.translation: [Something] was pretty; lovely; beautiful, wasn't it?
phrases.source: Terrace House-Boys x Girls Next Door

phrases.japanese: 考えたこともなかったです
phrases.reading: かんがえた こと も なかった です
phrases.lemmaField: 考える こと も ない です
phrases.translation: Thinking matter wasn't even there -> [I] didn't even think about [this].
phrases.notes:
Note that "mo" does not mean "too" here, but "even". Especially in negative sentences, "mo" is often used like this, more examples follow later.
nakatta: negative past of aru

phrases.reading: わたし は ずっと しあわせ です
phrases.lemmaField: 私 は ずっと 幸せ です
phrases.translation: As for me, [I]'ve been happy the whole time [since I learned about this].

phrases.reading: ひろしま へ かえります
phrases.lemmaField: 広島 へ 帰る
phrases.translation: [I] return to Hiroshima.
phrases.notes: hiroshima: city in Japan

phrases.reading: いい じゃない です か
phrases.lemmaField: いい じゃ です か
phrases.translation: Isn't [this idea] good -> isn't this a good idea?

phrases.japanese: すみません大丈夫ですか
phrases.reading: すみません だいじょうぶ です か
phrases.lemmaField: すみません 大丈夫 です か
phrases.translation: Excuse me, are [you] ok?

phrases.japanese: ここにいるじゃないですか
phrases.reading: ここ に いる じゃない です か
phrases.lemmaField: ここ に いる じゃ です か
phrases.romaji: koko ni iru janai desu ka
phrases.translation:
Isn't [someone supposed to be] here?!
[Should] not [someone] be here?!
phrases.notes: It's always amazing how much information is packed into context in Japanese: The entire "supposed to be" or "should be" is completely transmitted by the intonation.

phrases.reading: わたし も よく しる おとこ です
phrases.lemmaField: 私 も よく 知る 男 です
phrases.romaji: watashi mo yoku shiru otoko desu
phrases.translation: [He's] a guy I know well myself
phrases.notes: Or less literal: I know this guy well myself.

phrases.reading: ばか で は ありません
phrases.lemmaField: バカ で は ある
phrases.translation: [Someone] is not an idiot (expressed in a polite way :D).
phrases.notes: "de ha arimasen" is the grammatically correct way to express polite negative state of being. In practice, you'll encounter "janai desu" more often.
phrases.source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure スターダストクルセイダース

phrases.reading: うそ で は ありません
phrases.lemmaField: 嘘 で は ある
phrases.translation: uso: lie
phrases.notes:
[Something said before] is not a lie.

"de ha arimasen" is the grammatically correct way to express polite negative state of being. In practice, you'll encounter "janai desu" more often.

phrases.reading: じょうだん じゃ ありません
phrases.lemmaField: 冗談 じゃ ある
phrases.translation: [Something said before] is not a joke.
phrases.notes: "ja arimasen" is slightly less formal than "de ha arimasen", refer to this question for details.

phrases.japanese: 全然大丈夫じゃありませんでしたよ
phrases.reading: ぜんぜん だいじょうぶ じゃ ありません でした よ
phrases.lemmaField: 全然 大丈夫 じゃ ある です よ
phrases.romaji: zenzen daijoubu ja arimasen deshita yo
phrases.translation: [Someone or something done] was totally not ok.
phrases.notes: "ja arimasen" is slightly less formal than "de ha arimasen", refer to this question for details.

phrases.reading: ただいま
phrases.lemmaField: ただいま
phrases.translation: tadaima: Here I am; I'm home! (Phrase people say when returning home)

phrases.reading: おかえり
phrases.lemmaField: おかえり
phrases.translation: okaeri: welcome home (informal)

phrases.reading: おかえりなさい
phrases.lemmaField: おかえりなさい
phrases.translation: okaerinasai: welcome home (more formal / polite than okaeri)

phrases.reading: おじゃまします
phrases.lemmaField: おじゃまします
phrases.translation: ojamashimasu: Excuse me for disturbing (interrupting) you; greeting used when entering someone's home

phrases.reading: うみ に いきます
phrases.lemmaField: 海 に 行く
phrases.translation: [I] go to the sea.
phrases.grammarNote: Sometimes I put cards in between without any new terms, e.g. to repeat words in a different context. If you immediately understand these, I'd recommend to suspend them ("@" or "!" in desktop Anki). If you delete them, they will be reimported when the deck is updated.

phrases.reading: ただ の にく じゃねえ
phrases.lemmaField: ただ の 肉 だ
phrases.translation: Isn't [this] just ordinary meat? -> The conversation revolves around a piece of meat that is considered special, but looks ordinary to the speaker, so he asks this question.
phrases.grammarNote: Listen closely, we have a question without question marker here.
phrases.notes:
The ending "janee" here is a slurred, casual form of "janai". It's not the empathic sentence ending particle "ne/ね".

tada: ordinary; common; usual​

Internal remark: gintama s5 e15 15:00 - and yes, it's ordinary meat

phrases.reading: おれ の けいたい
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 の 携帯
phrases.translation: keitai: Abbreviation for mobile telephone; cellular telephone

phrases.reading: そして わたし の ねがい だ
phrases.lemmaField: そして 私 の 願い だ
phrases.translation: ...and this is my wish.
phrases.notes: negai: desire; wish; hope

phrases.japanese: 気づくことができなかったんだ
phrases.reading: きづく こと が できなかった ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: 気づく こと が できる ん だ
phrases.romaji: kidzuku koto ga dekinakatta n da
phrases.translation: [I] wasn't able to notice [this].
phrases.grammarNote: Notice the weird spelling of the first word: ki-dzu-ku. What the heck is "dsu" supposed to mean? It represents the Japanese "voiced" tsu-character. This is simply a "tsu/つ" with an additional small mark: づ. This changes the pronunciation a bit, press "r" to play the audio again. In Hepbun romanization, this is usually just spelled as it is pronounced: "zu". However, the pronunciation of the voiced "su/す"-character "ず" is the same, therefore it is also spelled "zu" in the Hepburn system. Jlab therefore spells these cases different in order to get a 1:1 mapping to Japanese without any ambiguities. Fortunately, there are only two of them. Have a look at the romanization section of the jlab manual for more details.
phrases.notes:
kidsuku: to notice
dekinakatta: past negative of dekiru (to be able to do)

I added only few examples for the plain negative past tense so far, I'll add a few more in the following. Quick reminder: Build the negative form (dekinai) and replace the "i" with "katta".

phrases.reading: きづかなかった か
phrases.lemmaField: 気づく か
phrases.translation: kidzukanakatta: negative past of kidzuku (to notice)
phrases.grammarNote: Notice the weird spelling of the first word: ki-dzu-ku. What the heck is "dsu" supposed to mean? It represents the Japanese "voiced" tsu-character. This is simply a "tsu/つ" with an additional small mark: づ. This changes the pronunciation a bit, press "r" to play the audio again. In Hepbun romanization, this is usually just spelled as it is pronounced: "zu". However, the pronunciation of the voiced "su/す"-character "ず" is the same, therefore it is also spelled "zu" in the Hepburn system. Jlab therefore spells these cases different in order to get a 1:1 mapping to Japanese without any ambiguities. Fortunately, there are only two of them. Have a look at the romanization section of the jlab manual for more details.
phrases.notes: I added only few examples for the plain negative past tense so far, I'll add a few more in the following. Quick reminder: Build the negative form (kidzukanai) and replace the "i" with "katta".

phrases.reading: さけ のみます か
phrases.lemmaField: 酒 飲む か
phrases.translation: [Do you like to] drink alcohol/wine? If the conversation already revolves around drinking some alcoholic beverage, this is a perfectly valid way of asking, if someone likes to drink it (i.e. without all the "do you like").
phrases.notes: Remark: In western languages, "sake" refers to Japanese rice wine. In Japanese, sake is a broader category that refers to any type of alcoholic beverage, no matter where it comes from. The Japanese rice wine is called nihonshuu/日本酒 in Japanese.

phrases.japanese: でもお酒飲まなかった
phrases.reading: でも おさけ のまなかった
phrases.lemmaField: でも お酒 飲む
phrases.translation: ...but [person known from context] didn't drink alcohol.
phrases.notes:
demo: but; however; though;
nomanakatta: past negative of nomu (to drink)

The context is usually important. Depending on the conversation, this sentence can express:
[We went out] but [I] didn't drink sake. Or: [He wanted to have a drink at the bar] but [he] didn't drink sake [in the end].

I sometimes put a specific context into the square brackets or a more general one as in this case. I hope you're not confused by this!
phrases.source: Terrace House-Boys x Girls Next Door

phrases.reading: たいが みなかった
phrases.lemmaField: 大河 見る
phrases.translation: Didn't [you] see taiga?
phrases.grammarNote: taiga is the name of a character.
phrases.notes: minakatta: negative past of miru (to see)

phrases.reading: きづかなかった の か
phrases.lemmaField: 気づく の か
phrases.translation: [You] didn't notice?
phrases.notes: remember: no in the end of a sentence adds an explanatory tone. Together with the question marker "ka" this indicates that the speaker is looking for an explanation.
phrases.source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure スターダストクルセイダース

phrases.reading: でも わたし は おもう の
phrases.lemmaField: でも 私 は 思う の
phrases.translation: ... but as for me, [i] believe [it / think this way]. The "no" adds an explanatory tone. A less literal translation would be: [that's] what I think / believe.
phrases.notes: omou: to think; to consider; to believe

phrases.reading: わたし は おもわない
phrases.lemmaField: 私 は 思う
phrases.translation: As for me, [I] don't believe [something clear from context].
phrases.notes: omowanai: negative of omou (to think; to consider; to believe)

phrases.reading: おもわなかった
phrases.lemmaField: 思う
phrases.translation: omowanakatta: negative past of omou (to think; to consider; to believe)

phrases.reading: おいしい です か
phrases.lemmaField: おいしい です か
phrases.translation: Is [it] tasty?

phrases.reading: たのしかった です ね
phrases.lemmaField: 楽しい です ね
phrases.translation: [It] was enjoyable/fun, wasn't it?

phrases.japanese: 今日は学校は楽しかったですか
phrases.reading: きょう は がっこう は たのしかった です か
phrases.lemmaField: 今日 は 学校 は 楽しい です か
phrases.romaji: kyou ha gakkou ha tanoshikatta desu ka
phrases.translation: Was school fun today?
phrases.notes: Note the two "ha" in this sentence, the topic is both today and the school. This is rather rare though.

phrases.japanese: おはようございますお父さん
phrases.reading: おはよう ございます おとうさん
phrases.lemmaField: おはよう ござる お父さん
phrases.translation: otousan: father (polite)
phrases.notes: otousan is the polite word for father. In this example, the speaker uses it to address her own father. She's also using the more polite version of "good morning".

phrases.reading: ちち は しらなかった
phrases.lemmaField: 父 は 知る
phrases.translation: chichi: father
phrases.notes: chichi is a less formal word for "father". It's not rude, but usually used to refer to one's own father when talking to others. So this sentence means: As for [my] father [he] didn't know.

phrases.reading: おとうさん どこ いく の
phrases.lemmaField: お父さん どこ 行く の
phrases.translation: Father, where [do you] go?
phrases.notes:
otousan: father

otousan is the polite word for father. In this example, the speaker uses it to address her own father. Note, that she further says "doko iku no" (colloquial) and not "doko ni ikimasu no ka". So don't worry about when to use which forms together, just listen to many more examples.

As far as I know, most families in Japan speak plain Japanese at home, but "otousan" is used to address ones own father directly or someone else's father. When talking about one's own father to others, "chichi" is used instead, but I think "otousan" can be used as well.
phrases.source: 今からあなたを脅迫します

phrases.japanese: でお父さんは何してるの
phrases.reading: で おとうさん は なに してる の
phrases.lemmaField: で お父さん は 何 する の
phrases.romaji: de otousan ha nani shiteru no
phrases.translation: The speaker talks about someone else's father and asks: As for [your] father, what is [he] doing (at the moment)?
phrases.grammarNote: Ignore "shiteru" for now, I'll cover this form later. It's the shortened present progressive tense of "suru - to do" and means "doing".
phrases.notes: The "de" is an informal conjuction (shortened "sorede"). You often hear in conversations, it means: so; therefore; and; (and) then

phrases.reading: わたし の ちち です
phrases.lemmaField: 私 の 父 です
phrases.translation: This can be the answer to the question: Who did it? [It was] my father.

phrases.reading: だいじょうぶ です おかあさん
phrases.lemmaField: 大丈夫 です お母さん
phrases.translation: [I'm] ok, mother!
phrases.notes: okaasan: mother (polite)

phrases.reading: おかあさん も いない
phrases.lemmaField: お母さん も いる
phrases.translation: Mother is not there either.
phrases.notes: You often find "mo" in negative sentences, I'll cover that in more detail later.

phrases.reading: わたし の はは です
phrases.lemmaField: わたし の 母 です
phrases.translation: [This] is my mother.
phrases.notes:
haha: mother

okaasan and haha follow the same rules as otousan and chichi: Use the polite version when referring to someone else's father or talking to your own father. Use the casual version, when talking to someone about your own father. It's not too strict in practice though...

phrases.reading: かぞく です
phrases.lemmaField: 家族 です
phrases.translation: [This] is [my] family.
phrases.notes: kazoku: family

phrases.japanese: お酒を買うこともできませんし
phrases.reading: おさけ を かう こと も できません し
phrases.lemmaField: お酒 を 買う こと も できる し
phrases.romaji: osake wo kau koto mo dekimasen shi
phrases.translation: [The conversation revolves around the question of why the people are drinking at one of the guy's home. One (among other) reasons is that outside we] can't buy any alcoholic beverages.
phrases.grammarNote: "shi" marks an incomplete set of reasons here, it's covered in more detail later - ignore it for now.
phrases.notes:
Remember sake (alcoholic beverage)? The prefix "o" makes it more polite. This prefix can't be added to any noun though.

Remark: "xxx koto ga dekiru" is one out of several ways to express the ability to do something. This is covered later in more detail. In negative sentences, "ga" is sometimes replaced by "mo" to add emphasis. "mo" translates to something like "even" in this case. I.e. we can't even buy alcohol. Have a look at the reference.

phrases.japanese: すみません注文いいですか
phrases.reading: すみません ちゅうもん いい です か
phrases.lemmaField: すみません 注文 いい です か
phrases.translation: Excuse me, [is] order ok? -> Can I order something?
phrases.notes: chuumon: order (in a restaurant)

phrases.reading: ごちゅうもん なん に します か
phrases.lemmaField: ご注文 何 に する か
phrases.translation: What [do you want to] order?
phrases.notes:
The prefix "go" makes chuumon more polite in this example. "o" and "go" are the only two prefixes used like this. I can't exactly tell you all the rules of when to use what and as always recommend to consume lots of materials. I will add good resources towards the end of the course.

Remark 1: In many cases, you can translate "ni suru" as "to decide on", see https://jlptsensei.com/learn-japanese-grammar/%E3%81%AB%E3%81%99%E3%82%8B-ni-suru-meaning/.
Remark 2: Here, we have "何にしますか/nan ni shimasu ka" and NOT "何しますか/nani shimasu ka" - note the different spelling of "nan", the pronunciation is also slightly different. In the first one, key grammar is nan ni suru - what do you decide on, in the second one, the grammar is nani wo suru with a dropped "wo"-particle - what do you want to do.

Don't worry about the details of Remark 2, "ni suru" is covered in more detail later.

phrases.reading: どこ に たべ に いく
phrases.lemmaField: どこ に 食べる に 行く
phrases.translation: Where do [you] go to eat?
phrases.notes:
tabe: stem of taberu (to eat)

Remember: The stem is retrieved by removing the "-masu" or teineigo ending. For a technically more correct way, refer to Tae Kim p. 76 or this website.

Verb stems (= special nouns) are mostly used together with "ni" or "he" + motion verb. I.e. the verb stem is the target of the motion verb. This can be translated as "to go (in order) to".

phrases.reading: きょう どこ み に いく
phrases.lemmaField: 今日 どこ 見る に 行く
phrases.translation: Today, where [do we] go to see [something, maybe a movie]?
phrases.notes:
Caution, this is a casual sentence, some particles are missing here.

Verb stems (= special nouns) are mostly used together with "ni" or "he" + motion verb. I.e. the verb stem is the target of the motion verb. This can be translated as "to go (in order) to".
phrases.source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure スターダストクルセイダース

phrases.reading: ぜったい み に いく ね
phrases.lemmaField: 絶対 見る に 行く ね
phrases.translation: Definitely go to see [it].
phrases.notes: mi: stem of miru (to see)

phrases.reading: み に いきません か
phrases.lemmaField: 見る に 行く か
phrases.translation: Shouldn't [we] go to see [something together]?

phrases.reading: なに し に いく の
phrases.lemmaField: 何 する に 行く の
phrases.translation: shi: stem of suru (to do)
phrases.notes:
This sentence is super interesting, because it's very hard to translate to English directly: "shi ni iku" means: "to go to do" or "to go in order to do". The speaker combines it with "nani/what" to ask something like: "what are you going to do"?

A more literal translation would be: [you] go in order to do what?

There's a show on Japanese TV called "you ha nani shi ni nihon he", which roughly translates to "why did you come to Japan?" It uses the same construction: As for you (you ha), came in order to do what?

phrases.reading: よび に いく
phrases.lemmaField: 呼ぶ に 行く
phrases.translation: [He] goes [there] to call [someone]?
phrases.notes: yobi: stem of yobu (to call)
phrases.source: ももへの手紙(A Letter to Momo)

phrases.reading: ‪こんど はなし に いく ‬
phrases.lemmaField: ‪今度 話す に 行く
phrases.translation: Next time [I] go to talk / have a conversation.
phrases.notes:
kondo: next time
hanashi: stem of hanasu (to talk)

phrases.reading: きょう のみ に いかない
phrases.lemmaField: 今日 飲む に 行く
phrases.translation: As for today (particle missing), don't [we] go in order to drink? -> Let's go out for a drink.
phrases.notes: nomi: stem of nomu (to drink)

phrases.reading: あそび に いく の
phrases.lemmaField: 遊び に 行く の
phrases.translation: [Do you] go to to visit [them] or just: Do you visit them?
phrases.notes:
asobi: verb stem of asobu (to play)

Literally, the sentence means: [Do you] go to play (with a desire for explanation due to "no"). However, the term "asobi ni iku" also means: "To go out on a trip" or "to go out to visit". Have a look at the dictionary if you like.

phrases.japanese: 今日はどこに遊びに行くかな
phrases.reading: きょう は どこ に あそび に いく か な
phrases.lemmaField: 今日 は どこ に 遊び に 行く か な
phrases.romaji: kyou ha doko ni asobi ni iku ka na
phrases.translation: As for today, [I] wonder where [I] should go out on a trip / go out to visit?
phrases.notes:
doko: where; what place

"ka na" can be translated as "I wonder".
phrases.source: Ore no Imouto ga konna ni Kawaii Wake ga Nai_

phrases.reading: なに を し に きた
phrases.lemmaField: 何 を する に くる
phrases.translation: [You] came [here] to do what? In English, you'd rather just say: Why did you come here?
phrases.notes:
shi: stem of suru
shi ni kuru: to come in order to do.

Remark: "nani wo shi ni kita" is past tense. It's used when person A already arrived and B wants to know what A came to do for. "nani wo shi ni kuru" is present tense. Since Japanese has no dedicated future, this is also used when A wants to come tomorrow, then B asks: Oh, you come tomorrow for doing what...?

phrases.japanese: 私ね今日謝りに来たの
phrases.reading: わたし ね きょう あやまり に きた の
phrases.lemmaField: 私 ね 今日 謝る に 来る の
phrases.romaji: watashi ne kyou ayamari ni kita no
phrases.translation: I today came to apologize.
phrases.notes:
ayamari: stem of ayamaru (to apologize)

Note that the "ne/ね" after watashi makes the sentence sound more feminine. Refer to this article for more details. I'll probably add more elaborate information on gender specific language later.

phrases.japanese: 私と友達にならないか
phrases.reading: わたし と ともだち に ならない か
phrases.lemmaField: 私 と 友達 に なる か
phrases.romaji: watashi to tomodachi ni naranai ka
phrases.translation: Don't [you] become friend with me?
phrases.source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure スターダストクルセイダース

phrases.reading: いま どこ に いる
phrases.lemmaField: 今 どこ に いる
phrases.translation: Where is [he] now?
phrases.notes: ima: now; the present time

phrases.reading: また おなじ ゆめ
phrases.lemmaField: また 同じ 夢
phrases.translation: Again, [the] same dream.
phrases.notes: onaji: same; identical; equal

phrases.reading: わたし も がんばる
phrases.lemmaField: 私 も 頑張る がんばれ
phrases.translation: I too do [my] best.
phrases.notes: ganbaru: to do one's best; to persist; to keep at it; to hang on

phrases.japanese: 頑張ることができたから
phrases.reading: がんばる こと が できた から
phrases.lemmaField: 頑張る こと が できる から
phrases.translation: As usual, a little bit of context is missing here, e.g. [I succeeded] because I could manage to do my best / keep at it.
phrases.notes:
ganbaru: to do one's best; to persist; to keep at it; to hang on

Note that Tae Kim covers "kara" later. It usually connects two sentences in the following fashion: Reason kara result, meaning: because of reason, result happened. If the result is clear from context, it is often omitted, just as in this example. I'll pick this up in more detail later.
phrases.source: Toaru Kagaku no Railgun S (Railgun S02, JP only)

phrases.reading: もんだい ありません ね
phrases.lemmaField: 問題 ある ね
phrases.translation: There is no problem [with something clear from context].
phrases.notes: mondai: problem (e.g. societal, political); question; issue

phrases.reading: しごと の じかん だ
phrases.lemmaField: 仕事 の 時間 だ
phrases.translation: It's the hour/time of work -> It's time for work.
phrases.notes: shigoto: work; job; business

phrases.reading: おれ に も なまえ が ある
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 に も 名前 が ある
phrases.romaji: ore ni mo namae ga aru
phrases.translation: I also have a name (maybe someone didn't call the speaker by his name).
phrases.notes:
namae: name

Remark: The key grammar point here is: x ni y ga aru. Or, as Tae Kim explained it: "ni" sets the preceding word as target of something (namae ga aru in this case). In casual Japanese, you could omit the "ni". I wasn't sure of this, but a native speaker confirmed this.

phrases.reading: こんど は わたし が たすける
phrases.lemmaField: 今度 は 私 が 助ける
phrases.translation: Next time I will help you.
phrases.notes:
tasukeru: to save; to rescue / to help; to assist

Remark: "kondo" can mean both next time and this time, which I found a bit confusing. See ref.

phrases.reading: おれ は はずかしい よ
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 は 恥ずかしい よ
phrases.translation: hazukashii: embarrassing; embarrassed

phrases.japanese: 全然恥ずかしいことじゃないですよ
phrases.reading: ぜんぜん はずかしい こと じゃない です よ
phrases.lemmaField: 全然 恥ずかしい こと じゃ です よ
phrases.romaji: zenzen hazukashii koto janai desu yo
phrases.translation: [Something] is totally not an embarassing thing.
phrases.source: 下ネタという概念が存在しない退屈な世界 (uncensored)

phrases.reading: おかね は ある
phrases.lemmaField: お金 は ある
phrases.translation: [Do you] have money? Literally: As for money, is it there?
phrases.notes:
okane: money

Here's the teneigo prefix again: "o". In this case I think it became more common to say "okane" instead of just "kane".

phrases.reading: おかね なくなった
phrases.lemmaField: お金 なくなる
phrases.translation: [I] used up [my / the] money. Note again that this is informal speech, there's a particle missing (e.g. a "ga" after okane).
phrases.notes: nakunaru: to be used up; to be missing

phrases.reading: めいわく な はなし だ
phrases.lemmaField: 迷惑 だ 話 だ
phrases.translation: [This] is an annoying conversation.
phrases.notes: meiwaku: trouble; bother; annoyance

phrases.reading: まいにち み に くる ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: 毎日 見る に 来る ん だ
phrases.romaji: mainichi mi ni kuru n da
phrases.translation: [I] come daily to watch (in an explanatory tone).
phrases.notes: mainichi: daily
phrases.source: Higurashi no Naku Koro ni S1 (JP Eng)

phrases.reading: いえ は ちかい の
phrases.lemmaField: 家 は 近い の
phrases.translation: As for [your] house [is it] close?
phrases.notes: chikai: near; close; short (distance & in time)

phrases.reading: それ が わたし の ゆめ
phrases.lemmaField: それ が 私 の 夢
phrases.translation:
that [it] my dream [hitting my resignment right in the face of my boss].
sore: that; it (indicates closeness to the listener and may refer to almost everything: Object, person or something on the listener's mind)
phrases.notes:
Note the similarity to socchi/sochira, which referred to a direction.

Remark: the "ga" sounds very much like "ha" here, don't worry about it. If you want to check the context: Aggretsuko, S1, E2, 13:30

phrases.reading: それ は わたし も おなじ です
phrases.lemmaField: それ は 私 も 同じ です
phrases.romaji: sore ha watashi mo onaji desu
phrases.translation: As for that [on your mind], same here -> I agree with you and think the same about it.
phrases.notes: sore: that; it (indicates closeness to the listener and may refer to almost everything: Object, person or something on the listener's mind)

phrases.reading: それ は なに
phrases.lemmaField: それ は 何
phrases.translation: As for that [close to listener], what? -> What is that?
phrases.notes: sore: that; it (indicates closeness to the listener and may refer to almost everything: Object, person or something on the listener's mind)
phrases.source: Boku no Hero Academia S2 (ep 1-25 jp_en)

phrases.reading: わたし は それ を うしなった
phrases.lemmaField: 私 は それ を 失う
phrases.translation: As for me, [I] lost it. What was lost can be an item the listener still has or for example faith (they seem to be in space, after all).

phrases.reading: これ は なに
phrases.lemmaField: これ は 何
phrases.translation: Note the similarity to kocchi/kochira, which referred to a direction.
phrases.grammarNote: Have a look at the picture. What's lying on the bench?
phrases.notes: kore: this; it (indicates closeness to the speaker and may refer to almost everything: Object, person or something on the speaker's mind)

phrases.reading: これ は おれ の もんだい
phrases.lemmaField: これ は 俺 の 問題
phrases.translation: As for this, [it is] my problem / task to solve.

phrases.reading: これ は おれ の もの だ
phrases.lemmaField: これ は 俺 の もの だ
phrases.romaji: kore ha ore no mono da
phrases.translation: As for this, [it is] my thing/object/item.

phrases.reading: あれ は なに
phrases.lemmaField: あれ は 何
phrases.translation: In this sentence, the two might be talking about strange behavior of someone else: "What's that supposed to mean?"
phrases.notes: are: that; that thing (indicates distance to both speaker and listener and may refer to almost everything: Object, person or something on someone's mind)

phrases.reading: あれ は いもうと
phrases.lemmaField: あれ は 妹
phrases.translation: That over there, [your] younger sister? -> Is that your sister over there?
phrases.notes: Remark: Here, the guy is really talking about someone else's sister. Most resources teach that you'd rather use "imoutosan" here, but this is a casual conversation among friends and anime, after all.

phrases.reading: あれ は いぬ
phrases.lemmaField: あれ は 犬
phrases.translation: As for that over there, a dog?!

phrases.reading: せんせい の おかげ です
phrases.lemmaField: 先生 の おかげ です
phrases.translation: [Something] is the teacher's help / influence. -> This means that e.g. something worked out well thanks to the teacher's help.
phrases.notes: okage: assistance; help / effect, influence

phrases.japanese: さあごはんできましたよ
phrases.reading: さあ ごはん できました よ
phrases.lemmaField: さあ ごはん できる よ
phrases.translation: Food is ready.
phrases.notes:
gohan: cooked rice, meal -> cooked rice is so important in Japanese, that the word for it is used for describing an entire meal
dekiru: besides to do / to be able to / to be ready

phrases.reading: おみまい に きた よ
phrases.lemmaField: お見舞い に 来る よ
phrases.translation: omimai: calling on / visiting someone who is ill

phrases.japanese: 皆さんこっちに来ましたよ
phrases.reading: みなさん こっち に きました よ
phrases.lemmaField: 皆さん こっち に 来る よ
phrases.translation: Everybody came over here (towards the speaker).

phrases.reading: なんで ここ に きた の
phrases.lemmaField: なんで ここ に 来る の
phrases.translation: Why did [you] come here?

phrases.japanese: 大丈夫ですか佐藤先生
phrases.reading: だいじょうぶ です か さとう せんせい
phrases.lemmaField: 大丈夫 です か 佐藤 先生
phrases.translation: Are [you] ok, satou-sensei?
phrases.notes:
sensei (teacher) is an example for referring to someone by their title or position. It can be used to "just" refer to a teacher - just as in English. In Japanese however, you can use it to directly address your teacher in a polite way. It acknowledges the teacher's (higher) position.

In this example, the speaker directly addresses his teacher with the name (satou), sensei is used as suffix.

phrases.reading: せんせい は おうえん します
phrases.lemmaField: 先生 は 応援 する
phrases.translation: The teacher helps / supports [us].
phrases.notes:
ouen: aid; assistance; help. Also: to cheer someone up.

Here's the true context (which is a bit harder to understand than the above translation):
[Please don't join the demons. Let's start over again together] I will help you [the speaker is the teacher and she is referring to herself in 3rd person. This is covered in more detail throughout the deck, don't worry if you don't get it right away]. As usual in Japanese, it depends on the context ;).

phrases.reading: あの たかはし せんせい は
phrases.lemmaField: あの 高橋 先生 は あの人
phrases.translation: ano: say; well (filler word)
phrases.notes: This sentence is again ambiguous without context. Just as in the last example, the speaker could be directly addressing her teacher with the name (takahashi) + suffix, meaning: As for you, takahashi-sensei... what are you doing tonight? However, she can also use this to talk about takahashi sensei with someone else in a polite way.

phrases.reading: ひさしぶり だ な せんせい
phrases.lemmaField: 久しぶり だ な 先生
phrases.translation: It's been a while, teacher!
phrases.notes:
