hisashiburi: a long time (since the last time. Mostly used as phrase when meeting someone not seen for a while, e.g. "long time no see").

Here, the teacher ist directly addressed without using the name.

phrases.japanese: 高橋先生いい人だったな
phrases.reading: たかはし せんせい いい ひと だった な
phrases.lemmaField: 高橋 先生 いい 人 だ な
phrases.romaji: takahashi sensei ii hito datta na
phrases.translation: Takahashi-sensei was a good person, wasn't he?

phrases.japanese: 私が部長だから私が書く
phrases.reading: わたし が ぶちょう だ から わたし が かく
phrases.lemmaField: 私 が 部長 だ から 私 が 書く
phrases.romaji: watashi ga buchou da kara watashi ga kaku
phrases.translation: Because I am the head of the club, I write [it] down. (They are talking about the sheet of paper on the image. It's a "bukatsu shinsei youshi" - application form for extracurricular activities, and the head of the club wants to fill it out herself for some reason.
phrases.notes: buchou: head of a (school) club; it also means "head (chief, director) of a section or department", but in school anime, you'll hear this sometimes.

phrases.japanese: はいはっ失礼します部長
phrases.reading: はい はっしつれい します ぶちょう
phrases.lemmaField: はい はっ する 部長
phrases.translation: "shitsurei shimasu" in this sentence is a polite way to say goodbye to his boss (buchou), in this case probably because the speaker leaves work earlier than the others. It can also mean "excuse me".
phrases.notes: shitsurei: discourtesy; impoliteness​
phrases.source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure ダイヤモンドは砕けない

phrases.reading: ふじみや さん
phrases.lemmaField: 藤宮 さん
phrases.translation: -san: Suffix for mostly names adding politeness.
phrases.notes: It's similar to addressing someone with mr. or mrs. in English, but not the same. Here, the guy e.g. talks to a girl in school - you'd rather not address her with mrs. in English. An interesting explanation is found on quora (see reference link).

phrases.reading: みなさん こんにちは
phrases.lemmaField: 皆さん こんにちは
phrases.translation: -san can also be added to other words than just names. In this case to "minna" to address everyone in a polite way.

phrases.japanese: 大丈夫お父さん怖くないぞ
phrases.reading: だいじょうぶ おとうさん こわくない ぞ
phrases.lemmaField: 大丈夫 お父さん 怖い ぞ
phrases.translation: It's ok, [I] am not scared. -> The father is referring to himself in third person. He's dissecting a fish to prepare it for a meal in front of his very young daughter, and he is reassuring her that she shouldn't be afraid because he is not. But actually, he is!
phrases.notes: Note that "kowai" is an adjective, but it means both scary and scared. Have a look at the reference.

phrases.reading: ひめ は しんだ
phrases.lemmaField: 姫 は 死ぬ
phrases.translation: As for the princess, [she] died.
phrases.notes: hime: princess

phrases.reading: だいじょうぶ です か ひめさま
phrases.lemmaField: 大丈夫 です か 姫様
phrases.translation: Are [you] ok, princess?
phrases.notes: -sama: a politer version of "-san", more on this (honorific) language later. I wanted to add this here, because you'll hear versions of this every once in a while in anime.

phrases.reading: きれい な おひめさま
phrases.lemmaField: きれい だ お姫様
phrases.translation: A pretty princess.
phrases.notes: ohimesama: an even more respectful / honorific way to address the princess. All three versions (hime, himesama, ohimesama) are also found in the dictionary. Interestingly, this version also ironically refers to a spoiled girl ;).

phrases.reading: きょう は つかれた
phrases.lemmaField: 今日 は 疲れる
phrases.translation: tsukareru: to get tired; to tire; to get fatigued; to become exhausted

phrases.japanese: 休憩疲れましたね疲れた
phrases.reading: きゅうけい つかれました ね つかれた
phrases.lemmaField: 休憩 疲れる ね 疲れる
phrases.translation: Break! I got tired.
phrases.notes:
kyuukei: break, rest

These two seem to be tired from playing table tennis. Do you remember the verb stem? Just omit the "-masu/-mashita" part and you'll get a noun to be used for some specific cases. Do it for tsukareru/tsukaremashita now and then have a look at the next cards.

phrases.reading: おつかれ
phrases.lemmaField: お疲れ 疲れ おつかれ
phrases.translation:
otsukare: goodbye (especially after some work was done together, casual)
BUT ALSO: A casual "hi" --> check the answers on japanese stackexchange.
phrases.notes:
wasabi-jpn writes: "Since it cannot be translated because of the wide context, people consider it very difficult".
I'd say most of the time, this is means "goodbye" after some joint effort, but is also used as greeting. This will be covered again later in videos by native speakers, so try not to worry too much for now.

The origin is interesting: It's the verb stem plus "o"-prefix of "tsukareru - to become tired". I have no idea how to translate this into English, a literal translation would be: "The honored tiredness" or something.

phrases.reading: おつかれさま です
phrases.lemmaField: おつかれさま です お疲れ様 お疲れさま
phrases.translation: Thank you for your efforts (phrase often used as goodbye at the office)
phrases.notes:
"otsukare / sama" is complicated, check the answers on japanese stackexchange.

wasabi-jpn writes: "Since it cannot be translated because of the wide context, people consider it very difficult".
I'd say most of the time, this is means "goodbye" after some joint effort, but is also used as greeting. This will be covered again later in videos by native speakers, so try not to worry too much for now.

phrases.reading: ぱんだ くん
phrases.lemmaField: パンダ くん
phrases.translation: -kun: Usually used for addressing males of equal or lower status. You'll hear this a lot in school anime. Wikipedia however states, that it "is generally used by people of senior status addressing or referring to those of junior status".
phrases.notes:
The panda in this example sentence is always hanging out at the polar bear's cafe and the person speaking belongs to the staff.

I'd highly recommend this anime (Shirokuma cafe) for Japanese learners by the way, it's easier to understand than others.

phrases.japanese: 香織ちゃんこんにちは
phrases.reading: かおり ちゃん こんにちは
phrases.lemmaField: 香織 ちゃん こんにちは
phrases.translation: -chan: cute suffix for a familiar person, sounds a bit girlish
phrases.notes: "kaori" is the first name of the girl with the red hair. In this series, the small girl usually addresses her in a familiar and cute way. I also found this anime quite easy to understand by the way.

phrases.reading: はい ひろえ せんぱい
phrases.lemmaField: はい ヒロエ 先輩
phrases.translation: -senpai: used to address or refer to one's older or more senior colleagues in a school, workplace, dojo or sports club. Teachers are not senpai, but sensei (from wikipedia).

phrases.reading: あなた の おかげ です
phrases.lemmaField: あなた の おかげ です
phrases.translation: [Something good] is [thanks to] your assistance, help.
phrases.notes:
anata: you

So finally, after 500+ cards, a word for "you". It is important to realize that this is used in a very different way than the English "you" and can easily sound rude. By now you should be aware of the fact that pronouns are usually omitted in Japanese. The entire thing with pronouns being rude is explained in more detail here. Note that it's not automatically rude to use "anata", but explaining this is beyond the scope of this course. As always: Listen to many examples!

phrases.reading: きみ に はなし が ある
phrases.lemmaField: 君 に 話 が ある
phrases.translation: [I] need to talk to you!
phrases.notes: kimi: another word for "you", mostly used by men toward people of lower status. You'll hear this a lot in anime. I think it's rarely used in real life.

phrases.reading: きみ の あいて は ぼく だ
phrases.lemmaField: 君 の 相手 は 僕 だ
phrases.romaji: kimi no aite ha boku da
phrases.translation: [I] am your ally / partner.
phrases.notes: Explanation by a Japanese person from the discussion on quora: "Usually bosses can call lower rank person "kimi" or family name with "-kun" to male employees" - just as in this example...

phrases.japanese: お前はなぜ来なかった
phrases.reading: おまえ は なぜ こなかった
phrases.lemmaField: お前 は なぜ 来る
phrases.translation: As for you, why didn't [you] come?
phrases.notes:
omae: very casual, rough way to say "you".
naze: why

You'll hear this in anime a lot, it's not automatically rude, but more casual than "anata". You'd better avoid using this in a conversation unless you're really sure what you're saying.

phrases.reading: てめえ の せい だ
phrases.lemmaField: てめえ の せい だ
phrases.translation: [Everything is] your fault!
phrases.notes:
temee: derogatory "you".

Again, you'll sometimes hear this in anime, but never use it in a conversation - it's unfriendly by definition and rather used to cause trouble or insult someone.

phrases.reading: きさま なに を する
phrases.lemmaField: 貴様 何 を する
phrases.translation: What are you doing, you bastard!
phrases.notes:
kisama: you; you bastard; you son of a bitch

Another very unfriendly "you", you'll sometimes hear this in anime.

phrases.japanese: 春原妹さんから電話よ
phrases.reading: すのはら いもうとさん から でんわ よ
phrases.lemmaField: 春原 妹さん から 電話 よ
phrases.translation: "Sunohara, call from [your] younger sister".
phrases.notes: imouto: younger sister (+ san here)

phrases.japanese: でも私はいい姉じゃなかった
phrases.reading: でも わたし は いい あね じゃなかった
phrases.lemmaField: でも 私 は いい 姉 じゃ
phrases.romaji: demo watashi ha ii ane janakatta
phrases.translation: ...but as for me, [I] wasn't [a] good older sister.
phrases.notes: ane: older sister

phrases.japanese: 今日はありがとうお姉さん
phrases.reading: きょう は ありがとう おねえさん
phrases.lemmaField: 今日 は ありがとう お姉さん
phrases.translation: oneesan: more polite way to refer to one's older sister. It also means "young lady" or "miss", which might sound confusing sometimes.

phrases.reading: ぼく の あに だ よ
phrases.lemmaField: 僕 の 兄 だ よ
phrases.translation: [Who is this person over there?] It's my older brother.
phrases.notes: ani: older brother

phrases.reading: わたし の あに です よ
phrases.lemmaField: 私 の 兄 です よ
phrases.translation: [Who is this over there?] It's my older brother.

phrases.reading: せんせい の おにいさん
phrases.lemmaField: 先生 の お兄さん
phrases.translation: oniisan: more polite way for one's older brother
phrases.source: さよなら絶望先生 (Sayonara, Zetsubou-Sensei)

phrases.reading: おれ の おとうと は にんげん だ
phrases.lemmaField: オレ の 弟 は 人間 だ
phrases.romaji: ore no otouto ha ningen da
phrases.translation: My younger brother is a human [the younger brother lost his body, and his soul is bound to a piece of armor, so he does not seem "human"].
phrases.notes: otouto: younger brother

phrases.japanese: ハニー先輩の弟さんだよ
phrases.reading: はにー せんぱい の おとうとさん だ よ
phrases.lemmaField: ハニー 先輩 の 弟さん だ よ
phrases.romaji: hani- senpai no otoutosan da yo
phrases.translation: otoutosan: younger brother (polite)
phrases.source: Ouran High School Host Club (jp eng)

phrases.reading: かれ は すごい な
phrases.lemmaField: 彼 は すごい な
phrases.translation: He's great, I tell you!
phrases.notes:
kare: he

It's also possible to refer to others in third person, but as you might have guessed already: It's rather uncommon. Just as the other pronouns (I, you), "he" and "she" are almost never used like they are used in English. Most of the time, they are omitted. Only if it is not clear who's being talked about, they are sometimes used.

So if you omit "kare ha" in this sentence for example, the remaining "sugoi na" just means that something is great. However, the speaker might refer to the person standing behind him, doesn't know his name and thus adds "kare ha".

phrases.reading: かれ を ころす の
phrases.lemmaField: 彼 を 殺す の
phrases.translation: [You want to] kill him? (with a tone asking for explanation).

phrases.reading: かのじょ は いない です ね
phrases.lemmaField: 彼女 は いる です ね
phrases.translation: kanojo: she (or girlfriend)
phrases.notes: We already had the female counterpart to "kare" on earlier cards, it's "kanojo" and in this sentence, "she is not here".

phrases.reading: かのじょ は かわしま あみ
phrases.lemmaField: 彼女 は 川嶋 亜美
phrases.translation: The speaker introduces the person accompanying him as "kawashima ami". Note that ami is her first name, in Japanese the names are often mentioned or introduced lastname-first. This also matches the way to address people: If you would address ami directly, you'd probably say "kawashima-san".

phrases.reading: かれし は います か
phrases.lemmaField: 彼氏 は いる か
phrases.translation: [Do you] have a boyfriend?
phrases.notes:
kareshi: boyfriend

The same way kanojo means "she" and "girlfriend", kare means "he" and "boyfriend". However, "kareshi" is used as word for boyfriend more often. This sentence means: Do [you] have a boyfriend? Literally: As for boyfriend, is [he] there?
phrases.source: Terrace House- Boys & Girls in the City

phrases.japanese: でも会うのは今日が最後だ
phrases.reading: でも あう の は きょう が さいご だ
phrases.lemmaField: でも 会う の は 今日 が 最後 だ
phrases.romaji: demo au no ha kyou ga saigo da
phrases.translation: But as for meeting [him], today is last time.
phrases.notes:
au: to meet; to encounter; to see
saigo: end, conclusion (from previous card) and also last; final (this card).

phrases.japanese: そして僕は彼女の息子に会った
phrases.reading: そして ぼく は かのじょ の むすこ に あった
phrases.lemmaField: そして 僕 は 彼女 の 息子 に 会う
phrases.romaji: soshite boku ha kanojo no musuko ni atta
phrases.translation: And as for me, [I] met her son.
phrases.notes:
musuko: son
atta: past tense of au (to meet; to encounter; to see). Remark: "atta" is also the past of "aru". In written Japanese they are easily distinguished by the kanji, but in spoken Japanese it's the context that will help you.

phrases.japanese: 息子さんの仕事仲間です
phrases.reading: むすこさん の しごと なかま です
phrases.lemmaField: 息子さん の 仕事 仲間 です
phrases.translation: [Someone] is the work comrade of [someone's] son.
phrases.notes:
Even though you don't know the context here, the use of "san" tells you that the speaker is most likely referring to someone else's son. Interesting is also the use of "shigoto nakama". In Japanese, you can chain nouns together without particle, if they form one logical entity. The same thing is possible e.g. in German, but in Japanese it is not used that often. The explanation for this is well hidden in Tae Kim's book: P. 59 or this section.

Keep in mind, that Japanese has no whitespaces, so "shigoto nakama" is actually one word.

phrases.reading: むすめ を たのむ
phrases.lemmaField: 娘 を 頼む
phrases.translation: [Please] take care of [my] daughter. Or more literally: "I commend my daughter to you". This is the real context here (FMA brotherhood, episode 30, 3:20).
phrases.notes:
Depending on the context, this can also mean: Ask [my / someone's] daughter (in order to do something, not to answer a question. Asking a question requires a different word introduced after about 200 cards).

If this is too weird, only try to remember "musume"!

musume: daughter
tanomu: to entrust to (in addition to to request; to beg; to ask)

phrases.japanese: その意味がよく分かりました
phrases.reading: その いみ が よく わかりました
phrases.lemmaField: その 意味 が よく 分かる
phrases.translation: [I] well understood that meaning or less literal: I understood the significance [of something] well.
phrases.notes: sono: that; the (distant from the speaker, close to the listener, follows the same pattern as sore/socchi/sochira)

phrases.reading: その りす かわいい ね
phrases.lemmaField: その リス かわいい ね
phrases.translation:
risu: squirrel
sono: that; the (distant from the speaker, close to the listener, follows the same pattern as sore/socchi/sochira)

phrases.reading: その おとこ の なまえ よ
phrases.lemmaField: その 男 の 名前 よ
phrases.translation: [This is] the name of that guy.
phrases.notes: sono: that; the (distant from the speaker, close to the listener, follows the same pattern as sore/socchi/sochira)

phrases.reading: その はなし を し に きた
phrases.lemmaField: その 話 を する に 来る
phrases.romaji: sono hanashi wo shi ni kita
phrases.translation: I came to talk about that (topic the listener would like to talk about) or more literal: [I] came to do that conversation.
phrases.notes: sono: that; the (distant from the speaker, close to the listener, follows the same pattern as sore/socchi/sochira)

phrases.japanese: この学校は好きですか
phrases.reading: この がっこう は すき です か
phrases.lemmaField: この 学校 は 好き です か
phrases.romaji: kono gakkou ha suki desu ka
phrases.translation: As for this school [do you] like it? The listener probably transferred from a different school to the speaker's and the speaker wants to know if the listener likes it.
phrases.notes: kono: this (close to the speaker, distant to the listener, follows the same pattern as kore/kocchi/kochira)

phrases.reading: なに この ねこ
phrases.lemmaField: 何 この 猫
phrases.translation: What's up with this cat?
phrases.notes: kono: this (close to the speaker, distant to the listener, follows the same pattern as kore/kocchi/kochira)

phrases.reading: この もんだい わかる ひと
phrases.lemmaField: この 問題 分かる 人
phrases.translation: Another nice example for a clause: The teacher is asking for people, who understand this problem (i.e. "kono mondai (wo) wakaru" is a clause describing "hito"). They should probably come to the board and write down the answer.
phrases.notes: kono: this (close to the speaker, distant to the listener, follows the same pattern as kore/kocchi/kochira)

phrases.japanese: あのマンションですね
phrases.reading: あの まんしょん です ね
phrases.lemmaField: あの マンション です ね
phrases.translation: [A: Where does he live? B: ] It's that apartment building [over there].
phrases.notes: While a "mansion" is a large, luxurious house in English, "manshon" means apartment building in Japanese.

phrases.japanese: この時間がとても好き
phrases.reading: この じかん が とても すき
phrases.lemmaField: この 時間 が とても 好き
phrases.translation: As for this hour/time of the day, [I] like it very much.

phrases.reading: あの こと は わすれない
phrases.lemmaField: あの こと は 忘れる
phrases.translation: As for that thing/matter, don't forget.
phrases.notes:
ano: that (distant to both speaker and listener, follows the same pattern as are/acchi/achira)

We already had "ano" as filler, meaning "say; well; um; er" at the beginning of a sentence.

phrases.japanese: あの男は人間じゃない
phrases.reading: あの おとこ は にんげん じゃない
phrases.lemmaField: あの 男 は 人間 じゃ
phrases.translation: As for that guy over there, [he] is not human.
phrases.notes: ano: that (distant to both speaker and listener, follows the same pattern as are/acchi/achira)

phrases.reading: あの ゆめ は それ か
phrases.lemmaField: あの 夢 は それ か
phrases.translation: As for that dream [I had a while ago], is it that [what you just explained]?
phrases.notes: That's an interesting sentence using both ano and sore, if it doesn't make sense without context, just skip it.

phrases.japanese: 私あの勝負に勝ちましたの
phrases.reading: わたくし あの しょうぶ に かちました の
phrases.lemmaField: 私 あの 勝負 に 勝つ の
phrases.romaji: watakushi ano shoubu ni kachimashita no
phrases.translation: I won that battle/competition (in an explanatory tone). E.g. why are you so happy? Because I won that competition.
phrases.notes:
kachimashita: polite past tense of katsu - to win.
shoubu: battle / competition
watakushi: slightly more formal and feminine version of "watashi"
phrases.source: 下ネタという概念が存在しない退屈な世界 (uncensored)

phrases.reading: あの ね うえはら くん
phrases.lemmaField: あの ね 上原 君
phrases.translation: It's a colloquial phase you'll hear quite often. -kun fits here too as it's used to address males of rather lower status. I just added this because of the "ano"-context here ;).
phrases.notes: ano ne; look here; I say; well (familiar language)

phrases.reading: わたし もう いきます ね
phrases.lemmaField: 私 もう 行く ね
phrases.translation: I go now.
phrases.notes: mou: now; soon; shortly

phrases.japanese: 俺はもう家に帰るんだから
phrases.reading: おれ は もう いえ に かえる ん だ から
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 は もう 家 に 帰る ん だ から
phrases.romaji: ore ha mou ie ni kaeru n da kara
phrases.translation: The speaker doesn't want the kids to follow him and gives the reason: "[Don't follow me] because as for me, [I] now/soon return home".
phrases.notes:
mou: now; soon; shortly

Note that Tae Kim covers "kara" later. It usually connects two sentences in the following fashion: Reason kara result, meaning: because of reason, result happened. If the result is clear from context, it is often omitted, just as in this example. I'll pick this up in more detail later.

phrases.reading: これ は もう みました
phrases.lemmaField: これ は もう 見る
phrases.translation: As for this [I] already saw it.
phrases.notes: mou also means: already; yet

phrases.reading: いつも おなじ ゆめ を みる
phrases.lemmaField: いつも 同じ 夢 を 見る
phrases.translation: [I] always dream the same dream.
phrases.notes:
itsumo: always; usually; every time

The "ru" is cut off unfortunately, This happens sometimes due to inaccurate timings of the subtitles use for creating the deck.

phrases.reading: ぱんだ くん いつも の
phrases.lemmaField: パンダ くん いつも の
phrases.translation: The speaker works at the polarbear's cafe and asks the panda (regular guest): "The same as always"?
phrases.notes: itsumo: always; usually; every time

phrases.japanese: お前はいつも強くない
phrases.reading: おまえ は いつも つよくない
phrases.lemmaField: お前 は いつも 強い
phrases.translation: As for you (rough) [you are] never strong. Literally, this reads: always not strong, but in English you'd say "never strong".
phrases.notes: itsumo: never (with negative verb)

phrases.reading: とうきょう の だいがく に いく
phrases.lemmaField: 東京 の 大学 に 行く
phrases.translation: [I] go to Tokyo university.
phrases.notes: daigaku: university; college

phrases.reading: ぼく の だいがく の ともだち です
phrases.lemmaField: 僕 の 大学 の 友達 です
phrases.romaji: boku no daigaku no tomodachi desu
phrases.translation: [These people] are my college friends.
phrases.notes:
daigaku: university; college

Note the chain of two "no" here, it's quite common to do this.

phrases.reading: とくべつ な ともだち
phrases.lemmaField: 特別 だ 友達
phrases.translation: [Someone] is a special friend.
phrases.notes: tokubetsu: special; particular; extraordinary

phrases.reading: とくべつ な としょかん
phrases.lemmaField: 特別 だ 図書館
phrases.translation: [This is] a special library.
phrases.notes: tokubetsu: special; particular; extraordinary

phrases.japanese: それは僕にはできない特別なことだ
phrases.reading: それ は ぼく に は できない とくべつ な こと だ
phrases.lemmaField: それ は 僕 に は できる 特別 だ こと だ
phrases.romaji: sore ha boku ni ha dekinai tokubetsu na koto da
phrases.translation: As for that, it's a special thing I'm not able to do.
phrases.notes:
The sentence is a bit more difficult, "boku ni ha dekinai" is a clause describing "tokubetsu na koto".

The "ni ha" emphasizes, that "boku" is the one not being able to do the "tokubetsu na koto", have a look at the references. However, you can also just ignore it for now ;).

phrases.reading: しつもん が あります
phrases.lemmaField: 質問 が ある
phrases.translation: Question is there -> I have a question.
phrases.notes: shitsumon: question

phrases.reading: でも かのじょ は うつくしい
phrases.lemmaField: でも 彼女 は 美しい
phrases.translation: utsukushii: beautiful; pretty; lovely

phrases.reading: じぶん の せい だ ね
phrases.lemmaField: 自分 の せい だ ね
phrases.translation: jibun: myself; yourself; oneself
phrases.notes: The dictionary definition of jibun might read weird, but I found it always easy to understand from context what it refers to. It always means "someone self", the someone can be anyone clear from context. So in this sentence: [something] is [someone's] own fault.

phrases.japanese: お前と戦うつもりはない
phrases.reading: おまえ と たたかう つもり は ない
phrases.lemmaField: お前 と 戦う つもり は ない
phrases.romaji: omae to tatakau tsumori ha nai
phrases.translation: tsumori: intention; plan
phrases.notes: "tsumori" is a noun very often used together with a relative clause, just as in this sentence: As for "fight-with-you"-intention, not there. Or less literal: I don't have the intention to fight with you.

phrases.japanese: 分かるかはい分かるつもりです
phrases.reading: わかる か はい わかる つもり です
phrases.lemmaField: 分かる か はい 分かる つもり です
phrases.romaji: wakaru ka hai wakaru tsumori desu
phrases.translation:
Person A: [Do you] understand?
Person B: Yes, [I] assume/think [I] understand.
phrases.notes:
So obviously, B doesn't yet understand it.

tsumori: intention; plan; but also: belief, assumtion, thus "I assume/think".
phrases.source: Legend of the Galactic Heroes (JP Eng) (Media Added)

phrases.japanese: 今度は何するつもりですか
phrases.reading: こんど は なに する つもり です か
phrases.lemmaField: 今度 は 何 する つもり です か
phrases.romaji: kondo ha nani suru tsumori desu ka
phrases.translation: What are [we] going to do this time? Or literally: As for this time, what-do intention is it?
phrases.notes: kondo: this time; now OR next time (I always found kondo a bit weird because of this ambiguous definition, but it's usually clear from context what it means).
phrases.source: 下ネタという概念が存在しない退屈な世界 (uncensored)

phrases.japanese: 何をするつもりですの
phrases.reading: なに を する つもり です の
phrases.lemmaField: 何 を する つもり です の
phrases.romaji: nani wo suru tsumori desu no
phrases.translation: The speaker wants to know what the others are up to and asks literally: "what-do intention is it" in a tone looking for explanation.
phrases.source: Toaru Kagaku no Railgun S (Railgun S02, JP only)

phrases.reading: わたし に は むり ね
phrases.lemmaField: 私 に は 無理 ね
phrases.translation: [Something] is impossible for me.
phrases.notes: muri: impossible; unreasonable
phrases.source: The World God Only Knows S3 (jp eng)

phrases.reading: むり な もの は むり よ
phrases.lemmaField: 無理 だ もの は 無理 よ
phrases.romaji: muri na mono ha muri yo
phrases.translation: An impossible thing is, well... impossible (it seems like the guy wants to do something the girl considers hard or unreasonable).

phrases.japanese: そして僕はもうあの夢を見ることもなくなった
phrases.reading: そして ぼく は もう あの ゆめ を みる こと も なくなった
phrases.lemmaField: そして 僕 は もう あの 夢 を 見る こと も なくなる
phrases.romaji: soshite boku ha mou ano yume wo miru koto mo nakunatta
phrases.translation: ...and as for me, [I] already stopped having that dream.
phrases.grammarNote: Nothing new here, just a long sentence. If it's too difficult yet, delete the card.
phrases.notes: Reminder: In Japanese, dreaming is expressed as "seeing a dream".

phrases.reading: いつ まで いる ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: いつ まで いる ん だ
phrases.translation: Until when are [you] there?
phrases.notes: itsu: when; at what time; how soon

phrases.reading: いつ から なくなった
phrases.lemmaField: いつ から なくなる
phrases.translation: Since when did [your glasses] disappear [the listener has lost his glasses and the speaker wants to know when he lost them]?
phrases.notes: itsu: when; at what time; how soon

phrases.reading: いつ から いく の
phrases.lemmaField: いつ から 行く の
phrases.translation: Since when [do you] go [somewhere]?
phrases.notes:
itsu: when; at what time; how soon

Somewhere can again be almost everything: Work, a language class, etc.
phrases.source: Terrace House-Boys x Girls Next Door

phrases.reading: なに が すき だ
phrases.lemmaField: 何 が 好き だ
phrases.translation: What [do you] like?
phrases.notes: nani/nan/何: what (pronunciation depends a bit on the context)

phrases.reading: な なん です か
phrases.lemmaField: な 何 です か
phrases.translation: What is it? (Maybe the guy was staring at the girl).
phrases.notes:
nani/nan/何: what

Note that the question word for "what" is spelled "何" in native Japanese. The pronunciation is ambiguous, sometimes it's "nani", sometimes it's "nan".

phrases.reading: だれ の せい だ だれ が わるい
phrases.lemmaField: 誰 の せい だ 誰 が 悪い
phrases.romaji: dare no sei da dare ga warui
phrases.translation: Whose fault is [it], who [is] at fault
phrases.notes:
dare: who

Note that the adjective "warui" generally means "bad", but can also mean "at fault".

phrases.reading: どこ に いく つもり だ
phrases.lemmaField: どこ に 行く つもり だ
phrases.translation: Where do [you] intend to go?
phrases.notes:
doko: where

Again, a nice example for a verb clause: "doko ni iku" describes "tsumori", so literally: Where go-intention it is?

phrases.reading: どれ が いい
phrases.lemmaField: どれ が いい
phrases.translation: Which [one] is good? (E.g. when choosing something at the supermarket).
phrases.notes: dore: which
phrases.source: Sakurasou no Pet na Kanojo (jp eng)

phrases.japanese: どれくらい大きいんだ
phrases.reading: どれ くらい おおきい ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: どれ くらい 大きい ん だ
phrases.translation: How big is [it] approximately?
phrases.notes:
kurai: approximately; about (note that this also means "dark, gloomy"). In some cases, it is spelled "gurai". You'll face this "softening" of characters often, I'll cover this in more detail on another card.

Maybe a monster or something.

Remark: "dore" means "which". But especially when used together with "gurai", it rather translates to "how" (long/far/big...), have a look at the reference.

phrases.reading: いくら だ
phrases.lemmaField: いくら だ
phrases.translation: How much [is it / something]?
phrases.notes: ikura: how much

phrases.reading: いくら です か
phrases.lemmaField: いくら です か
phrases.translation: How much [is it / something], a bit more polite.
phrases.notes: ikura: how much

phrases.japanese: 買いますおいくらですか
phrases.reading: かいます お いくら です か
phrases.lemmaField: 買う お いくら です か
phrases.translation: [I] buy [it]. How much is [it]?
phrases.notes: Notice the politeness prefix "o" here.
phrases.source: 今からあなたを脅迫します

phrases.reading: これ どう おもいます
phrases.lemmaField: これ どう 思う
phrases.translation: As for this, how do [you] think?
phrases.notes: dou: how; in what way; how about​

phrases.reading: どう だった きょう は
phrases.lemmaField: どう だ 今日 は
phrases.translation: How was [it]? Today [I mean].

phrases.reading: どう します か
phrases.lemmaField: どう する か
phrases.translation: How should [we] do [it]? What should we do?
phrases.notes: The English equivalent is: What should we do? But in Japanese, this is expressed using "dou - how / in what way should we do [it]".

phrases.reading: おかえり どう だった
phrases.lemmaField: おかえり どう だ
phrases.translation: Welcome back! How was [it]?
phrases.source: BOFURI - Itai no wa Iya nano de Bougyoryoku ni Kyokufuri Shitai to Omoimasu (ep 1-12 w_en)

phrases.reading: おまえ は どう おもう
phrases.lemmaField: お前 は どう 思う
phrases.translation: As for you, how / in what way [do you] think?

phrases.reading: どうして
phrases.lemmaField: どうして
phrases.translation: doushite: why, for what reason?
phrases.notes: This is slightly more polite than "nande".

phrases.reading: おかあさん どうして
phrases.lemmaField: お母さん どうして
phrases.translation: Mother, why [did you say this]?

phrases.reading: かなしい はなし だ
phrases.lemmaField: 悲しい 話 だ
phrases.translation: [Something] is a sad story. The speaker however sounds like he's not serious, also the music is not very sad ;).
phrases.notes: kanashii: sad; miserable

phrases.reading: こわい えいが じゃない よ
phrases.lemmaField: 怖い 映画 じゃ よ
phrases.translation: [Something] is not a scary movie.
phrases.notes: eiga: movie

phrases.reading: げんいん なに です
phrases.lemmaField: 原因 何 です
phrases.translation: Cause - what is it?
phrases.grammarNote:
In case you're using the latin transcription on the cards, you might wonder what the weird spelling means here (gen'in). [n'] simply stands for the the Japanese "syllabic n" character (ん) in case of ambiguous spelling. Basically, Japanese has two spellings which end up in the latin character combination of "n" + "i". These are "に" and "んい". The first one is most common, but some words are also spelled the second way. Read more about the syllabic n on wikipedia.

One common criticism of romanizing Japanese is that it does not accurately represent the spelling. Therefore, I adapted the jlab romanization to all corner cases. It can be mapped to real Japanese 1:1 without ambiguities, the weird [n'] is a consequence of this.
phrases.notes: gen'in: cause; origin; source
phrases.source: Boku no Hero Academia S3 (ep 1-25 jp_en)

phrases.reading: きょう たんじょうび だ よ ね
phrases.lemmaField: 今日 誕生日 だ よ ね
phrases.translation: Today is [your] birthday, isn't it?
phrases.notes: tanjoubi: birthday

phrases.japanese: 先生お誕生日おめでとうございます
phrases.reading: せんせい おたんじょうび おめでとう ございます
phrases.lemmaField: 先生 お誕生日 おめでとう ござる
phrases.translation: A polite way to congratulate someone to his birthday.
phrases.notes:
omedetou: congratulations!; well done!; best wishes!; all the best!
This word is used e.g. for congratulating someone to their birthday, but also for wishing a happy new year and others.
phrases.source: 今からあなたを脅迫します

phrases.japanese: お誕生日 おめでとう
phrases.reading: おたんじょうび おめでとう
phrases.lemmaField: お誕生日 おめでとう
phrases.translation: A more casual way to congratulate someone.
phrases.source: 私に天使が舞い降りた! (wataten)

phrases.reading: だれか いる の
phrases.lemmaField: 誰か いる の
phrases.translation: Is someone there?
phrases.notes: dareka: someone (it's dare + ka, but I spell it together, because it's also found like this in the dictionary. Remember: Japanese has no whitespaces, so don't worry about this).

phrases.reading: だれか いない の か
phrases.lemmaField: 誰か いる の か
phrases.translation: Isn't someone there?
phrases.notes: dareka: someone (it's dare + ka, but I spell it together, because it's also found like this in the dictionary. Remember: Japanese has no whitespaces, so don't worry about this).

phrases.reading: だれ か いない か な
phrases.lemmaField: 誰 か いる か な
phrases.translation: Isn't someone there?
phrases.notes: dareka: someone (it's dare + ka, but I spell it together, because it's also found like this in the dictionary. Remember: Japanese has no whitespaces, so don't worry about this).

phrases.reading: だれか きた
phrases.lemmaField: 誰か 来る
phrases.translation: Oh, someone came!

phrases.japanese: 誰かこっちに来ますあ
phrases.reading: だれか こっち に きます あ
phrases.lemmaField: 誰か こっち に 来る あ
phrases.translation: Someone comes over here (towards the speaker)!

phrases.japanese: すみません誰かいませんか
phrases.reading: すみません だれか いません か
phrases.lemmaField: すみません 誰か いる か
phrases.translation: Excuse me! Isn't someone here?!

phrases.reading: なにか あった の
phrases.lemmaField: 何か ある の
phrases.translation: Literally, this translates to: Was something there? It's the Japanese way to ask: Did something happen? Was there something that bothered you?
phrases.notes: nanika: something (it's nani + ka, but I spell it together, because it's also found like this in the dictionary. Remember: Japanese has no whitespaces, so don't worry about this).

phrases.reading: なにか ありました か
phrases.lemmaField: 何か ある か
phrases.translation: Literally, this translates to: Was something there? It's the Japanese way to ask: Did something happen? Was there something that bothered you? The same as before, just a little more polite.
phrases.notes: nanika: something (it's nani + ka, but I spell it together, because it's also found like this in the dictionary. Remember: Japanese has no whitespaces, so don't worry about this).

phrases.reading: おれ に なにか した の か
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 に 何か する の か
phrases.romaji: ore ni nanika shita no ka
phrases.translation: Did [you] do something to me?
phrases.notes: nanika: something (it's nani + ka, but I spell it together, because it's also found like this in the dictionary. Remember: Japanese has no whitespaces, so don't worry about this).

phrases.reading: おれ が なにか した か
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 が 何か する か
phrases.translation: Did I do something [wrong]?

phrases.reading: ひと は いつか しぬ
phrases.lemmaField: 人 は いつか 死ぬ
phrases.translation: As for humans, [they] die someday.
phrases.notes: itsuka: someday

phrases.reading: いつか み に きて
phrases.lemmaField: いつか 見る に 来る
phrases.translation: Someday come to see.
phrases.grammarNote: Ignore "kite" for now. It's a soft imperative form of "kuru" and is covered soon.
phrases.source: Terrace House-Boys x Girls Next Door

phrases.japanese: でもいつか知るんだし
phrases.reading: でも いつか しる ん だ し
phrases.lemmaField: でも いつか 知る ん だ し
phrases.romaji: demo itsuka shiru n da shi
phrases.translation: ...but someday [you] will know.
phrases.grammarNote: Ignore the ending "shi" for now. It's used to list one out of several reasons.

phrases.japanese: どこかに遊びに行かない
phrases.reading: どこか に あそび に いかない
phrases.lemmaField: どこか に 遊び に 行く
phrases.translation: [Why] don't [we] go somewhere on a trip / go to visit?
phrases.notes:
dokoka: somewhere

(Refresher: "asobi ni iku" means: to go on a trip / to go to visit someone, it's a set phrase).
phrases.source: The World God Only Knows S3 (jp eng)

phrases.japanese: それがこの町のどこかにある
phrases.reading: それ が この まち の どこか に ある
phrases.lemmaField: それ が この 町 の どこか に ある
phrases.romaji: sore ga kono machi no dokoka ni aru
phrases.translation: That thing (on the listener's mind) is somewhere in this city.
phrases.notes:
Note the interesting way to express "somewhere in this city" using the "no"-particle (city no somewhere).

Remark: "sore" does not only mean that something is physically close to the listener, but the meaning is rather figurative. It's indicating an item or person near the listener, the action of the listener, or something on their mind.

phrases.japanese: どこかにいるはずだ絶対にいる
phrases.reading: どこか に いる はず だ ぜったい に いる
phrases.lemmaField: どこか に いる はず だ 絶対 に いる
phrases.romaji: dokoka ni iru hazu da zettai ni iru
phrases.translation: [He] should be somewhere! [He should] absolutely be there!
phrases.notes: hazu: should (be) -> this will be covered in more detail later.
phrases.source: JoJos Bizarre Adventure 黄金の風 (1-25)

phrases.reading: だれも いない
phrases.lemmaField: 誰も いる
phrases.translation: Nobody here?
phrases.notes: daremo: nobody (in negative sentence), everybody (in positive sentence, rare though)
phrases.source: BOFURI - Itai no wa Iya nano de Bougyoryoku ni Kyokufuri Shitai to Omoimasu (ep 1-12 w_en)

phrases.reading: いま は だれも いません
phrases.lemmaField: 今 は 誰も いる
phrases.translation: As for now, [there's] noone there.

phrases.reading: だれも がんばってる
phrases.lemmaField: 誰も 頑張る
phrases.translation: Everybody is doing [their] best.
phrases.grammarNote: Ignore the grammar of "ganbatteru" for now. It's a present progressive form of "ganbaru - to do one's best; to keep at it". It will be covered later.
phrases.notes: As a rule of thumb, "daremo" is more often used in negative sentences, where it means "noone". It can, however, also be used in positive sentences like this one. Remember that we already had "minna" to express "everybody", which is used more often.

phrases.reading: だれも こない な
phrases.lemmaField: 誰も 来る な
phrases.translation: Noone comes.

phrases.reading: ここ は だれも こない し
phrases.lemmaField: ここ は 誰も 来る し
phrases.translation: As for here, noone comes -> nobody comes to this place.
phrases.notes: We already had "shi" on an earlier card, it marks an incomplete list of of reasons in this case and will be covered again later. For this sentence, the speaker maybe tries to convince someone that this is a good place: Noone comes and sees what we're doing here (among other reasons).
phrases.source: Higurashi no Naku Koro ni S1 (JP Eng)

phrases.japanese: 君は悪くない誰も悪くない
phrases.reading: きみ は わるくない だれも わるくない
phrases.lemmaField: 君 は 悪い 誰も 悪い
phrases.translation: As for you, [you are] not at fault. Noone's at fault.

phrases.japanese: 誰も知るはずがありません
phrases.reading: だれも しる はず が ありません
phrases.lemmaField: 誰も 知る はず が ある
phrases.translation: Noone should be supposed to know.
phrases.notes:
hazu: should (be)

We have a clause (daremo shiru), which describes "hazu", "ga arimasen" then states that this is not there. For westerners this sounds weird, we're simply not used to express stuff this way. But you'll face many more sentences like this. If it's too difficult for now, just delete the card, it doesn't introduce anything new.
phrases.source: JoJos Bizarre Adventure 黄金の風 (1-25)

phrases.japanese: あそこには俺がいるはずだったのに｡
phrases.reading: あそこ に は おれ が いる はず だった のに ｡
phrases.lemmaField: あそこ に は 俺 が いる はず だ のに ｡
phrases.romaji: asoko ni ha ore ga iru hazu datta noni ｡
phrases.translation: [I didn't go] even though [I] should have been there.
phrases.notes:
hazu: should (be)
noni: even though (this is introduced in more detail later)

phrases.japanese: 勝てない勝てるはずがない
phrases.reading: かてない かてる はず が ない
phrases.lemmaField: 勝てる 勝てる はず が ない
phrases.translation: [They] can't win. [It] shouldn't be possible [for them] to win.
phrases.notes:
hazu: should (be)

Remark: "katenai" is the negative potential form and means "can't win". The negative is "katanai". The potential form is covered later, so please don't worry about this now. The point of this card is to remember "hazu". I didn't notice this when adding the card, this was corrected In v14.

phrases.reading: できる はず が ない
phrases.lemmaField: できる はず が ない
phrases.translation: [You] shouldn't be able to do [this].

phrases.japanese: 悲しいはずはないだろ
phrases.reading: かなしい はず は ない だろ
phrases.lemmaField: 悲しい はず は ない だ はずです
phrases.translation: [This] shouldn't be sad/sorrowful.
phrases.notes: darou: seems; I think; I guess; sometimes also used to seek agreement: right?; don't you agree?

phrases.japanese: 誰もいない恐ろしい世界で
phrases.reading: だれも いない おそろしい せかい で
phrases.lemmaField: 誰も いる 恐ろしい 世界 で
phrases.translation: It's a scary world where nobody lives [and we have to live in it now].
phrases.notes: Literally: It's a "noone-there-scary-world..." [and we have to live in it now]. Again, if it's too weird or you don't get it, just delete this card.

phrases.reading: なにも できない
phrases.lemmaField: 何も できる
phrases.translation: [Someone] can't do anything.
phrases.notes:
nanimo: nothing, (not) anything

In contrast to daremo, nanimo is exclusively used in negative sentences. It always means "nothing" or "(not) anything". Just in case you're wondering how to express "everything" in Japanese: We already had one example (subete), I'll add more on separate cards soon!

phrases.reading: おれ は なにも しらない
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 は 何も 知る
phrases.translation: As for me, [I] don't know anything.
phrases.notes:
nanimo: nothing, (not) anything

In contrast to daremo, nanimo is exclusively used in negative sentences. It always means "nothing" or "(not) anything". Just in case you're wondering how to express "everything" in Japanese: We already had one example (subete), I'll add more on separate cards soon!

phrases.japanese: 僕は君のこと何も知らないんだな
phrases.reading: ぼく は きみ の こと なにも しらない ん だ な
phrases.lemmaField: 僕 は 君 の こと 何も 知る ん だ な
phrases.romaji: boku ha kimi no koto nanimo shiranai n da na
phrases.translation: As for me, [I] don't know anything about you (in an explanatory tone).
phrases.notes: The "about you" is not explicitly stated here. There are words for this in Japanese, but expressing it like this is perfectly fine.

phrases.japanese: 私バカだから自分のこと何も知らなかった
phrases.reading: わたし ばか だ から じぶん の こと なにも しらなかった
phrases.lemmaField: 私 バカ だ から 自分 の こと 何も 知る
phrases.romaji: watashi baka da kara jibun no koto nanimo shiranakatta
phrases.translation: Because I am an idiot, [I] didn't know anything [about] me.
phrases.notes: Sounds a bit weird without context. The speaker is surprised about not having noticed something and is pondering about the reasons. Just delete this sentence if it's too difficult or doesn't make sense, it doesn't add anything new.

phrases.reading: でも なにも みなかった
phrases.lemmaField: でも 何も 見る
phrases.translation: ...but [I] didn't see anything.

phrases.reading: なにも たべない の
phrases.lemmaField: 何も 食べる の
phrases.translation: [You] don't eat anything (in tone asking for explanation)?

phrases.japanese: ごめんなさい何もない
phrases.reading: ごめんなさい なにも ない
phrases.lemmaField: ごめんなさい 何も ない
phrases.translation: "nanimo nai" literally means "nothing is there". The speaker says: Sorry, [it's] nothing.

phrases.reading: な なにも ない です
phrases.lemmaField: な 何も ない です
phrases.translation: It's nothing [forget about it]!

phrases.reading: なにも かいません よ
phrases.lemmaField: 何も 買う よ
phrases.translation: The kid wants her robot servant to go somewhere and buy something. She answers: [I] don't buy anything!

phrases.japanese: でもあそこには何もないわよ
phrases.reading: でも あそこ に は なにも ない わ よ
phrases.lemmaField: でも あそこ に は 何も ない わ よ
phrases.romaji: demo asoko ni ha nanimo nai wa yo
phrases.translation: As for "over there", nothing there.
phrases.notes: asoko: over there (distant from listener and speaker). This again follows the same "positional" pattern as achira, kochira, sochira.
phrases.source: blood c the last dark (jp eng)

phrases.reading: ぜんぶ あなた の せい
phrases.lemmaField: 全部 あなた の せい
phrases.translation: Everything is your fault! Remember: It's not very common and sometimes rude to address someone directly with "anata - you". But the speaker is pointing a gun at the people here, so he probably doesn't care anyways... ;).
phrases.notes: zenbu: everything; all; entire; whole; altogether

phrases.japanese: ごめんなさい私が全部悪いです
phrases.reading: ごめんなさい わたし が ぜんぶ わるい です
phrases.lemmaField: ごめんなさい 私 が 全部 悪い です
phrases.romaji: gomennasai watashi ga zenbu warui desu
phrases.translation: Sorry, everything is my fault!
phrases.notes: Note that "zenbu" does not just simply mean "everything". It rather carries the meaning of "something in its completeness", have a look at the dictionary. So while this sentence can be translated like above, a more accurate translation would be: Sorry, I am completely to blame. Don't worry about this, the meaning is pretty much the same and the meaning of "zenbu" is pretty much always clear from context!

phrases.japanese: 全部お前のせいじゃないか
phrases.reading: ぜんぶ おまえ の せい じゃない か
phrases.lemmaField: 全部 お前 の せい じゃ か
phrases.romaji: zenbu omae no sei janai ka
phrases.translation: Everything is your fault, isn't it?!
phrases.notes: Remark: "omae no sei janai" means: It isn't your fault. When used as a question like in this sentence however, "janai (ka)" often translates to the English "isn't it".
phrases.source: Kokoro ga Sakebitagatterunda (Anthem of the Heart)

phrases.reading: もう みました ぜんぶ
phrases.lemmaField: もう 見る 全部
phrases.translation: [I] already saw [it], everything.
phrases.notes: Or: I've already seen everything.

phrases.japanese: この時間が全てじゃない
phrases.reading: この じかん が すべて じゃない
phrases.lemmaField: この 時間 が 全て じゃ
phrases.translation:
This time isn't everything (in a sense: There's more to come).
It seems like the two are having a good time.

phrases.japanese: 全ての問題は人間の心から来るんだよ
phrases.reading: すべて の もんだい は にんげん の こころ から くる ん だ よ
phrases.lemmaField: 全て の 問題 は 人間 の 心 から 来る ん だ よ
phrases.romaji: subete no mondai ha ningen no kokoro kara kuru n da yo
phrases.translation: As for all problems, [they] come from the heart of humans.
phrases.notes: Seems like humans are to blame for something here. If the sentence is too weird, delete it! It didn't add any new points.

phrases.reading: すべて を うしなう か
phrases.lemmaField: 全て を 失う か
phrases.translation: [We] lose everything (profits, achievements, whatever)?
phrases.source: 今からあなたを脅迫します

phrases.japanese: ええあなたどこも怪我はない
phrases.reading: ええ あなた どこも けが は ない
phrases.lemmaField: ええ あなた どこも 怪我 は ない
phrases.romaji: ee anata dokomo kega ha nai
phrases.translation: You are injured nowhere -> literally: You, injury nowhere present.
phrases.notes:
dokomo: everywhere or nowhere (in negative sentence)
kega: injury, hurt

phrases.japanese: 海の匂いってどこも同じね
phrases.reading: うみ の におい って どこも おなじ ね
phrases.lemmaField: 海 の 匂い って どこも 同じ ね
phrases.romaji: umi no nioi tte dokomo onaji ne
phrases.translation: As for the smell of the sea, it's the same everywhere, isn't it.
phrases.notes:
tte: casual topic marker 

nioi: smell

phrases.japanese: いつものことじゃないですか
phrases.reading: いつも の こと じゃない です か
phrases.lemmaField: いつも の こと じゃ です か
phrases.romaji: itsumo no koto janai desu ka
phrases.translation: Isn't [it] the same thing as always?
phrases.notes: We already had itsu + mo on a previous card: It almost always means "always" and pretty much never means "never". Some more words on how to say "never" follow soon.

phrases.reading: いつも ありがとう
phrases.lemmaField: いつも ありがとう
phrases.translation: Always thank you.

phrases.japanese: ここいつもの図書館だ
phrases.reading: ここ いつも の としょかん だ
phrases.lemmaField: ここ いつも の 図書館 だ
phrases.translation: As for here, [it] is the same library as always.
phrases.notes: Note the interesting way for expressing "same xxx as always" using the "no"-particle.

phrases.japanese: 男の人はいつもずるい
phrases.reading: おとこ の ひと は いつも ずるい
phrases.lemmaField: 男 の 人 は いつも ずるい
phrases.romaji: otoko no hito ha itsumo zurui
phrases.translation: Guys are always sly/dishonest. Maybe someone cheated on her.
phrases.notes: zurui: sly; cunning; sneaky; crafty; unfair; dishonest

phrases.reading: いつも の あさ です
phrases.lemmaField: いつも の 朝 です 朝早く
phrases.translation: It's the same morning as always (I guess the speaker refers to some morning routine, which is always the same).
phrases.notes: asa: morning

phrases.japanese: 今まで全然気付かなかった
phrases.reading: いま まで ぜんぜん きづかなかった
phrases.lemmaField: 今 まで 全然 気付く
phrases.translation: Until now [I] totally did not notice (or never noticed).
phrases.notes:
zenzen: (not) at all / totally (not)  (in negative sentence)

In Japanese you can use "zenzen" + negative sentence to express "never" - just in case you've been wondering. This pattern is quite common, we already had it in the context of question words a few cards ago.

phrases.japanese: 友達も全然いないみたい
phrases.reading: ともだち も ぜんぜん いない みたい
phrases.lemmaField: 友達 も 全然 いる みたい
phrases.translation: Friends totally not exist, it seems - or less literal: It seems like [he] does not have any friends.
phrases.notes:
mitai: seems like -> this will be covered in more detail again later.
Moreover, ignore the "mo" for now: It's often used in negative sentences like this.

phrases.reading: ぜんぜん うれしくない よ
phrases.lemmaField: 全然 嬉しい よ
phrases.translation: [Something] is totally not happy; glad; joyful.

phrases.reading: ぜんぜん だめ
phrases.lemmaField: 全然 だめ
phrases.translation: [Something is] totally not good, maybe something that was suggested or done by someone. In Japanese, you can also use this to express that something is not possible or to refuse to do something.
phrases.notes: dame: no good

phrases.reading: ぜんぜん かまいません
phrases.lemmaField: 全然 かまう
phrases.translation: [I] totally don't mind.
phrases.notes: kamau: to mind

phrases.reading: だれ でも いい よ
phrases.lemmaField: 誰 でも いい よ
phrases.translation: Anyone is ok, anyone can do this job.
phrases.notes: dare demo: anyone / whoever

phrases.japanese: パンダくん誰でもいいの
phrases.reading: ぱんだ くん だれ でも いい の
phrases.lemmaField: パンダ くん 誰 でも いい の
phrases.romaji: panda kun dare demo ii no
phrases.translation: The panda in this anime is a totally lazy bum. In this episode hovever, he'd like to become an apprentice in order to learn something. The waitress asks: Panda, is anyone ok [as teacher]?

phrases.reading: だれ でも できる し
phrases.lemmaField: 誰 でも できる し
phrases.translation: Anyone can do this, among other reasons.
phrases.notes: shi: one reason out of many
phrases.source: 私に天使が舞い降りた! (wataten)

phrases.reading: だれ でも いい です か
phrases.lemmaField: 誰 でも いい です か
phrases.translation: The conversation is revolving around kissing and the question, if you'd kiss anyone. The speaker asks: Is anyone [really] ok?

phrases.japanese: いつでも相手になるよ
phrases.reading: いつ でも あいて に なる よ
phrases.lemmaField: いつ でも 相手 に なる よ
phrases.romaji: itsu demo aite ni naru yo
phrases.translation: [Let's] become partners any time.
phrases.notes: itsudemo: any time

phrases.japanese: ええっていつでも飲みに来てな
phrases.reading: ええ って いつ でも のみ に きて な
phrases.lemmaField: ええ って いつ でも 飲む に 来る な
phrases.romaji: ee tte itsu demo nomi ni kite na
phrases.translation: [A: Thank you for so many cups of tea! B:] It's ok, come to drink whenever [you like].
phrases.notes:
itsudemo: any time

Remark: "ee tte" is kansai dialect and means "ii yo".

phrases.reading: いつ でも いい よ
phrases.lemmaField: いつ でも いい よ
phrases.translation: Any time is ok.
phrases.notes: itsudemo: any time
phrases.source: Terrace House- Boys & Girls in the City

phrases.reading: どこ でも いい よ
phrases.lemmaField: どこ でも いい よ
phrases.translation: Anywhere [is] ok.
phrases.notes: dokodemo: anywhere / wereever
phrases.source: Terrace House- Boys & Girls in the City

phrases.reading: どこ でも いく ぞ
phrases.lemmaField: どこ でも 行く ぞ
phrases.translation: [Let's] go anywhere!
phrases.notes: A weird sentence, but it looks like these people are about to fight and ready to go anywhere.

phrases.japanese: 俺よく分からないからどこでもいいよ
phrases.reading: おれ よく わからない から どこ でも いい よ
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 よく 分かる から どこ でも いい よ
phrases.romaji: ore yoku wakaranai kara doko demo ii yo
phrases.translation: Looks like they want to go out in order to do something, but haven't decided where to go yet. The speaker says: Because I don't know anything [about it], anywhere is ok.
phrases.source: Wotakoi Otaku ni Koi ha Muzukashii

phrases.japanese: 別にどこでもいいじゃないですか
phrases.reading: べつに どこ でも いい じゃない です か
phrases.lemmaField: 別に どこ でも いい じゃ です か
phrases.romaji: betsuni doko demo ii janai desu ka
phrases.translation: Isn't anywhere ok?
phrases.grammarNote: Ignore "betsuni" for now.

phrases.japanese: どこでもいいです私は
phrases.reading: どこ でも いい です わたし は
phrases.lemmaField: どこ でも いう です 私 は
phrases.romaji: doko demo ii desu watashi ha
phrases.translation: As for me, anywhere is ok.

phrases.reading: かんたん な こと だ よ
phrases.lemmaField: 簡単 だ こと だ よ
phrases.translation: [Something] is an easy thing [to do].
phrases.notes: kantan: simple; easy; uncomplicated

phrases.reading: おかしい です よ ね
phrases.lemmaField: おかしい です よ ね
phrases.translation: [It's] strange, isn't it!
phrases.notes: okashii: strange; odd

phrases.reading: つぎ は ぼく だ
phrases.lemmaField: 次 は 僕 だ
phrases.translation: As for next, it's me -> It's my turn now.
phrases.notes: tsugi: next; following; subsequent

phrases.reading: わたし は げんき です
phrases.lemmaField: 私 は 元気 です 元気いっぱい
phrases.translation: As for me, I'm good!
phrases.notes:
genki: healthy; well; fit

Translating this to English literally sounds a bit weird: "I'm healthy". It's a common way to say: I'm good!

phrases.reading: きょう は あたたかい な
phrases.lemmaField: 今日 は 暖かい な
phrases.translation: As for today, it's warm (in a pleasant way), isn't it.
phrases.notes: atatakai: warm; mild; (pleasantly) hot

phrases.reading: きょう も あつい ね
phrases.lemmaField: 今日 も 暑い ね
phrases.translation: Today's hot too, isn't it.
phrases.notes: atsui: hot (temperature, not in a too pleasant way)

phrases.japanese: 今日はとても暑いですね
phrases.reading: きょう は とても あつい です ね
phrases.lemmaField: 今日 は とても 暑い です ね
phrases.romaji: kyou ha totemo atsui desu ne
phrases.translation: As for today, [it] is extremely hot, isn't it?

phrases.reading: とても つめたい ひと です
phrases.lemmaField: とても 冷たい 人 です
phrases.translation: [Someone] is a cold person.
phrases.notes:
tsumetai: (emotionally) cold

"tsumetai" also refers to temperature.
phrases.source: ぼくたちは勉強ができない

phrases.japanese: 友達が最近冷たいんだ
phrases.reading: ともだち が さいきん つめたい ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: 友達 が 最近 冷たい ん だ
phrases.romaji: tomodachi ga saikin tsumetai n da
phrases.translation: [My] friends are cold recently.
phrases.notes: saikin: recently

phrases.reading: あいかわらず つめたい ね
phrases.lemmaField: 相変わらず 冷たい ね
phrases.translation: [She is] cold as usual, isn't [she].
phrases.notes: aikawarazu: as ever; as usual

phrases.japanese: はいちょっと冷たいですよ
phrases.reading: はい ちょっと つめたい です よ
phrases.lemmaField: はい ちょっと 冷たい です よ
phrases.translation: The doctor is touching the patient with something cold and wants to express: It's getting cold now...
phrases.notes:
tsumetai: cold (to the touch)
chotto: a little; a bit; slightly​

You can't use "tsumetai" for the temperature outside, see next card!

phrases.reading: さむい です
phrases.lemmaField: 寒い デス
phrases.translation: It's cold!
phrases.notes: samui: cold (e.g. weather)

phrases.reading: さむい よ ここ は さむい よ
phrases.lemmaField: 寒い よ ここ は 寒い よ
phrases.romaji: samui yo koko ha samui yo
phrases.translation: It's cold! As for this place (close to the speaker), it's cold!

phrases.japanese: さすがにちょっと寒いですね
phrases.reading: さすが に ちょっと さむい です ね
phrases.lemmaField: さすが に ちょっと 寒い です ね
phrases.romaji: sasuga ni chotto samui desu ne
phrases.translation: As you'd expect, it is a bit cold [here].
phrases.notes:
sasuga: as one would expect; just as you'd expect
If you wonder about the difference to "tashika ni", have a look at the reference. If you don't know this word yet: It's covered in about 2000 cards, you'll find the reference again then.

phrases.reading: ぶしつ は さむい から な
phrases.lemmaField: 部室 は 寒い から な
phrases.translation: [It's uncomfortable in here] because the club room is cold.
phrases.notes:
bushitsu: club room

"butshitsu" might sound like an unusual word, but if you like school-related anime, you'll definitely hear this, because extracurricular activities are very common in Japan. Moreover, "bu" means "club" and "shitsu" means room (do you remember the word for bedroom from an earlier card?). Note that "shitsu" is used in compound words like this and rather not as standalone word for room. I'll add this a few cards later.

Note that Tae Kim covers "kara" later. It usually connects two sentences in the following fashion: Reason kara result, meaning: because of reason, result happened. If the result is clear from context, it is often omitted, just as in this example. I'll pick this up in more detail later.

phrases.japanese: 毎日こんなに寒いのか
phrases.reading: まいにち こんなに さむい の か
phrases.lemmaField: 毎日 こんなに 寒い の か
phrases.translation: Every day [it's] cold like this?!
phrases.notes:
konnani: like this; in this way (focused on the speaker's opinion)

The intonation together with "no ka" makes the sentence sound like:  "Is it really this cold every day [here]"?! Or, depending on the context: "Does it really have to be this cold every day"?!

phrases.japanese: こんなに寒いのが悪いんだ
phrases.reading: こんなに さむい の が わるい ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: こんなに 寒い の が 悪い ん だ
phrases.romaji: konnani samui no ga warui n da
phrases.translation: As for this cold / coldness like this, [it's] bad (in an explanatory tone).
phrases.notes:
konnani: like this; in this way (focused on the speaker's opinion)

Remember that "no" can also be used to nominalize adjectives (samui) in order to append noun-related particles.

phrases.reading: さむい わ この へや
phrases.lemmaField: 寒い わ この 部屋
phrases.translation: [It's] cold, this room [I mean].
phrases.notes:
heya: room

Remarks:
heya is a more general word for "room" and used to refer to rooms in general. The "shitsu" from previous cards is rather not used like this, it usually occurs as suffix.
The "wa" in here is the feminine sentence ending particle. It's in the middle, because the speaker seems to have forgotten the context: Note the pause after "samui wa". Have a look at the references for a repetition.

phrases.reading: そんなに うれしい か
phrases.lemmaField: そんなに 嬉しい か
phrases.translation: [Are you] really that happy?
phrases.notes: sonnani: so much; so; like that (focused on the listener's opinion)

phrases.reading: そんなに たいせつ な もの
phrases.lemmaField: そんなに 大切 だ もの
phrases.translation: [Is it really] such an important thing?
phrases.notes: sonnani: so much; so; like that (focused on the listener's opinion)

phrases.reading: そんなに つよい の か
phrases.lemmaField: そんなに 強い の か
phrases.translation: [Is it (drink, opponent, whatever) really] that strong?

phrases.japanese: そんなに長くなかったね
phrases.reading: そんなに ながくなかった ね
phrases.lemmaField: そんなに 長い ね
phrases.translation: [Something] was not that long, was it?

phrases.japanese: よく食べるなそんなにうまいか
phrases.reading: よく たべる な そんなに うまい か
phrases.lemmaField: よく 食べる な そんなに うまい か
phrases.romaji: yoku taberu na sonnani umai ka
phrases.translation: [You] eat [this] frequently, [is it] that tasty?
phrases.notes:
yoku: properly, well / frequently, often
Remember: "yoku" is the irregular conjugation of the adjective "ii - good, excellent, fine" to an adverb (i.e. it describes a verb in this case). Note that it can also be translated to "frequently, often", which fits in this case.

umai: tasty - same meaning as "oishii".

phrases.japanese: 実はそんなに長くない
phrases.reading: じつ は そんなに ながくない
phrases.lemmaField: 実 は そんなに 長い 実は
phrases.translation: Actually, [it] is not that long.
phrases.notes: jitsu: truth, reality. Note that this dictionary definition of "jitsu" is a bit technical. This word occurs together with the "ha" particle most of the time and almost always translates to "actually", "in fact" or "to tell you the truth". Therefore, "jitsu ha" also has its own dictionary entry.
phrases.source: Boku no Hero Academia S2 (ep 1-25 jp_en)

phrases.reading: あんなにかんたん に
phrases.lemmaField: あんなに 簡単 に
phrases.translation: In this example, the speaker seems to watch something happening at a certain distance. E.g. someone is doing something without much effort. Then he states: [did he really do it] that easily?
phrases.notes:
annani: to that extent; to that degree; so much; so

konnani, sonnani and annani follow the usual pattern of kore, sore and are. I.e. they refer to something related to the speaker, the listener or something unrelated.

The actual verb is omitted here, which is common in conversations. Just imagine a "shimashita" in the end.

phrases.reading: まけた の か
phrases.lemmaField: 負ける の か
phrases.translation: [You were] defeated?
phrases.notes: makeru: to lose; to be defeated

phrases.reading: あんなに はやい あいて に
phrases.lemmaField: あんなに 早い 相手 に 早く
phrases.translation: [I was defeated] by an opponent that fast (with "that fast" referring to the opponent).
phrases.notes:
During a natural conversation you often find incomplete sentences like this. Just add the "maketa" from the last card in the end and it makes more sense:

The card doesn't add anything new, just delete it if it makes no sense.

phrases.reading: ちょっと
phrases.lemmaField: ちょっと
phrases.translation: chotto not only means "a little; a bit; slightly​" as introduced on an earlier card, but it also means "hey! come on!" In the sense of "wait a minute" or "give me a break".

phrases.reading: ほんとう だ よ
phrases.lemmaField: 本当 だ よ
phrases.translation: It's the truth!
phrases.notes:
hontou: truth; reality; actuality; fact

What's the difference between "jitsu" and "hontou"? As already mentioned a few cards before, "jitsu" is usually used like the English "actually" or "in fact". hontou is used in a very similar way, but emphasizes "truth without lying" a bit more. Have a look at this question for more details.

As usual, don't focus on speaking yourself yet. It's usually very easy to get the meaning from context by just listening to many examples!

phrases.reading: ほんとう です か
phrases.lemmaField: 本当 です か
phrases.translation: Truth?! -> Is [this really] true?
phrases.notes: hontou: truth; reality; actuality; fact

phrases.reading: ほんとう です こまります
phrases.lemmaField: 本当 です 困る
phrases.translation: Is [this] true? [Now we're] in trouble!
phrases.notes: komaru: to be troubled; to have difficulty

phrases.reading: ほんとうに ごめん ね
phrases.lemmaField: 本当に ごめん ね
phrases.translation: I'm really sorry!
phrases.notes:
hontouni: really, truly

As a rule of thumb, "hontou" = truth, reality and "hontouni" = really. I never actually thought about the grammar of "hontou + ni", which I think is "na-adjective + ni = adverb", but this phrase often describes non-verbs, too. Just stick to the rule of thumb, it's usually very easy to understand. If you're really into grammar, I added two links to Japanese stackexchange below, but the answers there are not very sharp either. Don't worry and keep going :).

phrases.reading: ほんとうに ありがとう
phrases.lemmaField: 本当に ありがとう
phrases.translation: Thank you [I am really grateful].

phrases.reading: ほんとうに うまかった よ
phrases.lemmaField: 本当に うまい よ
phrases.translation: [It] was really tasty.

phrases.japanese: 本当にありがとうございました
phrases.reading: ほんとうに ありがとう ございました
phrases.lemmaField: 本当に ありがとう ござる
phrases.translation: Thank you [I am really grateful].

phrases.japanese: よく頑張ったよ本当に
phrases.reading: よく がんばった よ ほんとうに
phrases.lemmaField: よく 頑張る よ 本当に
phrases.translation:
[You] well hung in there. Really!
[You] well did your best. Really!
phrases.notes: Or less literal: You really did your best!

phrases.japanese: 本当に恐ろしかったんだ
phrases.reading: ほんとうに おそろしかった ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: 本当に 恐ろしい ん だ
phrases.translation: [It] was really scary.
phrases.source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure スターダストクルセイダース

phrases.japanese: 困ります本当に困ります
phrases.reading: こまります ほんとうに こまります
phrases.lemmaField: 困る 本当に 困る
phrases.translation: [We are] in trouble. Really in trouble.

phrases.reading: ほんとうに あつくない
phrases.lemmaField: 本当に 熱い
phrases.translation: [Is it] really not hot?
phrases.notes:
atsui/暑い: hot (weather)
atsui/熱い: hot (to the touch)

Note that "atsui" refers to both weather and touching things. In kanji however, the words are spelled differently. Here, the speaker (i.e. the child kneeling on the floor) was trying to touch the flame of a candle and asked if it was really OK to touch it.

phrases.reading: なんで わらう
phrases.lemmaField: 何で 笑う
phrases.translation: Why [do you] laugh?
phrases.notes: warau: to laugh

phrases.reading: ほんとうに わらわない
phrases.lemmaField: 本当に 笑う
phrases.translation: [You] really don't laugh [if I tell you]?

phrases.japanese: 誰か見ませんでしたか
phrases.reading: だれ か みません でした か
phrases.lemmaField: 誰 か 見る です か
phrases.translation: Didn't [you] see someone?
phrases.notes: Refresher: "mimasen deshita" is the grammatically correct teineigo-past of "miru". In spoken Japanese, you'd probably rather hear: "dareka minakatta desu"?

phrases.japanese: お父さんが誰かと来たの
phrases.reading: おとうさん が だれ か と きた の
phrases.lemmaField: お父さん が 誰 か と 来る の
phrases.romaji: otousan ga dare ka to kita no
phrases.translation: Did [your] father come together with someone?

phrases.japanese: かわいくてすてきです
phrases.reading: かわいくて すてき です
phrases.lemmaField: かわいい すてき です
phrases.translation: [Something] is cute and lovely.
phrases.notes: You can connect an i-adjective (or a sentence ending on an i-adjective) "x" to another sentence "y" by replacing -i with -kute. The meaning becomes "x and y". This grammar part is commonly referred to as "te-form".

phrases.reading: くらくて あぶない から
phrases.lemmaField: 暗い 危ない から
phrases.translation: [Don't go in there] because it is dark and dangerous.
phrases.notes:
You can connect an i-adjective (or a sentence ending on an i-adjective) "x" to another sentence "y" by replacing -i with -kute. The meaning becomes "x and y". This grammar part is commonly referred to as "te-form".

Remark: abunai is not a negative word, it means: dangerous.

phrases.japanese: 温かくて本当によかった
phrases.reading: あたたかくて ほんとうに よかった
phrases.lemmaField: 温かい 本当に よい
phrases.translation: The guy is talking about his hand. For some reason, [it] is warm and [this] was great -> He's glad that his hand is warm.
phrases.notes: You can connect an i-adjective (or a sentence ending on an i-adjective) "x" to another sentence "y" by replacing -i with -kute. The meaning becomes "x and y". This grammar part is commonly referred to as "te-form".

phrases.japanese: すごい冷たくて甘いですよこれ
phrases.reading: すごい つめたくて あまい です よ これ
phrases.lemmaField: すごい 冷たい 甘い です よ これ
phrases.romaji: sugoi tsumetakute amai desu yo kore
phrases.translation: Amazing, [it, judging from the picture maybe ice cream] is cold and sweet.
phrases.notes:
amai: sweet

You can connect an i-adjective (or a sentence ending on an i-adjective) "x" to another sentence "y" by replacing -i with -kute. The meaning becomes "x and y". This grammar part is commonly referred to as "te-form".

phrases.japanese: 天気がよくて気持ちいいね
phrases.reading: てんき が よくて きもちいい ね
phrases.lemmaField: 天気 が よい 気持ちいい ね
phrases.translation: The weather is great and [this is] feeling good.
phrases.notes:
kimochiii: good feeling; feeling good (from kimochi - feeling, sensation + ii - good)

You can connect an i-adjective (or a sentence ending on an i-adjective) "x" to another sentence "y" by replacing -i with -kute. The meaning becomes "x and y". This grammar part is commonly referred to as "te-form".

phrases.japanese: 優しくてすてきな人だなあって
phrases.reading: やさしくて すてき な ひと だ なあ って
phrases.lemmaField: 優しい すてき だ 人 だ なあ って
phrases.romaji: yasashikute suteki na hito da naa tte
phrases.translation: [He] is a kind and lovely person, isn't he.
phrases.notes:
yasashii: tender; kind; gentle

You can connect an i-adjective (or a sentence ending on an i-adjective) "x" to another sentence "y" by replacing -i with -kute. The meaning becomes "x and y". This grammar part is commonly referred to as "te-form".

phrases.japanese: ん甘くておいしいです
phrases.reading: ん あまくて おいしい です
phrases.lemmaField: ん 甘い おいしい です
phrases.translation: [It] is sweet and tasty.
phrases.notes: You can connect an i-adjective (or a sentence ending on an i-adjective) "x" to another sentence "y" by replacing -i with -kute. The meaning becomes "x and y". This grammar part is commonly referred to as "te-form".

phrases.reading: あまくて うまい ぞ
phrases.lemmaField: 甘い うまい ぞ
phrases.translation: [It] is sweet and delicious.
phrases.notes: umai and oishii can both refer to delicious food. umai also can mean "skillfull, clever", see next card.

phrases.reading: うまい よ わたし
phrases.lemmaField: うまい よ 私
phrases.translation: Skilled! Me, I mean. -> I'm skilled!
phrases.notes:
I guess it's clear that she's not saying: "I'm tasty" here ;).
The "umai" sounds a little bit like "komai", but it is indeed "umai". Sometimes, this is caused by background noise, music or others speaking, don't worry about this. The card is from mitsuboshi colors, ep. 8 around 11:50 if you want to check yourself.

phrases.reading: せまくて わるい ね
phrases.lemmaField: 狭い 悪い ね
phrases.translation: [This place] is small and bad, isn't it.
phrases.notes: semai: narrow; confined; small

phrases.reading: おおきくて おもい
phrases.lemmaField: 大きい 重い
phrases.translation: [It] is big and heavy. This anime revolves around music in a school orchestra, so I guess they are talking about an instrument.
phrases.notes: omoi: heavy

phrases.japanese: やっぱりすごく嬉しくて
phrases.reading: やっぱり すごく うれしくて
phrases.lemmaField: やっぱり すごい 嬉しい
phrases.translation: After all, [you] are very happy (and then the speaker gets doubts: Aren't you?)
phrases.notes:
yappari: as expected, after all

Note, that "sugoi" as a matter of expressing "very" is casual, a more proper way would be to use "totemo".
Reminder: Replacing "i" of an i-adjective with "ku" makes it an adverb, which allows to describe a verb.

By now I guess you got the pattern: All of the previous -kute examples could be translated to "x and y". Due to this "and"-nature, you'll often find the -te form at the end of an incomplete sentence (like in this example), indicating that the speaker is unsure or might want to add something else. Especially in this sentence, this is also clear from the intonation.

phrases.reading: しろくて つめたくて
phrases.lemmaField: 白い 冷たい
phrases.translation: [It's] white, cold and (...maybe something else will be added due to the ending -te).
phrases.notes: shiroi: white

phrases.japanese: 静かで悪くない部屋だ
phrases.reading: しずか で わるくない へや だ
phrases.lemmaField: 静か だ 悪い 部屋 だ
phrases.translation: [This] room is quiet and not so bad.
phrases.notes: The same chaining that we had for sentences ending on an i-adjective can be done for na-adjectives and nouns by appending "de" (to "shizuka" in this case):

phrases.japanese: キレイで優しいさわ子先生はどこに
phrases.reading: きれい で やさしい さわこ せんせい は どこ に
phrases.lemmaField: キレイ だ 優しい さわ子 先生 は どこ に
phrases.romaji: kirei de yasashii sawako sensei ha doko ni
phrases.translation: As for the lovely and kind sawako sensei, where [is she / did she go]? This refers to the character of the teacher, it seems like the teacher somehow changed, the speaker sounds pretty disappointed.
phrases.notes:
yasashii: tender; kind; gentle

The same chaining that we had for sentences ending on an i-adjective can be done for na-adjectives and nouns by appending "de". Reminder: Even though "kirei" ends on an i, it is still a na-adjective.

phrases.japanese: きれいで楽しくてカッコよくて
phrases.reading: きれい で たのしくて かっこよくて
phrases.lemmaField: きれい だ 楽しい カッコいい
phrases.translation: [Someone seems to be] lovely, cheerful and stylish.
phrases.notes:
kakkoii: attractive; good-looking; stylish; cool (conjugated like ii)

Here we have a chain of both na- and i-adjectives.

phrases.japanese: 髪が長くてキレイで優しい
phrases.reading: かみ が ながくて きれい で やさしい
phrases.lemmaField: 髪 が 長い キレイ だ 優しい
phrases.romaji: kami ga nagakute kirei de yasashii
phrases.translation: [Her] hair is long, lovely and tender.
phrases.notes: kami: hair

phrases.japanese: 朝ごはん食べて学校いくよ
phrases.reading: あさごはん たべて がっこう いく よ
phrases.lemmaField: 朝ごはん 食べる 学校 いく よ
phrases.translation: [I] eat breakfast and go to school.
phrases.notes:
asagohan: breakfast (it's "asa - morning" + "gohan - meal")

The te-form also exists for verbs: Conjugate the verb to past tense (e.g. taberu -> tabeta) and replace "ta" by "te". 

The meaning is the same as for the adjective examples here: The -te form connects the first sentence (asagohan (wo) tabete) to the second one (gakkou (ni) iku) by means of "and". Note that some particles are missing here.

phrases.japanese: 朝ごはん食べてこなかったの
phrases.reading: あさごはん たべて こなかった の
phrases.lemmaField: 朝ごはん 食べる くる の
phrases.translation: [You] ate breakfast and did not come? (maybe she missed the first lesson at school).
phrases.notes:
asagohan: breakfast

The te-form also exists for verbs: Conjugate the verb to past tense (e.g. taberu -> tabeta) and replace "ta" by "te".

phrases.reading: ごはん たべて のんで
phrases.lemmaField: ご飯 食べる 飲む
phrases.translation: [I go there and] eat a meal and drink [...and maybe have a dessert].
phrases.notes:
gohan: meal

The te-form also exists for verbs: Conjugate the verb to past tense (e.g. nomu -> nonda) and replace "da" by "de". When the past ends on "da" instead of "ta", you attach "de" instead of "te".
phrases.source: Terrace House- Boys & Girls in the City

phrases.reading: たべなくて よかった
phrases.lemmaField: 食べる よい
phrases.translation: [I] didn't eat [it] and this was good -> I'm happy that I didn't eat it.
phrases.notes:
The -te form also exists for negative verbs and is built in a similar way as for the adjectives: Take the negative verb (taberu -> tabenai) and replace "i" with "kute". Or: Replace the "nai" of the negative form with "nakute".
The -te form does not have a past tense. The tense is determined by the last verb, see ref.

phrases.japanese: 今日はもう疲れたから帰って寝る
phrases.reading: きょう は もう つかれた から かえって ねる
phrases.lemmaField: 今日 は もう 疲れる から 帰る 寝る
phrases.romaji: kyou ha mou tsukareta kara kaette neru
phrases.translation: As for today, because [I am] already tired, [I] go home and sleep.
phrases.notes:
kara: because; it can connect two sentences in the following sense: reason kara result, the meaning always is: Because of reason, result happens. Note that the result may be omitted, if it's clear from context.

Note that we already had "kara" on previous cards in different roles: To state a relative time (asa kara - since morning) or a direction (gakkou kara - from school).

phrases.japanese: 疲れたから私は寝るぞ
phrases.reading: つかれた から わたし は ねる ぞ
phrases.lemmaField: 疲れる から 私 は 寝る ぞ
phrases.romaji: tsukareta kara watashi ha neru zo
phrases.translation: Because [I] became tired, [I] sleep.
phrases.notes:
kara: because; it can connect two sentences in the following sense: reason kara result, the meaning always is: Because of reason, result happens. Note that the result may be omitted, if it's clear from context.

In English, this can also translate to "so": I became tired, so I sleep.

phrases.japanese: 食べたことないから楽しみだね
phrases.reading: たべた こと ない から たのしみ だ ね
phrases.lemmaField: 食べる こと ない から 楽しみ だ ね
phrases.romaji: tabeta koto nai kara tanoshimi da ne
phrases.translation: Very interesting sentence, it means: I'm excited to eat this, because I never ate it before.
phrases.notes:
"tabeta koto nai" -> [I] ate [it]-thing not there -> I never ate this.
"tanoshimi da" -> excitement is there -> I'm excited.
"kara" links the first as reason to the second.

Reminder: "koto" is a very generic sort of placeholder noun used to refer to a "thing" or "matter". The matter is usually described by a clause, just as in this example. Some more "koto"-examples follow soon.

phrases.japanese: ちょっと疲れたから休憩
phrases.reading: ちょっと つかれた から きゅうけい
phrases.lemmaField: ちょっと 疲れる から 休憩
phrases.translation: [Let's] take a break because [I] became a bit tired.
phrases.notes: Maybe you noticed an interesting pattern: In English, you'd rather say: I do x because of y. In Japanese, this is usually expressed vice versa. You'll notice this many times, Jay Rubin's book "Making Sense of Japanese" has an entire chapter dedicated to this. This book is totally worth reading, but not for beginners. I'll recommend it again at the end of this course.

phrases.reading: あぶない から
phrases.lemmaField: 危ない から
phrases.translation: [Don't go there] because it is dangerous.
phrases.notes: In this sentence, the result of our pattern "reason kara result" is omitted, because it seems to be clear from context.

phrases.reading: なかま だ から な
phrases.lemmaField: 仲間 だ から な
phrases.translation: [It's no problem] because [he] is [my] comrade.
phrases.notes:
Note that if the reason for something ends on a noun, you usually add "da" before "kara":

Without the "da", this might sound like kara in the role of "from", i.e. I received something from my comrade.

phrases.reading: ともだち だ から だ よ
phrases.lemmaField: 友達 だ から だ よ
phrases.translation: [It's no problem] because [I] am [your] friend.
phrases.notes:
Note that if the reason for something ends on a noun, you usually add "da" before "kara":

Without the "da", this might sound like kara in the role of "from", i.e. I received something from my comrade.

phrases.reading: しごと だ から な
phrases.lemmaField: 仕事 だ から な
phrases.translation: [I can't go] because of work.
phrases.notes:
Note that if the reason for something ends on a noun, you usually add "da" before "kara":

Without the "da", this might sound like kara in the role of "from", i.e. I received something from my comrade.
phrases.source: JoJos Bizarre Adventure 黄金の風 (26-39)

phrases.reading: いい から いい から
phrases.lemmaField: いい から いい から
phrases.translation: ii kara: never mind that; don't worry about that
phrases.notes: Note that in some cases, "kara" is used to express sympathy and can't be directly translated to "because / from / since".

phrases.reading: たき いま いくいく から
phrases.lemmaField: 多軌 今 行く行く から
phrases.translation: Taki [character name], I['ll] go now, I go [there now to rescue you].
phrases.notes: Note that in some cases, "kara" is used to express sympathy and can't be directly translated to "because / from / since". An example is this sentence, the guy is hurrying to save taki from an evil spirit.

phrases.japanese: 映画で見たことがある
phrases.reading: えいが で みた こと が ある
phrases.lemmaField: 映画 で 見る こと が ある
phrases.romaji: eiga de mita koto ga aru
phrases.translation: [I] saw [it] in a movie-thing is there -> I saw it in a movie.
phrases.notes: Reminder: "koto" is a very generic sort of placeholder noun used to refer to a "thing" or "matter". The matter is usually described by a clause, just as in this example. Tae Kim covers this much later, but it's very easy useful.
phrases.source: JoJos Bizarre Adventure 黄金の風 (1-25)

phrases.japanese: 会ったことがあるのか
phrases.reading: あった こと が ある の か
phrases.lemmaField: 会う こと が ある の か
phrases.romaji: atta koto ga aru no ka
phrases.translation: Met-thing exists? -> Did you meet him?
phrases.notes: Reminder: "koto" is a very generic sort of placeholder noun used to refer to a "thing" or "matter". The matter is usually described by a clause, just as in this example. Tae Kim covers this much later, but it's very easy useful.

phrases.japanese: テレビで見たことがあるぞ
phrases.reading: てれび で みた こと が ある ぞ
phrases.lemmaField: テレビ で 見る こと が ある ぞ
phrases.romaji: terebi de mita koto ga aru zo
phrases.translation: Saw on tv-thing exists -> I already saw it on TV.
phrases.notes: terebi: television

phrases.japanese: この道来たことがあるな
phrases.reading: この みち きた こと が ある な
phrases.lemmaField: この 道 来る こと が ある な
phrases.romaji: kono michi kita koto ga aru na
phrases.translation: Came to this street-thing exists -> I've already been to this street before.
phrases.notes:
michi: road; path; street

Pay attention to the past tense of "kuru - to come, to visit" here (kita) and keep this in mind for the next card.

phrases.reading: きいた こと が ある
phrases.lemmaField: 聞く こと が ある
phrases.translation: Heard-thing exists -> I've heard that before.
phrases.notes:
kiku: to hear, to listen to something

The past tense of kuru and kiku sound very similar and are sometimes hard to distinguish. The "i" is pronounced longer for "kiku".
phrases.source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure スターダストクルセイダース

phrases.reading: きいた こと が ある か
phrases.lemmaField: 聞く こと が ある か
phrases.translation: Did you [already] hear about this?

phrases.japanese: うんそれは俺も聞いたことがある
phrases.reading: うん それ は おれ も きいた こと が ある
phrases.lemmaField: うん それ は 俺 も 聞く こと が ある
phrases.romaji: un sore ha ore mo kiita koto ga aru
phrases.translation: As for this, I also heard-thing is there -> I've also heard of this.
