phrases.source: 私に天使が舞い降りた! (wataten)

phrases.reading: ようい は できた か
phrases.lemmaField: 用意 は できる か
phrases.translation: Are the preparations completed?
phrases.notes: youi: preparation; arrangements

phrases.japanese: 飲み物すぐ用意するから
phrases.reading: のみもの すぐ ようい する から
phrases.lemmaField: 飲み物 すぐ 用意 する から
phrases.translation: I immediately prepare beverages.
phrases.grammarNote: Ignore the "kara" here.
phrases.notes: sugu: immediately; at once; right away

phrases.reading: ようい して ある よ
phrases.lemmaField: 用意 する ある よ
phrases.translation: The preparations have been completed.
phrases.notes: You could also say: "youi ha dekita", which just means that some preparations where completed. This sentence puts more emphasis on the resulting state. If this is too hard to understand without context, just keep in mind: -te form + aru = resulting state after an action completed.

phrases.japanese: 僕の名前が書いてあります
phrases.reading: ぼく の なまえ が かいて あります
phrases.lemmaField: 僕 の 名前 が 書く ある
phrases.romaji: boku no namae ga kaite arimasu
phrases.translation: My name is written down [here -> on the thing the kid is handing over].
phrases.notes: -te form + aru: resulting state after an action completed, it is conjugated using "aru".

phrases.japanese: やっぱりあの手紙に何か書いてあったのかな
phrases.reading: やっぱり あの てがみ に なにか かいて あった の か な
phrases.lemmaField: やっぱり あの 手紙 に 何か 書く ある の か な
phrases.romaji: yappari ano tegami ni nanika kaite atta no ka na
phrases.translation: I wonder if something was written in that letter.
phrases.grammarNote: Ignore "yappari" here. The person on the picture received some letter and now is in a good mood. Look at her face!
phrases.notes:
The "I wonder if" is a result of "..no ka na", listen to the intonation.
The "no" here is again the explanatory one: Together with the question, this emphasizes that the speaker is looking for an explanation.

phrases.reading: ここ に おく よ
phrases.lemmaField: ここ に 置く よ
phrases.translation: [I] place [it] here.
phrases.notes: oku: to put, to place

phrases.reading: どこ に おいた っけ
phrases.lemmaField: どこ に 置く っけ
phrases.translation: Where did [I] put [it]?!
phrases.notes:
oku: to put, to place
-kke: indicates that the speaker is trying to recall some information

phrases.japanese: でも何か考えておくね
phrases.reading: でも なにか かんがえて おく ね
phrases.lemmaField: でも 何か 考える おく ね
phrases.translation: ... but [we] have to think [of something, a present in this case].
phrases.notes:
If "oku" is added to a verb in te-form, the verb is carried out explicitly with the future in mind, e.g. to prepare for something.
"-te oku": To do something in preparation of the future.

phrases.reading: まぁ かんがえて おく よ
phrases.lemmaField: まぁ 考える おく よ
phrases.translation: Well, [I] think [about it, an offer made to the guy in this case].
phrases.notes: "-te oku": To do something in preparation of the future.

phrases.reading: うん はなして おく ｡
phrases.lemmaField: うん 話す おく ｡
phrases.translation: Yes, [I] talk [to him, e.g. in order to solve some issue].
phrases.notes: "-te oku": To do something in preparation of the future.

phrases.japanese: ないしょにしておくね
phrases.reading: ないしょ に して おく ね
phrases.lemmaField: ないしょ に する おく ね
phrases.translation: Keep [this] a secret [such that I'm not in trouble in the future].
phrases.notes:
naisho: secret
"-te oku": To do something in preparation of the future.
phrases.source: 私に天使が舞い降りた! (wataten)

phrases.reading: まぁ かえして おく ぜ
phrases.lemmaField: まぁ 返す おく ぜ
phrases.translation: The guy accidentially found a love letter he wasn't supposed to read in his backpack. He's musing about how to return it without getting in trouble in the future and says: [I] return [it, such that you have it again and nothing happened].
phrases.notes:
kaesu: to return (something); to restore; to put back
"-te oku": To do something in preparation of the future.

phrases.reading: ごはん あたためて おく か
phrases.lemmaField: ご飯 温める おく か
phrases.translation: A person is leaving while the others are eating. The speaker asks: [Should I] warm dinner / keep dinner warm [such that it is warm when you return]?
phrases.notes:
atatameru: to warm; to heat
"-te oku": To do something in preparation of the future.
phrases.source: Sakurasou no Pet na Kanojo (jp eng)

phrases.japanese: ここに置いておきますね
phrases.reading: ここ に おいて おきます ね
phrases.lemmaField: ここ に 置く おく ね
phrases.translation: [I] put [it] here [for later].
phrases.notes: Interestingly, "oku" can be connected to itself using the "te oku"-pattern. The first oku simply means: "To put" and the second one indicates, that this is done in preparation for the future. Note that the second oku is conjugated here.
phrases.source: Fate Stay Night Unlimited Blade Works S1 (JP Eng)

phrases.japanese: 悪いけどここに置いておくわよ
phrases.reading: わるい けど ここ に おいて おく わ よ
phrases.lemmaField: 悪い けど ここ に 置く おく わ よ
phrases.romaji: warui kedo koko ni oite oku wa yo
phrases.translation: [It's] bad, but [I] put [it] here for later.
phrases.notes:
warui: bad, poor, undesireable, but also: sorry; (my) bad; unforgivable

"warui" is an interesting word. It means "bad, poor" most of the time but is also a way for apologizing in Japanese meaning "sorry; (my) bad; unforgivable". Just have a look at the dictionary.
Interestingly, "oku" can be connected to itself using the "te oku"-pattern. The first oku here is conjugated to "oite" and simply means "to put", while the second one indicates that this is done in preparation for the future.

phrases.reading: おちゃ いれます
phrases.lemmaField: お茶 入れる
phrases.translation: [I] make tea.
phrases.notes:
ireru: to put in; to let in; to take in; to bring in
Note that in the context of tea of coffee, "ocha/kohii wo ireru" simply means: to make coffee or tea. This is covered in a nice instructional video in about 1000 cards.

phrases.reading: ごはん いれて おく ね
phrases.lemmaField: ご飯 入れる おく ね
phrases.translation: [I] put food [into the box for later]. Maybe she's trying to send him somewhere by mail, weird...
phrases.grammarNote: Look at what's happening here...

phrases.reading: さがして おく から
phrases.lemmaField: 探す おく から
phrases.translation: [I] search [for it, such that you have it back later].
phrases.notes:
"-te oku": To do something in preparation of the future.
sagasu: to search

phrases.reading: よく あやまって おいた が
phrases.lemmaField: よく 謝る おく が
phrases.translation: [He is still mad] but [I] apologized [in order be good again].
phrases.notes: Just an example for "te oku" with oku in past tense. I'll add some more examples in a different context later. The "ga" here is the contrasting one meaning "but / even though".

phrases.reading: かんがえとく ね
phrases.lemmaField: 考える ね
phrases.translation: Think about it [e.g. about accepting an offer].
phrases.notes:
Sometimes the "e" in "te oku"-constructions is omitted, I found these forms often hard to understand in the beginning. Just as for the omitted "i" in "-te iru", these contractions look like standalone verbs.
kangaetoku: contraction of kangaete oku

phrases.reading: かえしとく ね
phrases.lemmaField: 返す ね
phrases.translation: [I] return [it, so that you have it back agan in the future].
phrases.notes:
Sometimes the "e" in "te oku"-constructions is omitted, I found these forms often hard to understand in the beginning. Just as for the omitted "i" in "-te iru", these contractions look like standalone verbs.
kaeshitoku: contraction of kaeshite oku

phrases.reading: じゃ おいとく わ よ
phrases.lemmaField: じゃ 置く わ よ
phrases.translation: Ok, then [I] put it / leave it here [it's better if I keep it at my place in the future].
phrases.notes:
Sometimes the "e" in "te oku"-constructions is omitted, I found these forms often hard to understand in the beginning. Just as for the omitted "i" in "-te iru", these contractions look like standalone verbs.
oitoku: contraction of oite oku

ja/じゃ: Then, well

phrases.japanese: おお菓子も用意しとくね
phrases.reading: お おかし も ようい しとく ね
phrases.lemmaField: お お菓子 も 用意 する ね
phrases.romaji: o okashi mo youi shitoku ne
phrases.translation: Sweets also [should be] prepared [for later].
phrases.notes:
Sometimes the "e" in "te oku"-constructions is omitted, I found these forms often hard to understand in the beginning. Just as for the omitted "i" in "-te iru", these contractions look like standalone verbs.
shitoku: contraction of shite oku

phrases.reading: いって みる
phrases.lemmaField: 行く みる
phrases.translation: [Should we] try to go [in there] or more literal: Go and see?
phrases.notes:
-te form + miru: To try something out in the sense: “To give something a try and see how it goes”. Note that it does not mean "to try hard" in most cases, Japanese has a different expression for that covered later.

Reminder: miru = to see
phrases.source: BOFURI - Itai no wa Iya nano de Bougyoryoku ni Kyokufuri Shitai to Omoimasu (ep 1-12 w_en)

phrases.reading: てつだって みる
phrases.lemmaField: 手伝う みる
phrases.translation: [Should I] try to help? Or, depending on the context: [Can you] try to help [me]?
phrases.notes: -te form + miru: To try something out in the sense: “To give something a try and see how it goes”. Note that it does not mean "to try hard" in most cases, Japanese has a different expression for that covered later.

phrases.reading: うん がんばって みる よ
phrases.lemmaField: うん 頑張る みる よ
phrases.translation: Yes, [I] try to do [my] best.
phrases.notes: -te form + miru: To try something out in the sense: “To give something a try and see how it goes”. Note that it does not mean "to try hard" in most cases, Japanese has a different expression for that covered later.

phrases.reading: おれ も がんばって みる
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 も 頑張る みる
phrases.translation: I also try to do [my] best.
phrases.notes: -te form + miru: To try something out in the sense: “To give something a try and see how it goes”. Note that it does not mean "to try hard" in most cases, Japanese has a different expression for that covered later.

phrases.japanese: お父さんに聞いてみるよ
phrases.reading: おとうさん に きいて みる よ
phrases.lemmaField: お父さん に 聞く みる よ
phrases.translation: [I don't know, but] try to ask [your] father.
phrases.notes:
-te form + miru: To try something out in the sense: “To give something a try and see how it goes”. Note that it does not mean "to try hard" in most cases, Japanese has a different expression for that covered later.

Remark: kiku means both to hear and to ask, have a look at the hinative link if this confuses you.

phrases.reading: わたし の たべて みる
phrases.lemmaField: 私 の 食べる みる
phrases.translation: [Do you want to] try to eat mine? -> Do you want to try my icecream?
phrases.notes: -te form + miru: To try something out in the sense: “To give something a try and see how it goes”. Note that it does not mean "to try hard" in most cases, Japanese has a different expression for that covered later.

phrases.japanese: 分かったよ帰って考えてみる
phrases.reading: わかった よ かえって かんがえて みる
phrases.lemmaField: 分かる よ 帰る 考える みる
phrases.translation: [I] got it. [I] go home and try to think [about it].
phrases.notes:
-te form + miru: To try something out in the sense: “To give something a try and see how it goes”. Note that it does not mean "to try hard" in most cases, Japanese has a different expression for that covered later.

Here we have 3 verbs chained by the te-form: "Go home, think and see".

phrases.japanese: どれがおいしかったか聞いてみるの
phrases.reading: どれ が おいしかった か きいて みる の
phrases.lemmaField: どれ が おいしい か 聞く みる の
phrases.romaji: dore ga oishikatta ka kiite miru no
phrases.translation: [I] try to ask which one was tasty -> I try to ask which one they liked.
phrases.notes:
-te form + miru: To try something out in the sense: “To give something a try and see how it goes”. Note that it does not mean "to try hard" in most cases, Japanese has a different expression for that covered later.

This also is a nice example for a relative clause ending on "ka". Remember: This allows you to talk about a question, the question of "dore ga oishikatta ka - which one was tasty?" in this case.
phrases.source: Honzuki - Ascendance of a Bookworm S1 (JP Only)

phrases.reading: けんじ に きいて みた
phrases.lemmaField: ケンジ に 聞く みる
phrases.translation: [I] tried to ask kenji.
phrases.notes: -te form + miru: To try something out (not: to try hard)

phrases.japanese: でも僕は目を閉じて考えてみた
phrases.reading: でも ぼく は め を とじて かんがえて みた
phrases.lemmaField: でも 僕 は 目 を 閉じる 考える みる
phrases.romaji: demo boku ha me wo tojite kangaete mita
phrases.translation: But as for me, [I] closed my eyes and tried to think [about it].
phrases.notes:
tojiru: to close (e.g. book, eyes, meeting, etc.); to shut
-te form + miru: To try something out (not: to try hard)

Note that the past tense of "miru" applies to the entire te-chain.

phrases.reading: かんがえて みます
phrases.lemmaField: 考える みる
phrases.translation: [I] try to think [about it].
phrases.notes: -te form + miru: To try something out (not: to try hard)

phrases.japanese: 分かりました聞いてみます
phrases.reading: わかりました きいて みます
phrases.lemmaField: 分かる 聞く みる
phrases.translation: Got it. [I] try to ask.
phrases.notes: -te form + miru: To try something out (not: to try hard)
phrases.source: Midnight Diner Tokyo Stories S1 (jp only)

phrases.japanese: 分かりました捜してみます
phrases.reading: わかりました さがして みます
phrases.lemmaField: 分かる 捜す みる
phrases.translation: Got it. [I] try to search [for it].
phrases.notes: -te form + miru: To try something out (not: to try hard)

phrases.japanese: 分かりましたもう少し待ってみます
phrases.reading: わかりました もうすこし まって みます
phrases.lemmaField: 分かる もう少し 待つ みる
phrases.translation: [Someone is being late here]. Got it, [I] try to wait a little longer.
phrases.notes:
mousukoshi: a bit more; a bit longer
-te form + miru: To try something out (not: to try hard)

phrases.japanese: なるほどやってみます
phrases.reading: なるほど やって みます
phrases.lemmaField: なるほど やる みる
phrases.translation: I see, [I] try to do [it, physical action; the conversation revolves around training fighting skills].
phrases.notes:
naruhodo: I see; that's right; indeed
-te form + miru: To try something out (not: to try hard)

phrases.reading: さがして みました
phrases.lemmaField: 探す みる
phrases.translation: [I] tried to search [for it].
phrases.notes: -te form + miru: To try something out (not: to try hard)

phrases.reading: つくって みました
phrases.lemmaField: 作る みる
phrases.translation: [I] tried to prepare / make [a set of photobooks in this case, but also e.g. a meal].
phrases.notes: -te form + miru: To try something out (not: to try hard)
phrases.source: Ouran High School Host Club (jp eng)

phrases.japanese: パンダくんに聞いて作ってみました
phrases.reading: ぱんだ くん に きいて つくって みました
phrases.lemmaField: パンダ くん に 聞く 作る みる
phrases.romaji: panda kun ni kiite tsukutte mimashita
phrases.translation: [I] asked Panda [about a weird dish he wanted to eat: Bamboo Parfait] and tried to prepare [it].
phrases.notes: -te form + miru: To try something out (not: to try hard)

phrases.reading: かえって いく ｡
phrases.lemmaField: 帰る いく ｡
phrases.translation: [I] go home.
phrases.notes:
-te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future).

This is already the dictionary definition of "kaeru", but together with iku it means to leave a certain place, i.e. the action is directed away from e.g. you friend's place. kaette kuru on the other hand means to return home, i.e. the "going home" is directed towards someone's home.

phrases.reading: かえって きません ねえ
phrases.lemmaField: 帰る くる ねえ
phrases.translation: [You] don't return home, do you?
phrases.notes:
-te kuru: directs the verb in te-form towards a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the past to the present).

Here's the "return home" counterpart with conjugated "kuru". The speaker e.g. already is at home and asks this question, i.e. the "returning home" is directed towards the joint home of the two.

phrases.reading: かさ かって いく か
phrases.lemmaField: 傘 買う 行く か
phrases.translation: [Should I] go out / away [from home] and buy an umbrella?
phrases.notes:
-te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future).

The "should" is a consequence of the "ka" in the end, this is a question the speaker asks himself.
phrases.source: Sakurasou no Pet na Kanojo (jp eng)

phrases.reading: かって くる
phrases.lemmaField: 買う くる
phrases.translation: [I] buy [it] and return.
phrases.notes:
-te kuru: directs the verb in te-form towards a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the past to the present).

Especially the "-te kuru" construct very often means to do something and then return. I.e. saying "katte kuru" while at home, this means to go out and buy something (you have to go out to do this of course, as you're at home), but then you return. Remember the previous "katte iku"? In this case, the speaker does not return anywhere, he just goes out to buy an umbrella, maybe while on his way somewhere else.

phrases.reading: かえって いった
phrases.lemmaField: 帰る いく
phrases.translation: [I] went home (emphasizing that the speaker left some place).
phrases.notes: -te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future).

phrases.reading: かえって きた
phrases.lemmaField: 帰る くる
phrases.translation: [I] came home  (emphasizing that the speaker returned).
phrases.notes: -te kuru: directs the verb in te-form towards a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the past to the present).
phrases.source: Fate Stay Night Unlimited Blade Works S02 (JP Eng)

phrases.japanese: それ持って行きますか
phrases.reading: それ もって いきます か
phrases.lemmaField: それ 持つ 行く か
phrases.translation: [Do you] take this with you [when you go]?
phrases.notes:
-te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future).

motsu (to hold (in one's hand)) is a good example for indicating direction, as it works well for both iku and kuru: Literally, "motte iku" means: to take something and go, i.e. the person leaves a place and takes something along. "motte kuru" means: to take something and come, i.e. to bring something along towards a certain place.

phrases.reading: てれび もって きた
phrases.lemmaField: テレビ 持つ くる
phrases.translation: [I] brought a television.
phrases.notes:
-te kuru: directs the verb in te-form towards a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the past to the present).

motsu (to hold (in one's hand)) is a good example for indicating direction, as it works well for both iku and kuru: Literally, "motte iku" means: to take something and go, i.e. the person leaves a place and takes something along. "motte kuru" means: to take something and come, i.e. to bring something along towards a certain place.

phrases.reading: きょう もって きた
phrases.lemmaField: 今日 持つ くる
phrases.translation: [I] brought [it] today.
phrases.notes:
-te kuru: directs the verb in te-form towards a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the past to the present).

motsu (to hold (in one's hand)) is a good example for indicating direction, as it works well for both iku and kuru: Literally, "motte iku" means: to take something and go, i.e. the person leaves a place and takes something along. "motte kuru" means: to take something and come, i.e. to bring something along towards a certain place.

phrases.japanese: 今度お酒でも持っていきます
phrases.reading: こんど おさけ でも もって いきます
phrases.lemmaField: 今度 お酒 でも 持つ いく
phrases.translation: Next time [we even] take alcohol (beverage) with us.
phrases.notes:
-te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future).
"demo" means "even" here, just ignore it if that confuses you.

phrases.reading: にげて いきます よ
phrases.lemmaField: 逃げる いく よ
phrases.translation: [I] flee [away from this place].
phrases.notes:
-te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future).

Note that -te iku can also direct an action away from the current point in time. In this case, -te iku refers to starting something - this could also apply here I'd say, see this page for more details.

phrases.reading: ちから が ぬけて いく
phrases.lemmaField: 力 が 抜ける いく
phrases.translation: [My] power is fading.
phrases.notes:
-te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future).
nukeru: to fade, to be missing (this has many more meanings, but together with "chikara" it means this).

Note that -te iku can also direct an action away from the current point in time, which is the case here. -te iku emphasizes a continuing change here, see this page for more details.

phrases.japanese: 僕の人生は変わっていく
phrases.reading: ぼく の じんせい は かわって いく
phrases.lemmaField: 僕 の 人生 は 変わる いく
phrases.romaji: boku no jinsei ha kawatte iku
phrases.translation: As for my life, [it] is changing.
phrases.notes:
-te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future).
kawaru: to change

phrases.japanese: だんだん強くなっていく
phrases.reading: だんだん つよく なって いく
phrases.lemmaField: だんだん 強い なる いく
phrases.translation: [He] gradually becomes stronger.
phrases.notes:
-te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future).
dandan: gradually; by degrees; little by little; more and more

I think you could also say "tsuyoku natte iru" to express the continuous state of becoming strong. However, "tsuyoku natte iku" puts more emphasis on the change over time, see this page for more details.

phrases.reading: れんしゅう して いく
phrases.lemmaField: 練習 する いく
phrases.translation: [I] go out to practice. Saying "renshuu ni shite kita" would direct this towards a certain place you're visiting - "I came to practice".
phrases.notes:
-te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future).
renshuu: practice; training; drill

phrases.reading: あるいて いく
phrases.lemmaField: 歩く いく
phrases.translation: [Do you want to] go for a walk?
phrases.notes:
-te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future).
aruku: to walk

phrases.japanese: 俺もこれから頑張っていくから
phrases.reading: おれ も これから がんばって いく から
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 も これから 頑張る いく から
phrases.romaji: ore mo korekara ganbatte iku kara
phrases.translation: [I] also do my best from now on.
phrases.grammarNote: Ignore the trailing "kara" here.
phrases.notes:
-te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future).
korekara: from now on; after this; in the future

Here, the -te iku again directs the verb away from a given point in time and emphasizes a continuing change.
phrases.source: Fate Stay Night Unlimited Blade Works S02 (JP Eng)

phrases.reading: はなれて いく よ
phrases.lemmaField: 離れる いく よ
phrases.translation: [I] let [it] go [from now on].
phrases.notes:
-te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future).
hanareru: to be separated, to lose connection with; to drift away from

Here, the -te iku again directs the verb away from a given point in time and emphasizes a continuing change.

phrases.reading: さがして くる
phrases.lemmaField: 捜す くる
phrases.translation: [I] come and search -> the searching is directed towards someone, maybe the speaker wants to help.
phrases.notes:
-te kuru: directs the verb in te-form towards a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the past to the present).
If the speaker says this to someone who is currently near to him, it would mean: I search something and then come back. Or in other words: "-te kuru" very often means: "I do xxx and come back".

phrases.japanese: 飲み物忘れた買ってくる
phrases.reading: のみもの わすれた かって くる
phrases.lemmaField: 飲み物 忘れる 買う くる
phrases.translation: [I] forgot [my] drink. [I] go buy one and return.
phrases.notes:
-te kuru: directs the verb in te-form towards a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the past to the present).

Especially the "-te kuru" construct very often means to do something and then return. I.e. saying "katte kuru" while at home, this means to go out and buy something (you have to go out to do this of course, as you're at home), but then you return. Remember the previous "katte iku"? In this case, the speaker does not return anywhere, he just goes out to buy an umbrella, maybe while on his way somewhere else.
phrases.source: The World God Only Knows S3 (jp eng)

phrases.reading: おちゃ いれて くる ね
phrases.lemmaField: お茶 入れる くる ね
phrases.translation: [I] go and make tea -> note that "I go and do xxx" is expressed not using "go" but "come" in Japanese (by means of -te kuru).
phrases.notes:
ireru: to put in; to let in; to take in; to bring in
Note that in the context of tea of coffee, "ocha/kohii wo ireru" simply means: to make coffee or tea. This is covered in a nice instructional video in about 1000 cards.

phrases.japanese: 相手は強くなっていく
phrases.reading: あいて は つよく なって いく
phrases.lemmaField: 相手 は 強い なる いく
phrases.translation: [You] opponent continuously becomes stronger.
phrases.notes:
-te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future).

-te iku refers to a change over time / away from the current point in time, see this page for more details.

phrases.reading: ちかく なって きた ぞ
phrases.lemmaField: 近く なる くる ぞ
phrases.translation: [Something] became close.
phrases.notes:
-te kuru: directs the verb in te-form towards a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the past to the present).

Here, "chikaku naru - to become close" is directed towards the current point in time. I'd say "natte iku/kuru" most of the time refer to a point in time.

phrases.japanese: 私も持ってきてるわよ
phrases.reading: わたし も もって きてる わ よ
phrases.lemmaField: 私 も 持つ くる わ よ
phrases.romaji: watashi mo motte kiteru wa yo
phrases.translation: [I am] also bringing [something] -> "motte kiteru -> motte kite iru" is the present progressive form of motte kuru.
phrases.notes:
Unfortunately, the "-te iku" constructions can be -te-connected further - "iku" is a verb and may be conjugated, after all! I found these chains of verbs to be one of the most difficult part to understand quickly by listening comprehension. I'll add more of them to the very end of this course, but this example gives you an idea how this looks like.

Just ignore this card, if it's still too difficult.

phrases.reading: なんで もって きてる の
phrases.lemmaField: 何で 持つ くる の
phrases.translation: Why are [you] bringing [this]? -> "motte kiteru -> motte kite iru" is the present progressive form of motte kuru.
phrases.notes:
Unfortunately, the "-te iku" constructions can be -te-connected further - "iku" is a verb and may be conjugated, after all! I found these chains of verbs to be one of the most difficult part to understand quickly by listening comprehension. I'll add more of them to the very end of this course, but this example gives you an idea how this looks like.

Just ignore this card, if it's still too difficult.

phrases.reading: いってきます
phrases.lemmaField: 行ってきます
phrases.translation: A very interesting expression you might now understand better is this one: "itte kimasu" is a common phrase people in Japan say when leaving the house. It means "I go and come back".

phrases.reading: いってらっしゃい
phrases.lemmaField: いってらっしゃい 行ってらっしゃい
phrases.translation: The answer to "ittekimasu" from someone who stays at home is "itterasshai - take care". The grammar of this will be covered later though.

phrases.reading: しまった
phrases.lemmaField: しまる
phrases.translation: "shimatta" is past tense of "shimau". In pretty much all cases, this means: "Oh no, I screwed [something] up". Just look at the guy's face...
phrases.notes: Interesting here is, that "shimau" is rarely used on its own. It almost always is used either in its past tense like on this card, or together with another verb in te-form (which comes next). Therefore I don't list its meanings in the deck, have a look at the dictionary, if you're interested.

phrases.reading: おりる か おまえ
phrases.lemmaField: 降りる か お前
phrases.translation: [Do] you [want to] get off [the scooter]?
phrases.notes:
oriru: to descend (e.g. a mountain); to go down; to come down​

Remark: There are dedicated ways to express "want to", covererd in about 300 cards.

phrases.reading: いちばん すき だった ふく だ
phrases.lemmaField: 一番 好き だ 服 だ 一番上
phrases.translation: [These are] the clothes [I] liked most.
phrases.notes: ichiban: number one; first; best; most

phrases.reading: ぜったい に みつける から
phrases.lemmaField: 絶対 に 見つける から
phrases.translation: [Someone is missing here. Don't worry] because [we] absolutely will find [her].
phrases.notes: mitsukeru: to discover; to find (e.g. an error in a book or someone who's missing), to locate

phrases.japanese: これトイレ行くときどうするの
phrases.reading: これ といれ いく とき どう する の
phrases.lemmaField: これ トイレ 行く とき どう する の ある時 あるとき そのとき
phrases.romaji: kore toire iku toki dou suru no
phrases.translation: When [I need to] go to the toilet, what [should I] do? -> The speaker is the girl on the bench, she wrapped her sleeping bag with foil to make it warmer and can't move anymore.
phrases.grammarNote: The speaker is the girl on the bench, she wrapped her sleeping bag with foil to make it warmer and can't move anymore.
phrases.notes: toki: time; hour; moment​. One important use of this word is to express "when doing X, then", just as in this sentence. In such a construction, "toki" is always described by a preceding clause ("toire iku" in this case). More examples later...

phrases.reading: わらって しまう わ
phrases.lemmaField: 笑う しまう わ
phrases.translation: To laugh (unintentionally). Note that "-te shimau" sounds rather formal, even though it's in plain form. The more casual forms will be covered a few cards later.
phrases.notes: -te shimau: The verb in -te form was done unintentionally, often with bad or unsatisfactory result.

phrases.japanese: 殺すことになってしまう
phrases.reading: ころす こと に なって しまう
phrases.lemmaField: 殺す こと に なる しまう
phrases.translation: [If we go there, we] will get killed (which of course is unintended and a pretty unsatisfactory result).
phrases.notes:
-te shimau: The verb in -te form was done unintentionally, often with bad or unsatisfactory result.

Note that "-te shimau" sounds rather formal, even though it's in plain form. The more casual forms will be covered a few cards later.

phrases.reading: まけて しまう
phrases.lemmaField: 負ける しまう
phrases.translation: [I am] defeated.
phrases.notes:
-te shimau: The verb in -te form was done unintentionally, often with bad or unsatisfactory result.

Note that "-te shimau" sounds rather formal, even though it's in plain form. The more casual forms will be covered a few cards later.
phrases.source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure スターダストクルセイダース

phrases.reading: きいて しまう
phrases.lemmaField: 聞く しまう
phrases.translation: [I] unintentionally heard [it]. Depending on the context, it could also mean: [He] heard [what I said, even though it was not intended for him].
phrases.notes:
-te shimau: The verb in -te form was done unintentionally, often with bad or unsatisfactory result.

Note that "-te shimau" sounds rather formal, even though it's in plain form. The more casual forms will be covered a few cards later.

phrases.reading: どう なって しまう の
phrases.lemmaField: どう なる しまう の
phrases.translation: How / in what way will it go / become? The "shimau" here indicates that something out of the speaker's control changes.
phrases.notes:
-te shimau: The verb in -te form was done unintentionally, often with bad or unsatisfactory result.

Note that "-te shimau" sounds rather formal, even though it's in plain form. The more casual forms will be covered a few cards later.

phrases.japanese: それじゃバレてしまいますよ
phrases.reading: それ じゃ ばれて しまいます よ
phrases.lemmaField: それ じゃ バレる しまう よ
phrases.translation: Well then, [it] comes out [e.g. the secret the listener wants to keep].
phrases.notes:
-te shimau: The verb in -te form was done unintentionally, often with bad or unsatisfactory result.
bareru: to leak out (a secret); to be exposed (a lie, improper behaviour, etc.)

phrases.reading: かわって しまった の
phrases.lemmaField: 変わる しまう の
phrases.translation: [He] has changed [possibly to the bad].
phrases.notes: -te shimau: The verb in -te form was done unintentionally, often with bad or unsatisfactory result.

phrases.japanese: 全てなくなってしまった
phrases.reading: すべて なくなって しまった
phrases.lemmaField: 全て なくなる しまう
phrases.translation: Everthing is lost.
phrases.notes: -te shimau: The verb in -te form was done unintentionally, often with bad or unsatisfactory result.
phrases.source: Boku no Hero Academia_ Futari no Hero

phrases.japanese: 俺が失ってしまった時間
phrases.reading: おれ が うしなって しまった じかん
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 が 失う しまう 時間
phrases.translation: [I can't get back] the time I lost.
phrases.notes: -te shimau: The verb in -te form was done unintentionally, often with bad or unsatisfactory result.
phrases.source: Erased - 僕だけがいない街

phrases.japanese: また強くなってしまったか
phrases.reading: また つよく なって しまった か
phrases.lemmaField: また 強い なる しまう か
phrases.translation: [I] wonder if [it] became strong again [maybe a monster the guy is fighting].
phrases.notes: -te shimau: The verb in -te form was done unintentionally, often with bad or unsatisfactory result.

phrases.japanese: ごめんなさい迷惑かけてしまいます
phrases.reading: ごめんなさい めいわく かけて しまいます
phrases.lemmaField: ごめんなさい 迷惑 かける しまう
phrases.translation: meiwaku wo kakeru: to cause someone trouble. "kakeru" is a word with many meanings, I'll add a few examples later.
phrases.notes: -te shimau: The verb in -te form was done unintentionally, often with bad or unsatisfactory result.

phrases.reading: おそく なって しまった
phrases.lemmaField: 遅い なる しまう
phrases.translation: [I] became late.
phrases.notes: -te shimau: The verb in -te form was done unintentionally, often with bad or unsatisfactory result.

phrases.japanese: どうしてそんなに変わってしまったの
phrases.reading: どうして そんなにかわって しまった の
phrases.lemmaField: どうして そんなに 変わる しまう の
phrases.translation: [I wonder] why [he] has changed that much.
phrases.notes: -te shimau: The verb in -te form was done unintentionally, often with bad or unsatisfactory result.

phrases.japanese: わたしの世界はまるで変わってしまった
phrases.reading: わたし の せかい は まるで かわって しまった
phrases.lemmaField: わたし の 世界 は まるで 変わる しまう
phrases.romaji: watashi no sekai ha marude kawatte shimatta
phrases.translation: My world has changed completely.
phrases.notes:
-te shimau: The verb in -te form was done unintentionally, often with bad or unsatisfactory result.
marude: quite; entirely; completely

phrases.reading: まよう ね
phrases.lemmaField: 迷う ね
phrases.translation: [You're] lost, aren't you?
phrases.notes: mayou: to lose one's way; to get lost

phrases.reading: まよった
phrases.lemmaField: 迷う
phrases.translation: [I] got lost.

phrases.reading: まよって いる の か
phrases.lemmaField: 迷う いる の か
phrases.translation: Are [you] lost?

phrases.reading: まよって しまった
phrases.lemmaField: 迷う しまう
phrases.translation: [I] got lost -> now with a more negative connotation.
phrases.notes: -te shimau: The verb in -te form was done unintentionally, often with bad or unsatisfactory result.

phrases.reading: まけ ちゃう よ
phrases.lemmaField: 負ける ちゃう よ
phrases.translation: [We] are (or also, depending on context) will be defeated.
phrases.notes:
In casual speech, the entire "-te shimau" is replaced by "chau". I.e. the "-te" of the -te form is omitted. The combination again looks like a standalone verb, I keep them separated for clarity.
make chau: short for makete shimau

phrases.reading: わすれ ちゃう の
phrases.lemmaField: 忘れる ちゃう の
phrases.translation: [I can't do this] because [I] will forget [it - the protagonist of this anime loses her memory every week].
phrases.notes:
In casual speech, the entire "-te shimau" is replaced by "chau". I.e. the "-te" of the -te form is omitted. The combination again looks like a standalone verb, I keep them separated for clarity.
wasure chau: short for wasurete shimau

phrases.reading: たべ ちゃう ぞ
phrases.lemmaField: 食べる ちゃう ぞ
phrases.translation: [I] can't help but eat [it].
phrases.notes:
In casual speech, the entire "-te shimau" is replaced by "chau". I.e. the "-te" of the -te form is omitted. The combination again looks like a standalone verb, I keep them separated for clarity.
tabe chau: short for tabete shimau

Remark: In past tense (tabechatta) you could also translate this as "I ate [e.g. your sweets] by accident.

phrases.reading: せんせい ない ちゃう ぞ
phrases.lemmaField: 先生 泣く ちゃう ぞ
phrases.translation: The teacher cries [maybe the outcome of some bad action or prank].
phrases.notes:
In casual speech, the entire "-te shimau" is replaced by "chau". I.e. the "-te" of the -te form is omitted. The combination again looks like a standalone verb.
nai chau: short for naite shimau

phrases.reading: わらっちゃう わ よ ね
phrases.lemmaField: 笑う わ よ ね
phrases.translation: [They] laugh, don't they! [e.g. the speaker mentioned something and didn't expect the audience to laugh].
phrases.notes:
In casual speech, the entire "-te shimau" is replaced by "chau". I.e. the "-te" of the -te form is omitted. The combination again looks like a standalone verb.

If the -te form contains a "tt" (warau -> waratte, i.e. prolonged pronunciation of the consonant "t"), the casual "chau" becomes "cchau", i.e. it also has a prolonged consonant. Reminder: In real Japanese, the small "tsu/っ"-character is used for expressing this, it prolongs pronunciation of the following consonant-based sound.

waracchau: short for waratte shimau

phrases.reading: ほんとうに かえっちゃう の
phrases.lemmaField: 本当に 帰る の
phrases.translation: Do you really return / go home? Maybe the speaker said something that made the others go home, so their return is unexpected.
phrases.notes:
In casual speech, the entire "-te shimau" is replaced by "chau". I.e. the "-te" of the -te form is omitted. The combination again looks like a standalone verb.

If the -te form contains a "tt" (warau -> waratte, i.e. prolonged pronunciation of the consonant "t"), the casual "chau" becomes "cchau", i.e. it also has a prolonged consonant. Reminder: In real Japanese, the small "tsu/っ"-character is used for expressing this, it prolongs pronunciation of the following consonant-based sound.

kaecchau: short for kaette shimau

phrases.japanese: どうなっちゃうんだろう
phrases.reading: どう なっちゃう ん だろう
phrases.lemmaField: どう なる ん だ
phrases.translation: How will [it] become / turn out, I wonder? [There are things going on which are out of the speaker's control, i.e. the "naru" happens automatically].
phrases.notes:
In casual speech, the entire "-te shimau" is replaced by "chau". I.e. the "-te" of the -te form is omitted. The combination again looks like a standalone verb.

If the -te form contains a "tt" (warau -> waratte, i.e. prolonged pronunciation of the consonant "t"), the casual "chau" becomes "cchau", i.e. it also has a prolonged consonant. Reminder: In real Japanese, the small "tsu/っ"-character is used for expressing this, it prolongs pronunciation of the following consonant-based sound.

nacchau: short for natte shimau

phrases.japanese: これ見ちゃったからね
phrases.reading: これ み ちゃった から ね
phrases.lemmaField: これ 見る しまう から ね
phrases.translation: [Now that I] accidentially saw this [i.e. what the listeners did... I changed my mind] -> the speaker admitted that he works for the enemy and was asked why he suddenly decided to admit this.
phrases.notes:
The "chau"-part may be conjugated to past tense.

mi chatta: short for mite shimatta

phrases.reading: ぼく きづいちゃった よ
phrases.lemmaField: 僕 気付く よ
phrases.translation: [I] accidentially noticed [something I  wasn't supposed to notice].
phrases.notes:
The "chau"-part may be conjugated to past tense.

kidzui chatta: short for kidzuite shimatta

phrases.reading: あめ に なっちゃった ね
phrases.lemmaField: 雨 に なる ね
phrases.translation: [It] started to rain, didn't it?
phrases.notes:
The "chau"-part may be conjugated to past tense.

na chatta: short for natte shimatta

phrases.japanese: コンビニ飽きちゃったのよ
phrases.reading: こんびに あきちゃった の よ
phrases.lemmaField: コンビニ 飽きる の よ
phrases.translation: [I] became sick of convenience store [food] (the "food" you can buy there often is instant stuff like cup ramen. No wonder she became sick of it).
phrases.notes:
The "chau"-part may be conjugated to past tense.

aki chatta: short for akite shimatta (akiru - to grow sick of something)

phrases.japanese: お前が死んでしまうぞ
phrases.reading: おまえ が しんで しまう ぞ
phrases.lemmaField: お前 が 死ぬ しまう ぞ
phrases.translation: [If you go there] you will die.
phrases.notes:
-te shimau: The verb in -te form was done or happens unintentionally, often with bad or unsatisfactory result.
Reminder: For some verbs, the -te form ends on "de", "shinu - to die" is one of them.

phrases.reading: しん じゃう よ
phrases.lemmaField: 死ぬ じゃう よ
phrases.translation:
If the verb's -te form ends on "-de", the casual "chau" becomes "jau".
shin jau: short for shinde shimau
phrases.notes: Again, the whitespace in "shin jau" is for emphasizing that these are actually two different words.

phrases.reading: しん じゃった
phrases.lemmaField: 死ぬ じゃう
phrases.translation:
The "jau" part may be conjugated to past tense.
shin jatta: short for shinde shimatta.
phrases.notes: Again, the whitespace in "shin jau" is for emphasizing that these are actually two different words.

phrases.reading: のん じゃった
phrases.lemmaField: 飲む じゃう
phrases.translation:
The "jau" part may be conjugated to past tense.
non jatta: short for nonde shimatta.
phrases.notes: Again, the whitespace in "shin jau" is for emphasizing that these are actually two different words.

phrases.reading: たべられる もの
phrases.lemmaField: 食べる もの
phrases.translation: [This is] a can-eat-thing (a thing you can eat).
phrases.notes:
taberareru: potential form of taberu: can / be able to eat.

For -ru verbs, replace "ru" with "rareru" to get the potential form. This expresses the ability to perform the verb. Again: There are some -u verbs also ending on "ru". Don't worry about them for now and more important: Don't try to memorize these.

phrases.reading: やられる ぞ
phrases.lemmaField: やる ぞ
phrases.translation: [If I am not careful] I will be killed / physically harmed.
phrases.grammarNote: If you see this card for the first time, just ignore it. There was a wrong explanation on the back in the past and I left it in the deck for clarification.
phrases.notes:
IMPORTANT: There was a mistake on this card in the past. I had explained "yarareru" potential form of "yaru". However, it is the passive form - sorry for that and more on this later! Just ignore this card for now.

yarareru: passive form of "yaru": to be done (a physical action). Sometimes, yaru also means to be killed or physically harmed. It also has a meaning of its own: To suffer damage, see here.

phrases.reading: たすけられる の
phrases.lemmaField: 助ける の
phrases.translation: Can [you] help [me]?
phrases.notes:
tasukerareru: potential form of tasukeru: can / be able to help

For -ru verbs, replace "ru" with "rareru" to get the potential form. This expresses the ability to perform the verb.

phrases.reading: にげられる の わたしたち
phrases.lemmaField: 逃げる の 私たち
phrases.translation: Can we escape?
phrases.notes:
nigerareru: potential form of nigeru: can / be able to escape

For -ru verbs, replace "ru" with "rareru" to get the potential form. This expresses the ability to perform the verb.

phrases.reading: わすれられる もの か
phrases.lemmaField: 忘れる もの か
phrases.translation: [Is this] a can-forget thing -> are we ever able to forget this?
phrases.notes:
wasurerareru: potential form of wasureru: can / be able to forget

For -ru verbs, replace "ru" with "rareru" to get the potential form. This expresses the ability to perform the verb.

phrases.reading: かんがえられる の は
phrases.lemmaField: 考える の は
phrases.translation: kangaerareru: potential form of kangaeru: can / be able to think about something
phrases.grammarNote: Ignore the "no ha" part, it's an incomplete sentence.
phrases.notes: For -ru verbs, replace "ru" with "rareru" to get the potential form. This expresses the ability to perform the verb.

phrases.reading: ぜんぶ たべられる の か
phrases.lemmaField: 全部 食べる の か
phrases.translation: [Are] you able to eat everything [maybe a huge pile of food was served here]?
phrases.notes:
For -ru verbs, replace "ru" with "rareru" to get the potential form. This expresses the ability to perform the verb.

During a conversation however, speakers unfortunately don't have speech bubbles popping up over their heads ;).

phrases.japanese: 俺が見られない世界を見ることができる
phrases.reading: おれ が みられない せかい を みる こと が できる
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 が 見る 世界 を 見る こと が できる
phrases.romaji: ore ga mirarenai sekai wo miru koto ga dekiru
phrases.translation: [This guy] will be able to see a world I cannot see.
phrases.notes:
Here, The speaker is a runner participating in a competition. He's talking about a different runner, who is faster than him. So "world I cannot see" is probably something like the olympics. Interestingly, this sentence could also be translated to "I could see the world I was not able to see", depending on the context.  Suspend this card if it's still too difficult, it does not introduce anything new .

Together with a relative clause, "xxx-koto ga dekiru" is another way to express the ability to do something:

"Ore ga mirarenai sekai wo miru: to see the world I cannot see" is the relative clause in this case. Together with the rest the full sentence then literally means something like: [He] will be able to do the thing of seeing a world I cannot see.

phrases.japanese: 今日食べないとおいしくなくなるわ
phrases.reading: きょう たべない と おいしくなく なる わ
phrases.lemmaField: 今日 食べる と おいしい なる わ
phrases.romaji: kyou tabenai to oishikunaku naru wa
phrases.translation: If [you] don't eat [this] today, it will be not tasty [tomorrow].
phrases.notes:
Next, we learn how to say "if" in Japanese. One out of four (!) ways is to use the particle "to" in the following sense: [condition] to [result], which means: Whenever [condition] is fulfilled, [result] will for sure happen. Note that this often translates to "when/whenever xxx then yyy" instead of "if xxx then yyy" in English.

condition: kyou tabenai (don't eat today)
result: oishikunaku naru (will become untasty, refresher: oishii -> oshikunai -> oishikunaku (adverb describing the verb "naru")

phrases.japanese: 職員室ならあっちですけど

phrases.grammarNote: Ignore the "kedo" here.
phrases.notes:
The second way to express "if" is: [condition] nara [result]. Tae Kim calls this the "contextual condition", because the condition always requires a certain context in which it occurs. This context very often is a person saying a certain thing and you're drawing a conclusion from that: "If you say xxx, then I do yyy", or: "if you do xxx then I do yyy". The key difference to "to" is that we don't have a "natural consequence" of the form "whenever a then b" here.

Note that the "if" may not immediately visible here, it's sometimes hidden by what I put into square brackets.
phrases.source: Higurashi no Naku Koro ni S1 (JP Eng)

The key difference to "to" is that we don't have a "natural consequence" of the form "whenever a then b" here.

phrases.japanese: ここにいたら危ないよ

phrases.lemmaField: ここ に いる 危ない よ
phrases.translation: If [we] are here, it's dangerous -> it's dangerous to be here.
phrases.notes: The -tara form expresses a one time (or particular) result instead of the general consequence implied by "to". Construct it by verb past tense + "ra". For the next ~20 cards, just translate this to the English "if" - I'll explain the differences between the forms afterwards.

phrases.japanese: よく考えたら俺ここにくることはなかったんだよな
phrases.reading: よく かんがえたら おれ ここ に くる こと は なかった ん だ よ な
phrases.lemmaField: よく 考える 俺 ここ に くる こと は ない ん だ よ な
phrases.romaji: yoku kangaetara ore koko ni kuru koto ha nakatta n da yo na
phrases.translation: If [I] think well, [I] was not supposed to be here [in this world].
phrases.notes:
Remark: This is the real meaning of the sentence (it's from Angel Beats, ep. 14 around 17:00), but a bit hard to translate accurately. Actually, this sentence is very difficult, but since the translation was wrong in the past, I leave it in for now. Let's break this down:
koko ni kuru koto ha nakatta - come-here thing was not, which in this case means: The actual reason that makes people come to a special world of the dead (that's where he currently is) did not exist for him. This is what translates to "I was not supposed to be here in the first place" in English. If this is too weird, just ignore this card. It does not introduce anything new.

On the other hand, "koko ni kita koto ha nai" would mean:  came-here thing does not exist -> I didn't come here

The -tara form expresses a one time (or particular) result instead of the general consequence implied by "to". Construct it by verb past tense + "ra". For the next ~20 cards, just translate this to the English "if" - I'll explain the differences between the forms afterwards.

phrases.notes: The -tara form expresses a one time (or particular) result instead of the general consequence implied by "to". Construct it by verb past tense + "ra". For the next ~20 cards, just translate this to the English "if" - I'll explain the differences between the forms afterwards.

phrases.japanese: どこに置いたらいいかな

phrases.lemmaField: どこ に 置く いい か な
phrases.romaji: doko ni oitara ii ka na
phrases.translation: Very interesting sentence, it means: I wonder where should I put this.
phrases.notes:
It takes a while to get used to the way this is expressed in Japanese. Maybe consider this:
koko ni oitara ii desu - it is ok if you put it here. Then add "ka"
koko ni oitara ii desu ka - is it ok if I put it here? Then replace the "koko - here" with "doko - where".

The -tara form expresses a one time (or particular) result instead of the general consequence implied by "to". Construct it by verb past tense + "ra". For the next ~20 cards, just translate this to the English "if" - I'll explain the differences between the forms afterwards.

phrases.reading: みて は だめ よ
phrases.lemmaField: 見る は ダメ よ
phrases.translation: Looking is no good -> [You] must not look!
phrases.notes:
In order to express that you must not do something, put the verb in -te form, add "ha/は" and then either "dame", "ikenai" or "naranai" (I'll add examples for each of these starting with dame - no good). 

In short: The pattern "-te ha dame" is used to express that you must not do something, it means: "doing [something] is no good".

Note that the concept of "must not do something" is expressed in a completely different way in Japanese. It requires some time to get used to this, because it is expressed by a negation. Therefore, I'll add the literal translation and the English way to express this next to each other.
phrases.source: Sakurasou no Pet na Kanojo (jp eng)

phrases.reading: まって たたかって は だめ
phrases.lemmaField: 待つ 戦う は 駄目
phrases.translation: Wait! Fighting is no good -> you must not fight!
phrases.notes:
In order to express that you must not do something, put the verb in -te form, add "ha/は" and then either "dame", "ikenai" or "naranai" (I'll add examples for each of these starting with dame - no good). 

In short: The pattern "-te ha dame" is used to express that you must not do something, it means: "doing [something] is no good".

The literal translation can also mean something different in English (a general judgement). However, it's tied to the pattern "-te ha dame/ikenai/narani" and the "must not do"-context here.

phrases.reading: さあ たべよう
phrases.lemmaField: さあ 食べる
phrases.translation: Let's eat.
phrases.notes:
In Japanese, you can express "let's do ..." or "shall we do ..." using the volitional form. As a sloppy rule of thumb: If a verb somehow ends on "ou", it's in the (casual) volitional form (some exceptions apply).

Here are more precise rules: for ru verbs, replace the last "ru/る" with "you/よう", e.g. taberu -> tabeyou. For -u verbs, change the u-vowel sound to the respective o-vowel sound (ku/く -> ko/こ, su/す -> so/そ, etc.) and append "u", e.g. wakaru -> wakarou. I'll stick to the sloppy rule of thumb on the following cards ;).

I'll stick to the sloppy rule of thumb on the following cards ;).

phrases.reading: 「ありがとう」 と いった
phrases.lemmaField: 「ありがとう」 と 言う
phrases.translation: [He] said: "thank you".
phrases.notes:
In order to quote someone, you append "to itta" to the sentence the person said. "itta" is past tense of "iu - to say".

Note that the person who said "thank you" is not named here. It is known from context and therefore omitted as usual. If you want to name someone explicitly, you'd say: "tanaka-san ha arigatou to itta - Mr. tanaka said thank you". 

In Japanese, quotation marks look like this: 「」. In anime subtitles, they're usually not found, but on the following cards I added them for clarity. They have a special role, I'll comment on that again in a few cards.

phrases.japanese: 「話を聞きたい」と言ったのに

phrases.notes:
In order to quote someone, you append "to itta" to the sentence the person said. "itta" is past tense of "iu - to say".

Note that the person who said something is not named here. It is known from context and therefore omitted as usual.

phrases.japanese: いつ私が「あなたを好きだ」と言いましたか
phrases.reading: いつ わたし が 「あなた を すき だ」 と いいました か
phrases.lemmaField: いつ 私 が 「あなた を 好き だ」 と 言う か
phrases.romaji: itsu watashi ga 「anata wo suki da」 to iimashita ka
phrases.translation: When did I say: "I like you"?! -> Here the speaker is given, it's "watashi", so the speaker is quoting herself.
phrases.notes:
In order to quote someone, you append "to itta" to the sentence the person said. "itta" is past tense of "iu - to say".

Note that we do not have a direct quote here, because the speaker expresses that he never actually says "I like you". In this case (musing about something or "interpreted quotes" as Tae Kim calls it), the quotation marks are actually not used. I'll leave them on the following cards for clarity.

phrases.japanese: 誰が「寝ていい」と言った
phrases.reading: だれ が 「ねて いい」 と いった
phrases.lemmaField: 誰 が 「寝る いい」 と 言う
phrases.translation: Who said "it's ok to sleep"?! -> The player is lying on the floor, I guess he's not sleeping, but the trainer seems to be tough and strict.
phrases.notes: In order to quote someone, you append "to itta" to the sentence the person said. "itta" is past tense of "iu - to say".
phrases.source: Saiki Kusuo no Psi Nan S1 (斉木楠雄のΨ難 第1期)

phrases.japanese: 「分かっている」と言っただろう
phrases.reading: 「わかって いる」 と いった だろう
phrases.lemmaField: 「分かる いる」 と 言う だ
phrases.translation: [I] thought [you] said: "I'm getting it".
phrases.notes:
In order to quote someone, you append "to itta" to the sentence the person said. "itta" is past tense of "iu - to say".

Note that we again do not have a direct quote here, because the speaker is not sure if the other person really said something. In this case (musing about something or "interpreted quotes" as Tae Kim calls it), the quotation marks are actually not used. I'll leave them on the following cards for clarity.

phrases.japanese: 今日は「帰る」って言ったじゃないですか
phrases.reading: きょう は 「かえる」 って いった じゃない です か
phrases.lemmaField: 今日 は 「帰る」 って 言う じゃ です か
phrases.romaji: kyou ha 「kaeru」 tte itta janai desu ka
phrases.translation: Didn't [you] say that we go home today?
phrases.notes:
The "to" of "to iu / itta" is often abbreviated as "tte". Note that this only applies to this quotation context, not e.g. the conditional "to". We already had a few examples of this on earlier cards.

Again, no direct quote but quotation marks for clarity - the 「」-marks are only used for real, direct quotes. Since I practice Japanese pretty much only by listening comprehension myself, I can't tell you more ;).

phrases.japanese: 「聞こえない」って言ったじゃないか
phrases.reading: 「きこえない」 って いった じゃない か
phrases.lemmaField: 「聞こえる」 って 言う じゃ か っていう
phrases.translation:
Person A: Why are you screaming?!
Speaker: Didn't [you] say: [I] can't hear [you]?
phrases.notes: In practice, the "to" of "to iu" is often spelled "tte/って". It's easier pronounced and casual.

phrases.reading: さびしい って いったら
phrases.lemmaField: 寂しい って 言う
phrases.translation: If [you] say [you] are lonely, [then we need to do something].
phrases.notes:
So far, we had direct quotes (someone was quoted 1:1) and indirect quotes (the speaker mused about what someone might have said - the current card is another example for that). By conjugating "iu", you get even more possible meanings ("If you said" in this case). All of these have in common that you talk about what someone (might have) said.

In practice, the "to" of "to iu" is often spelled "tte/って". It's easier pronounced and casual.

phrases.japanese: 待ってるって言ったのに
phrases.reading: まってる って いった のに
phrases.lemmaField: 待つ って 言う のに
phrases.translation: [You already left] even though [you] said: [I] am waiting.
phrases.notes: In practice, the "to" of "to iu" is often spelled "tte/って". It's easier pronounced and casual.

phrases.japanese: きれいな名前だなって
phrases.reading: きれい な なまえ だ な って
phrases.lemmaField: きれい だ 名前 だ な って
phrases.romaji: kirei na namae da na tte
phrases.translation: [She] said: "It's a beautiful name".
phrases.notes:
In practice, the "to" of "to iu" is often spelled "tte/って". It's easier pronounced and casual.
In case of "tte", the "iu" can be skipped. Again, it's casual!

phrases.reading: つよい って きいた けど
phrases.lemmaField: 強い って 聞く けど
phrases.translation: [I wanted to drink booze] but [I] heard that it's strong. Or: [I wanted to fight the monster] but I heard that it's strong.
phrases.notes: Instead of "iu - to say", you can also use other words, for example "kiku - to hear" or "yobu - to call". Again, all of these expressions have in common, that you talk about something that someone said. With "kiku", you express that you heard something.

phrases.japanese: 昔私にも先生と呼ぶ人がいたの
phrases.reading: むかし わたし に も せんせい と よぶ ひと が いた の
phrases.lemmaField: 昔 私 に も 先生 と 呼ぶ 人 が いる の
phrases.romaji: mukashi watashi ni mo sensei to yobu hito ga ita no
phrases.translation: Long time ago, there were people who also called me "sensei".
phrases.notes:
Instead of "iu - to say", you can also use other words, for example "kiku - to hear" or "yobu - to call". Again, all of these expressions have in common, that you talk about something that someone said. With "to yobu", you explain how someone is called.

"to yobu" refers to "sensei" here. It's used as clause to describe "hito".

phrases.japanese: これからあなたをヒルダと呼ぶことにする
phrases.reading: これから あなた を ひるだ と よぶ こと に する
phrases.lemmaField: これから あなた を ヒルダ と 呼ぶ こと に する
phrases.romaji: korekara anata wo hiruda to yobu koto ni suru
phrases.translation: From now on, [I] will call you "hiruda".
phrases.notes:
Instead of "iu - to say", you can also use other words, for example "kiku - to hear" or "yobu - to call". Again, all of these expressions have in common, that you talk about something that someone said. With "to yobu", you explain how someone is called.

Remark: The "ni suru" at the end of the sentence usually means "to decide on"
phrases.source: Legend of the Galactic Heroes (JP Eng) (Media Added)

phrases.japanese: 遅くなると思うんだけど
