phrases.notes: "to omou" is another very useful example for talking about a relative clause. It allows to express what you think.

phrases.japanese: 私が話すと思うのかい
phrases.reading: わたし が はなす と おもう の かい
phrases.lemmaField: 私 が 話す と 思う の かい
phrases.romaji: watashi ga hanasu to omou no kai
phrases.translation: [You] think that I would say [it]?
phrases.notes: You can also use "to omou" to talk about what others think, but only if you formulate this as question. You don't know what's really on the person's mind! There are other ways to express this, which are covered later.

phrases.reading: たぶん ねこ だ と おもう
phrases.lemmaField: たぶん 猫 だ と 思う
phrases.translation: [I] think [this strange looking thing] is maybe a cat.

phrases.japanese: 何か意味があるんだと思う
phrases.reading: なにか いみ が ある ん だ と おもう
phrases.lemmaField: 何か 意味 が ある ん だ と 思う
phrases.romaji: nanika imi ga aru n da to omou
phrases.translation: [I] think there's some meaning [to this] -> maybe a strange thing is happening here.

phrases.japanese: 悪い話ではないと思うが
phrases.reading: わるい はなし で は ない と おもう が
phrases.lemmaField: 悪い 話 で は ない と 思う が
phrases.romaji: warui hanashi de ha nai to omou ga
phrases.translation: [I] don't think this is a bad conversation but...
phrases.notes:
Refreshers:
"ga" means "but" here.
de ha nai is a negative form of "da".

phrases.japanese: ‪多分温かくなると思うけど‬
phrases.reading: ‪ たぶん あたたかく なる と おもう けど ‬
phrases.lemmaField: ‪ 多分 温かい なる と 思う けど ‬
phrases.romaji: ‪ tabun atatakaku naru to omou kedo ‬
phrases.translation: [It is still cold] but [I] think it maybe gets warmer.

phrases.japanese: 夢じゃないかと思った
phrases.reading: ゆめ じゃない か と おもった
phrases.lemmaField: 夢 じゃ か と 思う
phrases.translation: [I] thought: Isn't this a dream?

phrases.reading: なつめ と いいます
phrases.lemmaField: 夏目 と 言う
phrases.translation: [I] am called "natsume" or: [You] call me "natsume".
phrases.notes:
I hope it became clear from the previous examples that the person who's actually saying something can be omitted very often and in general can be anybody. Moreover, it's not even necessary, that someone actually said something, which is the case here: There's no real speaker involved, but a generic one.

This sentence expresses, that people in general call the guy "natsume".

phrases.japanese: 相手はユウスケさんという人です
phrases.reading: あいて は ゆうすけ さん という ひと です
phrases.lemmaField: 相手 は ユウスケ さん という 人 です
phrases.romaji: aite ha yuusuke san toiu hito desu
phrases.translation: As for [your] opponent, it's a person called yuusuke.
phrases.notes: Together with "to", "iu" ultimately can become a generic verb that just allows to talk about a complete, "quoted" sentence. As Tae Kim explains, this can be used to describe anything. In many cases, this translates to "a thing called xxx", like in this example, but not always.

phrases.japanese: 俺はあなたを食べようとした
phrases.reading: おれ は あなた を たべよう と した
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 は あなた を 食べる と する
phrases.romaji: ore ha anata wo tabeyou to shita
phrases.translation: As for me, [I] attempted to eat you [which seemed to be hard].
phrases.notes: Do you remember "tabete miru" from previous cards? The "-te miru" construct means to try out some action and see how you like it. On this card, we have a similar construction: verb volitional (you/ou-form) + to suru, which means "to attempt to do something". Tae Kim actually explained these forms together, as both mean to try something. While no effort is required for "-te miru", an effort might be required with "verb-volitional to suru".

phrases.japanese: 僕はそれをやろうとしてるんだよ
phrases.reading: ぼく は それ を やろう と してる ん だ よ
phrases.lemmaField: 僕 は それ を やる と する ん だ よ
phrases.romaji: boku ha sore wo yarou to shiteru n da yo
phrases.translation: As for me, I'm attempting to do that [physical action]. This sounds weird in English, but matches the progressive form (-te iru / shiteru).
phrases.notes: Verb volitional (you/ou-form) + to suru: To attempt to do something.

phrases.japanese: でも誰も助けようとしなかったの
phrases.reading: でも だれも たすけよう と しなかった の
phrases.lemmaField: でも 誰も 助ける と する の
phrases.romaji: demo daremo tasukeyou to shinakatta no
phrases.translation: But didn't anyone attempt to save [you]?
phrases.notes: Verb volitional (you/ou-form) + to suru: To attempt to do something.

phrases.japanese: 何を隠そうとしてるの
phrases.reading: なに を かくそう と してる の
phrases.lemmaField: 何 を 隠す と する の
phrases.romaji: nani wo kakusou to shiteru no
phrases.translation: What are [you] attempting to hide?
phrases.notes: Verb volitional (you/ou-form) + to suru: To attempt to do something.

phrases.reading: にげよう と した のに
phrases.lemmaField: 逃げる と する のに
phrases.translation: [We're still here], even though [we] attempted to escape.
phrases.notes: Verb volitional (you/ou-form) + to suru: To attempt to do something.

phrases.reading: もどろう と して います
phrases.lemmaField: 戻る と する いる
phrases.translation: [I] am attempting to go back / return.
phrases.notes: Verb volitional (you/ou-form) + to suru: To attempt to do something.
phrases.source: JoJos Bizarre Adventure 黄金の風 (1-25)

phrases.japanese: よく分かったな俺が言おうとしたこと
phrases.reading: よく わかった な おれ が いおう と した こと
phrases.lemmaField: よく 分かる な 俺 が 言う と する こと
phrases.romaji: yoku wakatta na ore ga iou to shita koto
phrases.translation: [You] understood it well, what [I] attempted to say?!
phrases.notes: Verb volitional (you/ou-form) + to suru: To attempt to do something.

phrases.japanese: 仲良くしようとするのも
phrases.reading: なかよく しよう と する の も
phrases.lemmaField: 仲良く する と する の も
phrases.romaji: nakayoku shiyou to suru no mo
phrases.translation: [I] attempt to get along well [with you].
phrases.grammarNote: Ignore the "no mo" in the end.
phrases.notes:
nakayoku: on good terms with; on cordial terms with; getting along well with

Verb volitional (you/ou-form) + to suru: To attempt to do something.

phrases.japanese: 動きを止めようとしているんだ
phrases.reading: うごき を とめよう と して いる ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: 動き を 止める と する いる ん だ
phrases.romaji: ugoki wo tomeyou to shite iru n da
phrases.translation: [We] are attempting to stop the motion (maybe they are fighting something strong and are trying to come up with a good strategy).
phrases.notes:
ugoki: movement; move; motion

Verb volitional (you/ou-form) + to suru: To attempt to do something.

phrases.reading: みず を あげよう
phrases.lemmaField: 水 を あげる
phrases.translation: Let's give [them, people distant from speaker] some water.
phrases.grammarNote: Sorry for the weird song-card, but cards for handing over items are quite rare ;).
phrases.notes:
mizu: water

[xxx] wo ageru: Speaker or person close to speaker gives something to someone else. Never the other way round!

phrases.japanese: 私に勝ったら食べ物をあげる
phrases.reading: わたし に かったら たべもの を あげる
phrases.lemmaField: 私 に 勝つ 食べ物 を あげる
phrases.romaji: watashi ni kattara tabemono wo ageru
phrases.translation: If [you] win against me, [I] give you something to eat.
phrases.notes:
[xxx] wo ageru: Speaker or person close to speaker gives something to someone else. Never the other way round!

Remark: "katsu" means to win, "ni" defines "watashi" as target of the verb/katsu, so the meaning is: "If you win against me", which means if you beat me.

phrases.japanese: このチケットをあげましょう
phrases.reading: この ちけっと を あげましょう
phrases.lemmaField: この チケット を あげる
phrases.translation: Let's give [them] this ticket.
phrases.notes:
chiketto: ticket (English loan word, the Japanese word follows on the next card)

[xxx] wo ageru: Speaker or person close to speaker gives something to someone else. Never the other way round!

phrases.reading: これ むかし の きっぷ よ ね
phrases.lemmaField: これ 昔 の 切符 よ ね
phrases.romaji: kore mukashi no kippu yo ne
phrases.translation: This is an old ticket / ticket from the past.
phrases.notes: kippu: ticket

phrases.japanese: 頼まれてた切符買ってきたよ
phrases.reading: たのまれてた きっぷ かって きた よ
phrases.lemmaField: 頼む 切符 買う くる よ
phrases.translation: [I] bought the ticket [you] asked for (and returned).
phrases.notes: tanomareta is past passive tense of tanomu. Don't worry about this for now, this is introduced in about 150 cards. If you're curious, I added two references you can check in advance.

phrases.japanese: そっちに行ってあげるわよ
phrases.reading: そっち に いって あげる わ よ
phrases.lemmaField: そっち に 行く あげる わ よ
phrases.romaji: socchi ni itte ageru wa yo
phrases.translation: [I] give you the favor of going over there.
phrases.notes: If used together with the te-form, "ageru" means the speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else. I.e. the favor of doing something is given to someone.

phrases.reading: いい よ はなして あげる
phrases.lemmaField: いい よ 話す あげる
phrases.translation: [I] give [you] the favor of talking [to someone].
phrases.notes: If used together with the te-form, "ageru" means the speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else. I.e. the favor of doing something is given to someone.

phrases.reading: いい よ ゆるして あげる
phrases.lemmaField: いい よ 許す あげる
phrases.translation: [I] give you the favor of forgiving [you].
phrases.notes: If used together with the te-form, "ageru" means the speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else. I.e. the favor of doing something is given to someone.

phrases.reading: ゆるして あげよう
phrases.lemmaField: 許す あげる
phrases.translation: Let's give [them] the favor of forgiving them.
phrases.notes: If used together with the te-form, "ageru" means the speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else. I.e. the favor of doing something is given to someone.

phrases.reading: はんぶん もって あげる
phrases.lemmaField: 半分 持つ あげる
phrases.translation: [I] give [you] the favor of carrying half [of this heavy load].
phrases.notes: If used together with the te-form, "ageru" means the speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else. I.e. the favor of doing something is given to someone.
phrases.source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure ダイヤモンドは砕けない

phrases.japanese: 何か作ってあげるちょっと待っててね
phrases.reading: なにか つくって あげる ちょっと まってて ね
phrases.lemmaField: 何か 作る あげる ちょっと 待つ ね
phrases.romaji: nanika tsukutte ageru chotto mattete ne
phrases.translation: [I] prepare something [food]. Just wait a sec.
phrases.notes: "-te ageru": The speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else.

phrases.japanese: 聞かなかったことにしてあげる
phrases.reading: きかなかった こと に して あげる
phrases.lemmaField: 聞く こと に する あげる
phrases.translation: [I] give [you] the favor of not having heard this.
phrases.notes: "-te ageru": The speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else.

phrases.reading: しらべて あげる
phrases.lemmaField: 調べる あげる
phrases.translation: [I] give [you] the favor of checking it out.
phrases.notes: "-te ageru": The speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else.

phrases.reading: てつだって あげる ね
phrases.lemmaField: 手伝う あげる ね
phrases.translation: [I] give [you] the favor of helping.
phrases.notes: "-te ageru": The speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else.
phrases.source: Mahoutsukai no Yome (The Ancient Magus Bride) ep 13-24

phrases.reading: ぼく が いって あげる よ
phrases.lemmaField: 僕 が 言う あげる よ
phrases.translation: [I] give [you] the favor of saying [it for you]. They are talking about the crush of the penguin. He doesn't want to say something to her and the polar bear answers with this (he's not doing him a favor, though ;)).
phrases.notes: "-te ageru": The speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else.

phrases.japanese: みんなに温かいごはんを作ってあげよう
phrases.reading: みんな に あたたかい ごはん を つくって あげよう
phrases.lemmaField: みんな に 温かい ごはん を 作る あげる
phrases.romaji: minna ni atatakai gohan wo tsukutte ageyou
phrases.translation: Let's give the others the favor of preparing some warm food.
phrases.notes:
I on purpose leave "to give" in here, even though it sounds rather weird.

"-te ageru": The speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else.

phrases.japanese: まず名前をつけてあげないとね
phrases.reading: まず なまえ を つけて あげない と ね
phrases.lemmaField: まず 名前 を つける あげる と ね
phrases.romaji: mazu namae wo tsukete agenai to ne
phrases.translation: First, [we] must give [it] the favor of attaching a name (naming it).
phrases.notes: "-te ageru": The speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else.
phrases.source: BOFURI - Itai no wa Iya nano de Bougyoryoku ni Kyokufuri Shitai to Omoimasu (ep 1-12 w_en)

phrases.japanese: 何をしてあげればいいのか分かりません
phrases.reading: なに を して あげれば いい の か わかりません
phrases.lemmaField: 何 を する あげる いい の か 分かる
phrases.romaji: nani wo shite agereba ii no ka wakarimasen
phrases.translation: [I] don't understand, what [I] could do for [him].
phrases.notes: "-te ageru": The speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else.

phrases.japanese: 私は何もしてあげられなかった
phrases.reading: わたし は なにも して あげられなかった
phrases.lemmaField: 私 は 何も する あげる
phrases.translation: As for me, [I] could not do anything for them.
phrases.notes:
Here we have the potential past form: ageru -> agerareru (can give/do for) -> agerarenai -> agerarenakatta. It's covered later.

"-te ageru": The speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else.

phrases.japanese: 案内してあげるからついてきて
phrases.reading: あんない して あげる から ついて きて
phrases.lemmaField: 案内 する あげる から つく くる
phrases.romaji: annai shite ageru kara tsuite kite
phrases.translation: Follow me, because [I] give you the favor of leading the way.
phrases.notes:
annai: guidance; leading (the way)

We had several examples already: The te-form is used as soft, casual command/request here, we'll soon cover that in more detail.
phrases.source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure ダイヤモンドは砕けない

phrases.reading: みせて あげる よ
phrases.lemmaField: 見せる あげる よ
phrases.translation: [I] give [you] the favor of showing [you].
phrases.notes:
miseru: to show; to display

Note that this sentence never means: "show me". It's always the nature of "ageru" to go from speaker to someone else. Just in case you're wondering: It can also be used in third person, which is covered on the next card.
phrases.source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure ダイヤモンドは砕けない

phrases.japanese: それはお父さんがお母さんに買ってあげた大事なものなんだよ
phrases.reading: それ は おとうさん が おかあさん に かって あげた だいじ な もの なんだ よ
phrases.lemmaField: それ は お父さん が お母さん に 買う あげる 大事 だ もの なんだ よ
phrases.romaji: sore ha otousan ga okaasan ni katte ageta daiji na mono nanda yo
phrases.translation: As for that, it's a father-bought-it-for-mother-precious item (the "otousan ga okaasan ni katte ageta" describes, how "daiji" the item is: father bought it for mother).
phrases.notes: This is an example, where the speaker actually is not "-te ageru'ing" herself. Instead, her father is doing something for her mother. In this case, she and her father form a logical group or entity and from that group, something is given to someone else / outside of this group. Of course, she, her father and her mom are a group in terms of being a family, but it's the nature of "-te ageru" to never work towards the speaker, that's why I wrote: They form a "logical group".
phrases.source: ももへの手紙(A Letter to Momo)

phrases.japanese: お姉さんがしてあげますか
phrases.reading: おねえさん が して あげます か
phrases.lemmaField: お姉さん が する あげる か
phrases.translation: Can [you, older sister] do it for them?
phrases.grammarNote: See the two girls in the image? Imagine the younger to be talking to the older one.
phrases.notes: Let's assume the younger girl is saying this sentence to her older sister: She is not asking "can you do it for me", because "-te ageru" never works towards the speaker. So you know that something should be done for someone else here. I.e. the two girls form one group and the "-te ageru" acts from the group towards someone outside of this group.

phrases.japanese: 絵麻が手伝ってあげたりできないの
phrases.reading: えま が てつだって あげたり できない の
phrases.lemmaField: 絵麻 が 手伝う あげるたり できる の
phrases.romaji: ema ga tetsudatte agetari dekinai no
phrases.translation: Aren't [you, ema] able to give [them] the favor of helping [them] out? -> Can't you help them out somehow? The speaker is addressing the listener with her name here.
phrases.notes:
"-te ageru" never works towards the speaker, so this sentence can't mean "can't ema help me"? Instead, imagine two people who are supposed to help someone. One of them does not want to help and says: can't you do it?

Takeaway message: "-te ageru" never acts towards the speaker. This has an important influence on what is done for whom and sometimes also on who is doing something. It takes some time to get used to this.

phrases.japanese: 僕にちょっと時間をくれませんか
phrases.reading: ぼく に ちょっと じかん を くれません か
phrases.lemmaField: 僕 に ちょっと 時間 を くれる か
phrases.romaji: boku ni chotto jikan wo kuremasen ka
phrases.translation: Can't [you] give me some [of your] time?
phrases.notes: "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

phrases.japanese: 手紙をくれたのはお前か
phrases.reading: てがみ を くれた の は おまえ か
phrases.lemmaField: 手紙 を くれる の は お前 か
phrases.romaji: tegami wo kureta no ha omae ka
phrases.translation: As for the one who gave [me] the letter: Was it you?
phrases.notes: "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".
phrases.source: Saiki Kusuo no Psi Nan S1 (斉木楠雄のΨ難 第1期)

phrases.reading: てつだって くれる か
phrases.lemmaField: 手伝う くれる か
phrases.translation: Can you give [me] the favor of helping?
phrases.notes:
Just as for "ageru", it's much easier to find good example sentences where no real items, but favors are "given".

"kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

phrases.japanese: また食べに来てくれる
phrases.reading: また たべ に きて くれる
phrases.lemmaField: また 食べる に 来る くれる
phrases.translation: Can [you] give [me] the favor of coming again to eat?
phrases.notes: "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

phrases.reading: てがみ みて くれた ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: 手紙 見る くれる ん だ
phrases.translation: [He] gave me the favor of viewing the letter.
phrases.notes: "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

phrases.japanese: 来てくれてありがとう
phrases.reading: きて くれて ありがとう
phrases.lemmaField: 来る くれる ありがとう
phrases.translation: Thank you for giving [me] the favor of coming.
phrases.notes: "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

phrases.japanese: 助けに来てくれたんだ
phrases.reading: たすけ に きて くれた ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: 助け に 来る くれる ん だ
phrases.romaji: tasuke ni kite kureta n da
phrases.translation: [I'm grateful] because [he] gave [me] the favor of coming to save/help [me].
phrases.notes: "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

phrases.japanese: みんな応援してくれるんだ
phrases.reading: みんな おうえん して くれる ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: みんな 応援 する くれる ん だ
phrases.romaji: minna ouen shite kureru n da
phrases.translation: [I'm super happy] because everybody is giving [me] the favor of supporting/assisting.
phrases.notes: "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

phrases.reading: おうえん して くれた ひと
phrases.lemmaField: 応援 する くれる 人
phrases.translation: Someone here is a "gave [me] the favor of supporting"-person.
phrases.notes: "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

phrases.japanese: 学校で先生がすごいことしてくれたんだよ
phrases.reading: がっこう で せんせい が すごい こと して くれた ん だ よ
phrases.lemmaField: 学校 で 先生 が すごい こと する くれる ん だ よ
phrases.romaji: gakkou de sensei ga sugoi koto shite kureta n da yo
phrases.translation: At school, teacher gave [me / us] the favor of doing a big/amazing thing.
phrases.notes: "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

phrases.japanese: でも待ってくれている人がいるから
phrases.reading: でも まって くれて いる ひと が いる から
phrases.lemmaField: でも 待つ くれる いる 人 が いる から
phrases.romaji: demo matte kurete iru hito ga iru kara
phrases.translation: [I'd like to stay here] but there's a giving-me-favor-of-waiting-person there -> there's someone waiting for me at home. By using "kureru", the speaker is acknowledging that the person is waiting for him.
phrases.notes: "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

phrases.japanese: じゃあ約束してくれますか
phrases.reading: じゃあ やくそく して くれます か
phrases.lemmaField: じゃあ 約束 する くれる か
phrases.translation: Well, can [you] give [me] the favor of making a promise?

phrases.japanese: 月が出たらまた会いに来てくれるって
phrases.reading: つき が でたら また あい に きて くれる って
phrases.lemmaField: 月 が 出る また 会う に 来る くれる って てる
phrases.romaji: tsuki ga detara mata ai ni kite kureru tte
phrases.translation: If the moon comes out, [he] gives [me] the favor of coming again to meet.
phrases.grammarNote: Ignore the "tte" in the end.
phrases.notes:
tsuki: moon

"kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

phrases.japanese: 何お母さんに作ってくれたの
phrases.reading: なに おかあさん に つくって くれた の
phrases.lemmaField: 何 お母さん に 作る くれる の
phrases.romaji: nani okaasan ni tsukutte kureta no
phrases.translation: Here, a mother is talking to her child. She's referring to herself in third person and says: What, you gave [me, mother] the favor of making this? (the kid has made some handcrafted item).

phrases.japanese: 今日はお母さんに会いにきてくれたんだよ
phrases.reading: きょう は おかあさん に あい に きて くれた ん だ よ
phrases.lemmaField: 今日 は お母さん に 会う に くる くれる ん だ よ
phrases.romaji: kyou ha okaasan ni ai ni kite kureta n da yo
phrases.translation: As for today, [he] came to give [me] the favor of meeting you.
phrases.notes: Here, the speaker is introducing her husband to her passed away mother (they are standing in front of the mother's grave).

phrases.japanese: 去年お父さんが作ってくれたの
phrases.reading: きょねん おとうさん が つくって くれた の
phrases.lemmaField: 去年 お父さん が 作る くれる の
phrases.romaji: kyonen otousan ga tsukutte kureta no
phrases.translation: Last year, father gave [me] the favor of making this.
phrases.notes: kyonen: last year

phrases.japanese: 見送りに来てくれたのか
phrases.reading: みおくり に きて くれた の か
phrases.lemmaField: 見送り に 来る くれる の か
phrases.romaji: miokuri ni kite kureta no ka
phrases.translation: Did [she] come to see [me] off?
phrases.notes: miokuri: seeing one off; farewell

phrases.japanese: わざわざ見送りに来てくれたのか
phrases.reading: わざわざ みおくり に きて くれた の か
phrases.lemmaField: わざわざ 見送り に 来る くれる の か
phrases.romaji: wazawaza miokuri ni kite kureta no ka
phrases.translation: Did [you] especially come to see [me] off?
phrases.notes: wazawaza: expressly; especially; taking the trouble (to do)

phrases.japanese: おばあちゃんが教えてくれた
phrases.reading: おばあちゃん が おしえて くれた
phrases.lemmaField: おばあちゃん が 教える くれる
phrases.translation: Grandma gave [me] the favor of teaching [this to me].
phrases.notes: oshieru: to teach; to instruct

phrases.japanese: 案内してくれたお礼です
phrases.reading: あんない して くれた おれい です
phrases.lemmaField: 案内 する くれる お礼 です
phrases.translation: The adult gave something to the kid and says: [This is] the gratitude/"thank you" for giving me the favor of leading the way.
phrases.notes: orei: thanks; gratitude​ (teineigo, note the "o"-prefix)

phrases.japanese: まあまあそう言わないでくれる
phrases.reading: まあまあ そう いわないで くれる
phrases.lemmaField: まあまあ そう 言う くれる
phrases.translation: Give [me] the favor of not saying [it] this way.
phrases.notes: In order to ask someone to not do something, add "de" to the negative verb and add "kureru". Note that this is not the te-form.

phrases.japanese: 覚えてないなら無理しないでくれる
phrases.reading: おぼえてない なら むり しないで くれる
phrases.lemmaField: 覚える だ 無理 する くれる
phrases.translation: If [you] don't remember, give me the favor of not overdoing it (i.e. don't think too hard if you're not remembering it).
phrases.notes:
In order to ask someone to not do something, add "de" to the negative verb and add "kureru". Note that this is not the te-form.

muri: unreasonable, forced
muri suru: to try too hard

phrases.japanese: 忘れないでくれる私のこと
phrases.reading: わすれないで くれる わたし の こと
phrases.lemmaField: 忘れる くれる 私 の こと
phrases.translation: Give me the favor of not forgetting me.
phrases.notes: In order to ask someone to not do something, add "de" to the negative verb and add "kureru". Note that this is not the te-form.

phrases.japanese: からかわないでくれるかな
phrases.reading: からかわないで くれる か な
phrases.lemmaField: からかう くれる か な
phrases.translation: I wonder if [you] could give [me] the favor of not teasing me.
phrases.notes:
karakau: to tease; to make fun of

In order to ask someone to not do something, add "de" to the negative verb and add "kureru". Note that this is not the te-form.

phrases.japanese: お母さんが持ってきてくれたんだ
phrases.reading: おかあさん が もって きて くれた ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: お母さん が 持つ くる くれる ん だ
phrases.romaji: okaasan ga motte kite kureta n da
phrases.translation: [I am happy] because mother was giving me the favor of bringing [this].

phrases.japanese: お母さんが持って行ってあげるから
phrases.reading: おかあさん が もって いって あげる から
phrases.lemmaField: お母さん が 持つ 行く あげる から
phrases.romaji: okaasan ga motte itte ageru kara
phrases.translation: Here, the mother is speaking and referring to herself in third person: [You can leave it here] because [I, mother] give you the favor of taking it with me / bringing it [there].

phrases.japanese: 俺も応援に来てやったぜ
phrases.reading: おれ も おうえん に きて やった ぜ
phrases.lemmaField: 俺 も 応援 に 来る やる ぜ
phrases.romaji: ore mo ouen ni kite yatta ze
phrases.translation: I also came to support [you, inferior].
phrases.notes:
Caution, Tae Kim writes: "Usually used for pets, animals, and such, you can substitute yaru for ageru. You would normally never use this type of yaru for people". 
It's often used in anime though. It's very casual, less polite and usually used to express that the receiver of the item or favor is inferior. Have a look at the references if you're interested.

Remark: -te yaru has a second meaning that is less common and usually not found in any textbook. Keep this in mind for now, it's covered in about 700 cards.

phrases.japanese: 用意してやったぞさあ来い
phrases.reading: ようい して やった ぞ さあ こい
phrases.lemmaField: 用意 する やる ぞ さあ 来る
phrases.romaji: youi shite yatta zo saa koi
phrases.translation: [I] did the preparations for you! Come! (very casual, "koi" is the casual command form of "kuru", covered soon).
phrases.notes:
Caution, Tae Kim writes: "Usually used for pets, animals, and such, you can substitute yaru for ageru. You would normally never use this type of yaru for people". 
It's often used in anime though. It's very casual, less polite and usually used to express that the receiver of the item or favor is inferior. Have a look at the references if you're interested.

phrases.reading: てがみ もらった ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: 手紙 もらう ん だ
phrases.translation: [I'm super happy] because I received a letter!
phrases.notes:
morau: to receive

morau can be used as: [item] wo morau.
morau implies that something is received by the speaker or someone close to the speaker. If used in third person (e.g. he received), it means that "he" received something from another person, but not from the speaker. In other words, morau never means "he gets from me", so the giver is never the speaker or someone close to the speaker. This is explained very well in the book "making sense of Japanese", p. 54. Remark: This was corrected in v14, sorry for the mistake.

phrases.reading: へんじ もらった よ
phrases.lemmaField: 返事 もらう よ
phrases.translation: [I / you] received a reply!
phrases.notes:
morau can be used as: [item] wo morau (the "wo" is dropped here, it's casual speech).
morau implies that something is received by the speaker or someone close to the speaker. If used in third person (e.g. he received), it means that "he" received something from another person, but not from the speaker. In other words, morau never means "he gets from me", so the giver is never the speaker or someone close to the speaker. This is explained very well in the book "making sense of Japanese", p. 54. Remark: This was corrected in v14, sorry for the mistake.

phrases.japanese: 最後はお母さんに手伝って貰ったの
phrases.reading: さいご は おかあさん に てつだって もらった の
phrases.lemmaField: 最後 は お母さん に 手伝う 貰う の
phrases.romaji: saigo ha okaasan ni tetsudatte moratta no
phrases.translation: [I'm not good at this] so in the end, [I] received helping from mother.
phrases.notes:
morau can not only be used for receiving objects, but also for actions by using "-te morau".
morau implies that something is received by the speaker or someone close to the speaker. If used in third person (e.g. he received), it means that "he" received something from another person, but not from the speaker. In other words, morau never means "he gets from me", so the giver is never the speaker or someone close to the speaker. This is explained very well in the book "making sense of Japanese", p. 54. Remark: This was corrected in v14, sorry for the mistake.

saigo: end; conclusion, also: In the end.

phrases.japanese: この問題教えてもらっていいですか
phrases.reading: この もんだい おしえて もらって いい です か
phrases.lemmaField: この 問題 教える もらう いい です か
phrases.romaji: kono mondai oshiete moratte ii desu ka
phrases.translation: Can [I] receive the explaining of this problem -> Can you explain this problem to me?
phrases.notes:
morau can also used as: -te morau to receive an action that someone does for you.
morau implies that something is received by the speaker or someone close to the speaker. If used in third person (e.g. he received), it means that "he" received something from another person, but not from the speaker. In other words, morau never means "he gets from me", so the giver is never the speaker or someone close to the speaker. This is explained very well in the book "making sense of Japanese", p. 54. Remark: This was corrected in v14, sorry for the mistake.

phrases.japanese: 手伝ってもらいたいんだが
phrases.reading: てつだって もらいたい ん だ が
phrases.lemmaField: 手伝う もらう ん だ が
phrases.translation: [I] want to receive [your] helping / assisting, but...
phrases.notes:
morau can also used as: -te morau to receive an action that someone does for you.
morau implies that something is received by the speaker or someone close to the speaker. If used in third person (e.g. he received), it means that "he" received something from another person, but not from the speaker. In other words, morau never means "he gets from me", so the giver is never the speaker or someone close to the speaker. This is explained very well in the book "making sense of Japanese", p. 54. Remark: This was corrected in v14, sorry for the mistake.

phrases.japanese: いつか話してもらえるかな
phrases.reading: いつか はなして もらえる か な
phrases.lemmaField: いつか 話す もらえる か な
phrases.translation: [I] wonder if [I] can receive talking [from him] someday...
phrases.notes: This again sounds pretty weird in English, but I try to keep the translations close to Japanese. What the speaker wants to express is: "I wonder if he will talk to me someday".

phrases.reading: じかん を もらえる か な
phrases.lemmaField: 時間 を もらえる か な
phrases.translation: [I] wonder if [I] can receive [some of his] time.
phrases.notes:
Note the potential form: moraeru - can receive.

As you can see, "morau" is also useful when you want to ask for a favor. Usually, kureru and moraeru are used for this, Tae Kim covers this in a small section.

phrases.japanese: 許してもらえるだろうか
phrases.reading: ゆるして もらえる だろう か
phrases.lemmaField: 許す もらえる だ か
phrases.translation: [I] wonder if [I] can receive forgiving.
phrases.notes:
Here, forgiving is considered a favor that the speaker receives from someone.

As you can see, "morau" is also useful when you want to ask for a favor. Usually, kureru and moraeru are used for this, Tae Kim covers this in a small section.

phrases.japanese: 見せてもらえませんか
phrases.reading: みせて もらえません か
phrases.lemmaField: 見せる もらえる か
phrases.translation: Can't [I] receive [you] showing [this to me]?
phrases.notes:
The negative form of "-te morau" makes asking for favors a bit more polite. Note that we have the negative potential form here (negative: moraimasen - don't receive, potential: moraeru - can receive).

You could also simply ask: "misete?" but that's a lot less polite. "misete moraimasu ka" would be a better option. The negative "morau" then makes this request a bit more indirect and thus more polite.

phrases.japanese: 教えてはもらえませんか
phrases.reading: おしえて は もらえません か
phrases.lemmaField: 教える は もらえる か
phrases.translation: Can't [I] receive [you] explaining [this to me]?
phrases.grammarNote: Ignore the "ha" here, it's explained later.
phrases.notes:
The negative form of "-te morau" makes asking for favors a bit more polite. Note, that we have the negative potential form here (negative: moraimasen - don't receive, potential: moraeru - can receive).

As you can see, "morau" is also useful when you want to ask for a favor. Usually, kureru and moraeru are used for this, Tae Kim covers this in a small section.

phrases.reading: へや かたづける から
phrases.lemmaField: 部屋 片付ける から
phrases.translation: [I don't have time] because [I] am tidying up the room.
phrases.notes: katadzukeru: to tidy up; to put in order

phrases.japanese: 部屋の片づけ手伝ってくれませんか
phrases.reading: へや の かたづけ てつだって くれません か
phrases.lemmaField: 部屋 の 片づける 手伝う くれる か
phrases.romaji: heya no katadzuke tetsudatte kuremasen ka
phrases.translation: Cleaning of room, can [you] give [me] the favor of helping?

phrases.japanese: ちょっと待ってください
phrases.reading: ちょっと まって ください
phrases.lemmaField: ちょっと 待つ くださる
phrases.translation: Please wait a little bit.
phrases.notes:
-te kudasai: Polite way of making a request (i.e. please to "verb in -te form").

Making a request this way is more direct than asking for a favor with "kureru" or "moraeru".

phrases.japanese: 簡単に言わないでください
phrases.reading: かんたん に いわないで ください
phrases.lemmaField: 簡単 に 言う くださる
phrases.translation: Please don't say [this] so easily.
phrases.notes: To make a negative request, use "negative verb + de kudasai", just as we learned in the context of "morau" and "kureru" before.

phrases.reading: あの これ ください
phrases.lemmaField: あの これ くださる
phrases.translation: This, please.
phrases.notes: Just as for "ageru, kureru, morau", you can use "kudasai" for requesting both actions and items.

phrases.reading: おしえて ください
phrases.lemmaField: 教える くださる
phrases.translation: Please teach me!
phrases.notes: -te kudasai: Polite way of making a request (i.e. please to "verb in te form").

phrases.japanese: うわあついてこないでください
phrases.reading: うわあ ついて こないで ください
phrases.lemmaField: うわあ つく くる くださる
phrases.translation: Please don't follow me
phrases.notes:
-te kudasai: Polite way of making a request (i.e. please to "verb in te form").
To make a negative request, use "negative verb + de kudasai", just as we learned in the context of "morau" and "kureru" before.

phrases.reading: やめて ください
phrases.lemmaField: やめる 下さる
phrases.translation: Please stop [doing this].
phrases.notes: yameru: to stop

phrases.japanese: 冷静に考えてみてください
phrases.reading: れいせい に かんがえて みて ください
phrases.lemmaField: 冷静 に 考える みる くださる
phrases.translation: Please try to think [about it] calmly -> please calm down and try to think about it again.
phrases.notes: reisei: calmness; composure; coolness

phrases.reading: おべんとう を ください
phrases.lemmaField: お弁当 を くださる
phrases.translation: A box lunch, please.
phrases.notes: obentou: bento; Japanese box lunch

phrases.reading: みず を ください
phrases.lemmaField: 水 を くださる
phrases.translation: Water, please.

phrases.reading: みないで ください
phrases.lemmaField: 見る くださる
phrases.translation: Please don't watch!
phrases.notes: Again: minaide is not the -te form (this would be minakute).

phrases.japanese: 気にしないでくださいさあ
phrases.reading: き に しないで ください さあ
phrases.lemmaField: 気 に する くださる さあ
phrases.translation: Please don't worry about it.
phrases.notes:
ki: spirit; mind
ki ni suru: to mind
ki ni shinaide: don't worry about it; forget about it

phrases.japanese: あした行かないでください
phrases.reading: あした いかないで ください
phrases.lemmaField: あした 行く くださる
phrases.translation: Please don't go tomorrow.

phrases.japanese: 冗談言わないでください
phrases.reading: じょうだん いわないで ください
phrases.lemmaField: 冗談 言う くださる
phrases.translation: Please don't joke -> Please tell the truth.

phrases.reading: てつや あさって
phrases.lemmaField: 哲也 あさって
phrases.translation: asatte: day after tomorrow
phrases.source: Terrace House-Boys x Girls Next Door

phrases.japanese: それまたあさってとかやるんでしょう
phrases.reading: それ また あさって とか やる ん でしょう
phrases.lemmaField: それ また あさって とか やる ん です
phrases.romaji: sore mata asatte toka yaru n deshou
phrases.translation: As for that, I guess [we] do it again [physical action] the day after tomorrow?
phrases.notes:
deshou: right?; don't you agree? (if used in a question). If used without question, it means: I guess, I think -> more on this word later.

Remark: This audio type (real world dorama) is quite hard to understand, so don't worry if you don't understand the individual words yet.
phrases.source: Terrace House-Boys x Girls Next Door

phrases.reading: こないで
phrases.lemmaField: 来る
phrases.translation: Don't come!
phrases.notes: In casual speech, the "kudasai" can be dropped.

phrases.reading: き に しないで
phrases.lemmaField: 気 に する
phrases.translation: Don't worry / forget about it!
phrases.notes: In casual speech, the "kudasai" can be dropped.

phrases.reading: わたし を うみ に いれないで
phrases.lemmaField: 私 を 海 に 入れる
phrases.translation: Don't put / throw me into the sea!
phrases.notes: In casual speech, the "kudasai" can be dropped.

phrases.reading: がんばって
phrases.lemmaField: 頑張る
phrases.translation: Hang in there / do your best!
phrases.notes: In casual speech, the "kudasai" can be dropped. I think we already had a few examples of the -te form without "kudasai" on previous cards. It's sort of a soft command.

phrases.reading: ぼく と も あそんで よ
phrases.lemmaField: 僕 と も 遊ぶ よ
phrases.translation: Also play with me [not only with the others]!
phrases.notes:
In casual speech, the "kudasai" can be dropped. I think we already had a few examples of the -te form without "kudasai" on previous cards. It's sort of a soft command.

Here, we have the "to" particle as it was originally introduced: It means "with" in this case - just in case you forgot after all the other examples.

phrases.reading: わたし と ともだち で いて
phrases.lemmaField: 私 と 友達 で いる
phrases.translation: Stay friends with me!
phrases.notes: I think Tae Kim covers the meaning of "de iru" later. This just means "to remain in some state" - pretty easy I hope. Here, "iru" is in -te form and the "kudasai" is again missing. Have a look at the references if you're interested.

phrases.reading: たすけて くれ
phrases.lemmaField: 助ける くれる
phrases.translation: Help me!
phrases.notes:
"kure" is the command form of "kureru". It's often used in anime, but be careful: This is rough and casual, Tae Kim writes: "For those who want to sound particularly commanding and manly [when making a request], it is also possible to use kure".

I added this for the sake of completeness in the context of making requests, don't use it yourself in a conversation. More on the command form in a few cards...

phrases.japanese: 蒸しパンみんなで食ってくれ
phrases.reading: むしぱん みんな で くって くれ
phrases.lemmaField: 蒸しパン みんな で 食う くれる
phrases.translation: Eat the steamed bun with everybody!
phrases.notes:
"kure" is the command form of "kureru". It's often used in anime, but be careful: This is rough and casual, Tae Kim writes: "For those who want to sound particularly commanding and manly [when making a request], it is also possible to use kure".

The character saying this sentence always talks very casual. Don't imitate this (and suspend the card if you're unsure ;)).

phrases.japanese: 頼むから話を聞いてくれ
phrases.reading: たのむ から はなし を きいて くれ
phrases.lemmaField: 頼む から 話 を 聞く くれる
phrases.romaji: tanomu kara hanashi wo kiite kure
phrases.translation: I beg [you], listen to [my] talk / to what I have to say!

phrases.translation: Eat quickly! [I] leave [it, food] here.
phrases.notes:
sassato: quickly (caution: rude!)

Here we have the command form (taberu -> tabero). According to Tae Kim, it "is quite rude so you should use it with caution (if at all)". For -ru verbs, simply replace "ru/る" with "ro/ろ". Or vice versa: If a verb ends on "-ro", you have the command form.

phrases.reading: のめ よ
phrases.lemmaField: 飲む よ
phrases.translation: Drink!
phrases.notes:
Here we have the command form (nomu -> nome). According to Tae Kim, it "is quite rude so you should use it with caution (if at all)".

For -u verbs, simply replace the -u vowel sound (mu in this case) by an -e vowel sound (me in this case) to get this form. Or the sloppy listening comprehension rule: If a verb ends on ke/け, se/せ, te/て, ne/ね, me/め (or even sloppier*: if it ends on -e) and is not in -te form, you have the command form.

*Why sloppier? Because the -e in the end of a verb is an artifact of the romanization and does not exist as single character. The Japanese alphabet does have an "e" character, but this one is not used here - only the ones I listed above.

phrases.notes: Attaching "yagaru" to the verb stem shows contempt for an action. This indicates hatred and contempt, is extremely strong language and not used in everyday conversations.

phrases.reading: やめさせる
phrases.lemmaField: 止める
phrases.translation: Make [them] stop.
phrases.notes:
yamesaseru: casuative of yameru (to stop)

The causative form is the second to last verb conjugation. It's used to express "to make someone do something". For -ru verbs, replace "ru" with "saseru".

phrases.reading: させる か
phrases.lemmaField: する か
phrases.translation: [You think I] let [you] do [this]?
phrases.notes:
or: [He] made [you] do it?

saseru: causative of suru

Weird enough, the causative form not only means "to make someone do something", but also "to let someone do something. This really confused me, because I had only learned the causative as "make someone do something". In many cases I then wondered: Why are they forcing him to do it?! In fact, they allowed him to do it, though. Which one is actually meant must be derived from context.

So: Causative: to make or to let someone do something. For -ru verbs, replace "-ru" with "-saseru".

Weird enough, the causative form not only means "to make someone do something", but also "to let someone do something. This really confused me, because I had only learned the causative as "make someone do something". In many cases I then wondered: Why are they forcing him to do it?! In fact, they allowed him to do it, though. Note that by letting pikachu decide, they make him do the decision, so this is where the similarity might come from. They're not forcing him though.

So: Causative: to make or to let someone do something. For -ru verbs, replace "-ru" with "-saseru".

phrases.japanese: コーヒーを入れてきます
phrases.reading: こーひー を いれて きます
phrases.lemmaField: コーヒー を 入れる くる
phrases.translation: [I] make coffee and come back.
phrases.notes:
Remark 1: The expression "-te kuru" means: I go, do xxx and come back. In English, you'd probably just say: "I go [into the kitchen] and make coffee" instead of "I make coffee and come back". See ref.
Remark 2: literally, "ireru" means to put in or to pour in. In case of coffee or tea, it just means to make coffee or tea. There's a podcast episode in the follow-up deck that explains this in detail ;).

ko-hi-: coffee. The weird "-" marks prolong the vowels and are artifacts from romanizing katakana. This is a different Japanese writing system used for spelling loan words from other languages. In katakana, vowels are prolonged using "ー", which results in "-" in the romanization.

More causative soon...

Causative: to make or to let someone do something. For -u verbs, change the verb to negative form and then replace "nai" by "seru". Hacky rule of thumb for listening comprehension: If a verb ends on -seru, it's almost always causative. The only exception are -u verbs ending on -su, e.g. hanaseru is the potential form, while the causative e.g. is: hanasu -> hanasanai -> hanasaseru.

Hacky rule of thumb for listening comprehension: If a verb ends on -seru, it's almost always causative. If the causative is used together with ageru, kureru, morau or kudasai, it almost always means: to let someone do something, not to make someone do it.

Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further.

phrases.japanese: はい泳がせてください
phrases.reading: はい およがせて ください
phrases.lemmaField: はい 泳がせる くださる
phrases.translation: Yes, please let me swim.
phrases.notes:
If the causative is used together with ageru, kureru, morau or kudasai, it almost always means: to let someone do something, not to make someone do it.

Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further.

phrases.reading: およがせて くれ よ
phrases.lemmaField: 泳がせる くれる よ
phrases.translation: Let [me] swim!
phrases.notes:
If the causative is used together with ageru, kureru, morau or kudasai, it almost always means: to let someone do something, not to make someone do it.

Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further.

phrases.japanese: ごめんね待たせてしまって
phrases.reading: ごめん ね またせて しまって
phrases.lemmaField: ごめん ね 待つ しまう
phrases.translation: Sorry, [I] made [you] wait!
phrases.notes: Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further.

phrases.japanese: ここで待たせてくださいちょっと具合が悪くて
phrases.reading: ここ で またせて ください ちょっと ぐあい が わるくて
phrases.lemmaField: ここ で 待つ くださる ちょっと 具合 が 悪い
phrases.romaji: koko de matasete kudasai chotto guai ga warukute
phrases.translation: Please let [me] wait here. [My] condition is a bit bad.
phrases.notes:
guai: condition; health; state (of health)

Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further.
phrases.source: Honzuki - Ascendance of a Bookworm S1 (JP Only)

phrases.japanese: 静かに飲ませてくれる
phrases.reading: しずか に のませて くれる
phrases.lemmaField: 静か に 飲む くれる
phrases.translation:
The speaker is musing about how the owners of this restaurant let their customers enjoy sake to the fullest extend:
[In order to enjoy my sake, they] give [me] the favor of letting [me] drink [it] quietly [i.e. without talking to me / disturbing her].
phrases.notes:
Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further.

Remark: In the previous translation, I didn't consider the direction of "kureru", changed in v14.

phrases.reading: だれ に のませた ?
phrases.lemmaField: 誰 に 飲む ?
phrases.translation: Who [did you] allow to drink [it]? I.e. the listener let someone drink something and the speaker is upset about it.
phrases.notes:
Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further.

Remark: Corrected the translation in v14.

phrases.reading: おわらせる
phrases.lemmaField: 終わる
phrases.translation: Make [them] stop / come to an end!
phrases.notes: Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further.
phrases.source: Boku no Hero Academia S3 (ep 1-25 jp_en)

phrases.japanese: こんな悲しみ終わらせるんだ
phrases.reading: こんな かなしみ おわらせる ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: こんな 悲しみ 終わる ん だ
phrases.translation: [I] make this sorrow end.
phrases.grammarNote: Ignore the "no da".
phrases.notes: Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further.

phrases.reading: きょう は やすみ だ よ
phrases.lemmaField: 今日 は 休み だ よ 休み時間
phrases.translation: As for today, [he is on] vacation. Literally, it's "as for today, it's vacation", from context it is clear that it is "his" vacation (some person these guys talk about).
phrases.notes: yasumi: vacation; holiday; absence; suspension

phrases.reading: いわせる の か
phrases.lemmaField: 言う の か
phrases.translation: [You] make/let [them] say [it]?
phrases.notes:
Reminder: Negative of iu is iwanai.

Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further.
phrases.source: Boku no Hero Academia S3 (ep 1-25 jp_en)

phrases.japanese: 辞めた辞めたどうして
phrases.reading: やめた やめた どうして
phrases.lemmaField: 辞める 辞める どうして
phrases.translation: [I] quit. [You] quit?! Why?!
phrases.notes: yameru: to quit, to resign (it also means: to stop, but this word is written with a different kanji).

phrases.japanese: エゾリスたちにおいしいって言わせるまでに
phrases.reading: えぞりすたち に おいしい って いわせる まで に
phrases.lemmaField: エゾリスたち に おいしい って 言う まで に
phrases.romaji: ezorisutachi ni oishii tte iwaseru made ni
phrases.translation: Here we have the coffee apprentice once again. He's trying to learn how to make really good coffee and the "ezorisu - hokkaido squirrels" are judging his skills. However, the poor guy could not convince them. He says:
phrases.notes:
Until [I] make the squirrels say "tasty" [how much more time will it take?! -> next card]

Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further.

phrases.reading: ぱん です か
phrases.lemmaField: パン です か
phrases.translation: [Your favorite food] is bread?
phrases.notes: pan: bread; (sweet) pastry

phrases.reading: あれ ここ ぱんや な の
phrases.lemmaField: あれ ここ パン屋 だ の
phrases.translation: Huh? Is this a bakery?
phrases.notes:
panya: bakery; baker; pastry shop
-ya is a suffix used for certain shops. I.e. pan is bread, panya means bakery. The same for niku (meat) nikuya (butcher's shop).

phrases.japanese: どれだけかかるんだろう
phrases.reading: どれ だけ かかる ん だろう
phrases.lemmaField: どれ だけ かかる ん だ
phrases.translation: How much [time] will it take [until the squirrels finally like my coffee?!]
phrases.notes: kakaru: to take (a resource, e.g. time or money)

phrases.reading: やつ に こたえる な
phrases.lemmaField: やつ に 答える な
phrases.translation: Don't answer him!
phrases.notes:
kotaeru: to answer

Reminders:
verb + na: negative command form, rudeyatsu: Derogatory way to address someone, don't use this

phrases.japanese: 明日は学校に来るのか
phrases.reading: あした は がっこう に くる の か
phrases.lemmaField: 明日 は 学校 に 来る の か
phrases.romaji: ashita ha gakkou ni kuru no ka
phrases.translation: As for tomorrow, [will] you come to school?
phrases.notes: ashita: tomorrow

phrases.japanese: おいしいって言ってほしいんだ
phrases.reading: おいしい って いって ほしい ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: おいしい って 言う ほしい ん だ
phrases.romaji: oishii tte itte hoshii n da
phrases.translation: Now the polar bear gives some important advice: [You] want [them] to say "oishii".
phrases.grammarNote: Ignore the "no da" in the end.

phrases.reading: はなしかける な
phrases.lemmaField: 話しかける な
phrases.translation: Don't talk to me!
phrases.notes:
hanashikakeru: to address (someone), to start a conversation
Reminder: verb + na is the negative command form, rude.

phrases.reading: しらない ばんごう
phrases.lemmaField: 知る 番号
phrases.translation: An unknown number? (listen, someone is calling this guy, but he doesn't know the incoming number).
phrases.grammarNote: Listen, what do you hear in addition to the speaker's voice?
phrases.notes: bangou: number, series of digits

phrases.reading: 002 みた こと ない ばんごう だ
phrases.lemmaField: 002 見る こと ない 番号 だ
phrases.translation: 002 - this is a number [I] have not seen before.
phrases.notes: I cover numbers in a separate deck, which is linked later in this course. This one is easy though: zero-zero-ni (ni is Japanese for two, zero is sometimes used for 0).

phrases.reading: でんわばんごう しら なー い
phrases.lemmaField: 電話番号 知る なー いる
phrases.translation: [I] don't know [his] phone number.
phrases.notes: Remember denwa (phone)? denwabangou is a phone number, but as you learned from the previous card, you can also just say: bangou.
phrases.source: 今からあなたを脅迫します

phrases.japanese: 私の携帯が携帯電話が
phrases.reading: わたし の けいたい が けいたいでんわ が
phrases.lemmaField: 私 の 携帯 が 携帯電話 が
phrases.romaji: watashi no keitai ga keitaidenwa ga
phrases.translation: My phone, my cellphone... [seems like she lost it]
phrases.notes:
denwa: phone
keitaidenwa: cellphone
keitai: short for cellphone

phrases.japanese: スマホ持ってないから電話もできないし
phrases.reading: すまほ もってない から でんわ も できない し
phrases.lemmaField: スマホ 持つ から 電話 も できる し
phrases.romaji: sumaho mottenai kara denwa mo dekinai shi
phrases.translation: Since [I] don't have a smartphone [I] cannot call [him].
phrases.notes:
sumaho: smartphone
denwa is also a suru-verb: denwa suru - to call someone.
Reminder: dekiru is the (irregular) potential form of suru and means "to be able to do"

There's also a longer version of "sumaho", but I'll skip this for now.

phrases.reading: いい ほうほう が ある よ
phrases.lemmaField: いい 方法 が ある よ
phrases.translation: [You want them to like your coffee? Well...] A good method exists... [You know the result from an earlier card: Make them eat sweets before!
phrases.notes: houhou: method; process; manner

phrases.japanese: おかえりお風呂にするそれともごはんなんて
phrases.reading: おかえり おふろ に する それとも ごはん なんて
phrases.lemmaField: おかえり お風呂 に する それとも ごはん なんて
phrases.romaji: okaeri ofuro ni suru soretomo gohan nante
phrases.translation: Welcome home! [Do you want to] take a bath or have a meal?
phrases.notes:
soretomo: or

Remark: "ni suru" usually means "to decide on", have a look at the references if you want to know more.
phrases.source: 結婚できない男 (kekkon dekinai otoko S1)

phrases.japanese: 教室に戻るそれとも部室
phrases.reading: きょうしつ に もどる それとも ぶしつ
phrases.lemmaField: 教室 に 戻る それとも 部室
phrases.translation: [Do you] return to the classroom or the club room?
phrases.notes: soretomo: or

phrases.japanese: 椅子から下りてください
phrases.reading: いす から おりて ください
phrases.lemmaField: 椅子 から 下りる くださる
phrases.translation: Please climb / come down the chair.
phrases.notes: isu: chair
phrases.source: JoJos Bizarre Adventure 黄金の風 (1-25)

phrases.japanese: 私の写真誰にも見せないでね
phrases.reading: わたし の しゃしん だれ に も みせないで ね
phrases.lemmaField: 私 の 写真 誰 に も 見せる ね
phrases.romaji: watashi no shashin dare ni mo misenaide ne
phrases.translation: Please don't show my picture to anyone.
phrases.notes: shashin: picture, photo
phrases.source: からかい上手の高木さん

phrases.japanese: 僕帰ってもいいですか
phrases.reading: ぼく かえって も いい です か
phrases.lemmaField: 僕 帰る も いい です か
phrases.romaji: boku kaette mo ii desu ka
phrases.translation: Can I return home?
phrases.notes: If you want to ask for permission, the "-te mo ii" grammar is more common than the causative.

phrases.japanese: 少し見てきてもいいですか
phrases.reading: すこし みて きて も いい です か
phrases.lemmaField: 少し 見る くる も いい です か
phrases.romaji: sukoshi mite kite mo ii desu ka
phrases.translation: Can [I] quickly check [if we have more nice clothes] and come back?
phrases.notes:
The listener is a model who asks for more fancy clothes. The speaker has a lot of respect for her and asks if he can go and check. Also, "-te kuru" means "to xxx and come back", but in English you'd rather say: "I go and xxx", see ref.

If you want to ask for permission, the "-te mo ii" grammar is more common than the causative.

Translation changed in v14.

phrases.japanese: 先生私がやってもいいですか
phrases.reading: せんせい わたし が やって も いい です か
phrases.lemmaField: 先生 私 が やる も いい です か
phrases.romaji: sensei watashi ga yatte mo ii desu ka
phrases.translation: Sensei, can I do it [physical action]?
phrases.notes: If you want to ask for permission, the "-te mo ii" grammar is more common than the causative.

phrases.reading: あ すわって いい よ
phrases.lemmaField: あ 座る いい よ
phrases.translation: [You] can sit down.
phrases.notes: suwaru: to sit, to sit down

phrases.japanese: なんでこんなにいろいろあるんだ
phrases.reading: なんで こんなに いろいろ ある ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: なんで こんなに いろいろ ある ん だ 色々
phrases.romaji: nande konnani iroiro aru n da
phrases.translation: Why are there so many different [kinds of food] -> the speaker has trouble choosing the right dish.
phrases.notes: iroiro: various; all sorts of

phrases.reading: この どうが みた か
phrases.lemmaField: この 動画 見る か
phrases.translation: Did [you] see this video?
phrases.notes:
douga: video (esp. digital); video clip

Especially in Japanese YouTube videos, you will hear the word "douga" a lot, when people say: "In this video..."

phrases.reading: じゃ たつ ぞ
phrases.lemmaField: じゃ 立つ ぞ
phrases.translation: [I will] stand up (the speaker is carrying someone on the shoulders, who just got on).
phrases.notes: tatsu: to stand; to rise; to stand up​

phrases.japanese: 人が立ってるのかと思った
phrases.reading: ひと が たってる の か と おもった
phrases.lemmaField: 人 が 立つ の か と 思う
phrases.romaji: hito ga tatteru no ka to omotta
phrases.translation: [I was surprised and screamed] because [I] thought somebody is standing [there]?
phrases.notes:
tatsu: to stand; to rise; to stand up​
Reminder: tatteru is short for tatte iru.

The speaker was shocked and screamed, because he thought someone might be in the room. However, it was only dresses hanging there. He explains his screaming by saying this. So the "no" here is the typical explanatory one and the "ka" expresses his uncertainty by asking: Was someone there? Altogether, the sentence ending on "ka" is a clause the speaker talks about. Is it clearer now? I add this explanation to the card. It's from natsume's book of friends, s3 e5 after 5:40.

phrases.reading: とめられる
phrases.lemmaField: 止める
phrases.translation: Next we cover passive verbs, here are some good news: THIS IS THE LAST VERB CONJUGATION!!!!1 The remainder of Tae Kim's book is very easy I'd say. Hang in there!
phrases.notes:
Passive and potential are actually the same for -ru verbs, so this means:

[something] can be stopped (potential form)
[something] is being stopped (passive)

Passive: Something is done or was done, the "doer" is unknown or not relevant. For -ru verbs, replace -ru by -rareru.

phrases.reading: たべられる の か な
phrases.lemmaField: 食べる の か な
phrases.translation: Passive and potential are actually the same for -ru verbs, so this means:
phrases.notes:
[something] can be eaten (potential form)
[something] is being eaten (passive)

Passive: Something is done or was done, the "doer" is unknown or not relevant. For -ru verbs, replace -ru by -rareru.

phrases.japanese: この暗さで見られるか
phrases.reading: この くらさ で みられる か
phrases.lemmaField: この 暗い で 見る か
phrases.translation: Passive and potential are actually the same for -ru verbs, so this means:
phrases.notes:
[something] can be seen in this darkness (potential)?
[something] is being seen in this darkness (passive)?

kurasa: darkness (kurai - dark + sa (makes i-adjectives to nouns))

Passive: Something is done or was done, the "doer" is unknown or not relevant. For -ru verbs, replace -ru by -rareru.
phrases.source: Boku no Hero Academia S3 (ep 1-25 jp_en)

phrases.reading: きかれる だろう ばか
phrases.lemmaField: 聞く だ バカ
phrases.translation: [This] is heard [by someone], you moron!
phrases.notes:
Passive: Something is done or was done, the "doer" is unknown or not relevant. For -u verbs, use the negative form, but replace -nai with -reru. Hacky rule of thumb: If a verb ends on -reru, it's most likely passive (or potential).

Don't let this intimidate you, I'll add some general advice on the next card.

phrases.reading: きかれた ぜ
phrases.lemmaField: 聞く ぜ
phrases.translation: [It] was heard [by someone]
phrases.notes: Passive: Something is done or was done, the "doer" is unknown or not relevant. For -u verbs, use the negative form, but replace -nai with -reru. Passive verbs can be conjugated to past tense.
phrases.source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure ダイヤモンドは砕けない

phrases.reading: くわれる って
phrases.lemmaField: 食う って
phrases.translation: [We will] be eaten, you said?
phrases.notes: Passive: Something is done or was done, the "doer" is unknown or not relevant. For -u verbs, use the negative form, but replace -nai with -reru. Hacky rule of thumb: If a verb ends on -reru, it's most likely passive (or potential).

phrases.japanese: 仲間が目の前で食われた
phrases.reading: なかま が め の まえ で くわれた
phrases.lemmaField: 仲間 が 目 の 前 で 食う
phrases.romaji: nakama ga me no mae de kuwareta
phrases.translation: [It's dangerous out there, my] comrade was eaten in front of [my] eyes.

phrases.japanese: 言われるまで気づかなかった
phrases.reading: いわれる まで きづかなかった
phrases.lemmaField: 言う まで 気づく
phrases.translation: [I] didn't notice, until [it] was said.
phrases.notes: Passive: Something is done or was done, the "doer" is unknown or not relevant. For -u verbs, use the negative form, but replace -nai with -reru. Hacky rule of thumb: If a verb ends on -reru, it's most likely passive (or potential).

phrases.reading: どう する
phrases.lemmaField: どう する
phrases.translation: What will [you] do?

phrases.reading: どう します か
phrases.lemmaField: どう する か
phrases.translation: What will [you] do (regular polite)?

phrases.reading: どう されます の
phrases.lemmaField: どう する の
phrases.translation: What will [you] do (passive polite)?
phrases.notes: Using the passive can make a sentence more polite, because you're not addressing a person directly.
phrases.source: Boku no Hero Academia S3 (ep 1-25 jp_en)

phrases.japanese: どこへ行かれるのかな
phrases.reading: どこ へ いかれる の か な
phrases.lemmaField: どこ へ 行く の か な
phrases.romaji: doko he ikareru no ka na
phrases.translation: [I] wonder where [you] go (passive polite)
phrases.notes: Using the passive can make a sentence more polite, because you're not addressing a person directly.

phrases.japanese: ああ聞いたことがある
phrases.reading: ああ きいた こと が ある
phrases.lemmaField: ああ 聞く こと が ある
phrases.translation: [I] heard about [this].
phrases.notes: We already had a few "koto ga aru" examples before. A few more generic nouns follow now.

phrases.japanese: たくさん楽しいことがあったよ
phrases.reading: たくさん たのしい こと が あった よ
phrases.lemmaField: たくさん 楽しい こと が ある よ 沢山
phrases.romaji: takusan tanoshii koto ga atta yo
phrases.translation: A lot of enjoyable things happened.
phrases.notes: takusan: a lot; lots; plenty

phrases.reading: たいせつ な もの それ は なに
phrases.lemmaField: 大切 だ もの それ は 何
phrases.romaji: taisetsu na mono sore ha nani
phrases.translation: An important item? What is it?
phrases.notes: The difference between "koto" and "mono": mono is usually a tangible thing, such as a wallet, a cabbage, a door, or a coin, while koto is an intangible thing, such as a win, a habit, a wish, or an incident

phrases.japanese: 行きたい所だよ行きたい所
phrases.reading: いきたい ところ だ よ いきたい ところ
phrases.lemmaField: 行く 所 だ よ 行く 所
phrases.romaji: ikitai tokoro da yo ikitai tokoro
phrases.translation: [It is a] want-to-go-there place.
phrases.notes: Another abstract noun we already had is tokoro. In most cases, it refers to a physical location or place. However.... (next card)

phrases.japanese: 優しいところもいっぱいあるんだ
phrases.reading: やさしい ところ も いっぱい ある ん だ
phrases.lemmaField: 優しい ところ も いっぱい ある ん だ
phrases.romaji: yasashii tokoro mo ippai aru n da
phrases.translation: [He] has many gentle places -> He is gentle / kind in many ways.
phrases.notes: tokoro can also refer to characteristics or places in time.

phrases.japanese: 行ったら楽しいかも知れないよ
phrases.reading: いったら たのしい かもしれない よ
phrases.lemmaField: 行く 楽しい かも 知れる よ
phrases.translation: If [you] go [there], it's maybe enjoyable.
phrases.notes:
kamoshirenai: may; might; perhaps; may be; possibly. It's used to express uncertainty.

Technically, kamoshirenai actually is "[clause] ka mo shirenai". The "ka" makes the preceding clause an embedded question, whose answer is "shiru -> shireru (passive) -> shirenai -> not known".

phrases.japanese: 前にも言ったかもしれない
phrases.reading: まえ に も いった かもしれない
phrases.lemmaField: 前 に も 言う かもしれる
phrases.translation: [I] maybe also said [this] before.
phrases.notes:
kamoshirenai: may; might; perhaps; may be; possibly. It's used to express uncertainty.

Technically, kamoshirenai actually is "[clause] ka mo shirenai". The "ka" makes the preceding clause an embedded question, whose answer is "shiru -> shireru (passive) -> shirenai -> not known".
Note again, that iu (say) and iku (go) have the same past tense (itta).
